title: Supreme Court turns away appeal from alleged 9/11 mastermind
summary: The Supreme Court rebuffed an effort by alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to revive a plea deal reached with military prosecutors and revoked by the Biden administration.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday rebuffed a bid from accused Sept. 11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices to revive plea agreements that they reached with military prosecutors before being revoked by the Biden administration.

In an unsigned order, the high court turned away the appeals from Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash of a lower court decision that prevented a military judge from enforcing pretrial agreements they reached with military prosecutors in 2024, which were withdrawn by then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
In rejecting their case, the government's withdrawal of the plea deals remains in place. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in the court's consideration of the appeal.

Mohammed, Hawsawi and bin 'Atash, were captured in 2003 and charged before a military commission with several crimes for their alleged roles in crafting and perpetrating the Sept. 11 attacks, five of which carry the death penalty. In August, the judge overseeing their cases set a trial date of June 2028, which depends on the parties meeting certain deadlines and milestones on time.

The prosecutions have been mired in lengthy legal delays over whether evidence extracted during their interrogations could be used in court. The defendants were held at secret CIA prisons, where they were subjected to "enhanced interrogation techniques," or torture, before they were moved to Guantanamo Bay in 2006. They were formally charged in 2008.

In 2023, following the appointment of retired Brigadier General Susan Escallier as the Convening Authority for military commissions, military lawyers began discussing plea deals with the defendants. Agreements were subsequently reached in 2024 and approved by Escallier, who oversees the military court at Guantanamo Bay.

Under the terms of the deals, the defendants would plead guilty to all charges arising from their alleged roles in the 9/11 terror attacks and serve life sentences, avoiding the death penalty. But shortly after the agreements were announced, Austin said he was revoking them.

But a military judge ruled in November 2024 that Austin's nullification of the deals was unlawful, rendering the agreements valid and enforceable. A military appeals court then said Austin couldn't rescind the plea deals because the defendants had begun to perform one of the terms.

The Justice Department then asked the D.C. Circuit to step in and find that Austin validly withdrew from the pretrial agreements. The D.C. Circuit sided with the government in a decision last year and ruled that the defense secretary "indisputably" had the authority to withdraw from the plea deals.
"The Secretary acted within the bounds of his legal authority, and we decline to second-guess his judgment," the D.C. Circuit panel found.

title: Supreme Court to decide legality of ban on distilling liquor at home
summary: The Supreme Court on Monday said it will consider the constitutionality of a nearly 160-year-old federal ban on distilling liquor at home.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday said it will consider the constitutionality of a nearly 160-year-old federal ban on distilling liquor at home.
Arguments in the case, known as Department of Justice v. McNutt, will likely take place next year, with a decision coming by late June or early July.

For more than a century, Congress has limited the location of distilling to prevent tax evasion. Under the law at issue in the case, enacted in 1868, a "person may not produce distilled spirits at home for personal use." Any person who uses or possesses stills or other equipment to produce distilled spirits in "any dwelling house" or shed, yard or enclosure faces criminal penalties.
Violators face fines and up to five years in prison. The violator's home and property within it are also subject to forfeiture.

Congress approved the restrictions after determining that there was rampant tax evasion by commercial distillers. At that time, the tax rate for spirits was $2 per gallon, more than their market price, and commercial distillers found it cheaper to bribe revenue officers than pay the tax, according to a House report from 1867. Lawmakers determined that "at least seven-eights" of spirits went untaxed at the time.

The legislation that ultimately would prohibit home distilling cut the tax rate and required the duties to be paid before the spirits were removed from warehouses. There are no exceptions for distilled spirits made for personal or family use.

The dispute over the longstanding ban on home distilling was brought by the Hobby Distillers Association and one of its members, who wants to distill spirits at his home and argued that the home-distilling prohibition exceeded Congress' enumerated powers, including its taxing power. A federal district court sided with the plaintiffs and found the ban unconstitutional.
The location restrictions enacted by Congress in the 1800s "criminalize conduct of persons not subject to the tax" and don't "touch the product to be taxed," the district court said.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit then upheld most of that decision and said that the limits on home distilling are not "plainly adapted" to support the government's taxing power, since the restrictions reduce revenue by barring people from making distilled spirits that could be taxed.
The 5th Circuit said that upholding the ban would let Congress "criminalize nearly any at-home conduct only because it has the possibility of concealing taxable activity."
In urging the Supreme Court to take up the case, Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that the lower court decision striking down the ban is "erroneous."

Congress, he wrote in the appeal, restricted home distilling "because a distiller can more easily conceal a distilling operation or thwart necessary inspections — thereby evading the requisite tax — if the still is located in a dwelling-house or connected structure."

Lawyers for the would-be distillers agreed that the Supreme Court should step in and decide the constitutionality of the ban, which they said exceeds Congress's power under the Taxation and Necessary and Proper Clauses of the Constitution.
They warned in court papers that "there is no limit to the government's claim of power to criminalize local conduct that might conceal taxable activity."

title: National Guardsman injured in shooting in Washington, D.C.
summary: D.C. police said the National Guardsman suffered a non-life-threatening injury, and the suspect was also shot.
story: A National Guardsman and a suspect were both shot late Sunday night in Washington, D.C, near the U.S. Capitol as members of the National Guard attempted to intervene in a fight, police said.

Both the Guardsman and the suspect's injuries are not considered life-threatening, interim D.C. police chief Jeffrey Carroll said in a news conference early Monday. Both are being treated at area hospitals.

According to Carroll, the shooting began shortly after 11 p.m. when National Guardsmen were inside a van in the Capitol Hill neighborhood and observed a fight break out. The suspect allegedly took out a gun, and the Guardsmen told him to put the gun down, Carroll said. The suspect allegedly pointed the weapon toward the Guardsmen, who returned fire.
The suspect was shot in the leg, while one of the Guardsmen was shot in the leg, Carroll said.
The incident comes over a year after President Trump deployed the National Guard to Washington D.C. as part of national crackdown on crime.

In November 2025, two National Guardsmen who were deployed to D.C. were shot in an ambush-style attack near the White House, with one killed and the other critically wounded. Rahmanullah Lakanwal, a 29-year-old Afghan national, was charged with over a dozen federal counts related to the attack, including murder of a person assisting an officer of the United States and discharge of a firearm during a violent crime that causes death, both of which are death penalty-eligible. He has pleaded not guilty.

title: Trump spurs states to dump laws regulating new hospitals
summary: The Trump administration has tied billions in rural health funding for states partly to the policy commitments they make, including ending their certificate of need, or CON, laws governing the construction of new hospitals.
story: The Trump administration has hinged federal funding for states on whether they end or loosen powerful but controversial laws that regulate the construction of new hospitals — with a handful of states poised to comply.

A chunk of the $50 billion available to states through the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program is partly contingent on policy commitments. The administration told states it would score their applications higher if they walked back their certificate of need, or CON, laws, which give a state approval authority over the expansion or construction of any healthcare facility. Six states indicated plans to revisit their laws in their applications.

Certificate of need laws, which require that a healthcare provider prove a community need for a new service, were intended to curb monopolies and rising costs. But critics of the laws say they've instead raised healthcare prices, stalled needed facilities, and barred rural patients from new technology. More than 30 states, plus Washington, D.C., enforce some sort of certificate of need law, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Legislators in several states have been pushing to end the laws, which have faced scrutiny for decades — under Republican and Democratic administrations. But the Trump administration's aggressive approach to tie the policies to funding has forced states to reckon with their laws quickly.

The Rural Health Transformation Program was added to President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act as an initiative to modernize healthcare in remote areas. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, in its notice to states applying to the program, called certificate of need laws "an additional expense and burden on rural facilities" and explained how states with fewer certificate of need rules would get higher scores.

"It's not the first time the federal government used funding as a state carrot (versus using a stick) to encourage alignment on an administration's policy goal," Maureen Hensley-Quinn, a researcher at the National Academy for State Health Policy, said in an email. She noted that President Barack Obama's administration included millions of dollars in performance bonuses for states that made it easier for children to enroll in federally funded health insurance.
Hensley-Quinn said the funding "carrot" was an opportunity to take a hard look at whether policies like certificates of need were truly worth it.

"States need to carefully weigh the trade-offs of supporting a 'voluntary' federal policy no matter what," she said, "and additional federal financing, especially in tight state budget years, can tip the scale."
Obama, Trump on same page

Since the Rural Health Transformation Program became law last year, Tennessee has taken the most concrete action. In a bipartisan vote in April, state lawmakers passed a bill that will unravel most of its remaining certificate of need rules over the next four years. Alaska, Connecticut, Delaware, Iowa, and Mississippi have also said they would consider ending or loosening their laws.

"If there's an issue where you can have President Obama and President Trump in agreement on something, that tells you the idea probably has some merit," Wes Climer, a Republican state senator in South Carolina, said in 2021, supporting the repeal of that state's certificate of need law. The legislature voted in 2023 to end most rules in the law, and in January it will stop requiring certificate of need applications for new hospital construction or expansion, leaving them only for nursing homes.

Some certificate of need laws require approval for changes as minor as a new piece of expensive equipment. In North Carolina, a hospital that won a certificate of need to build a much-needed facility was mired in a court battle for three years before breaking ground in 2026.
As more states consider removing their certificate of need laws, Hensley-Quinn warns of unintended consequences: Fewer records will exist that help states track hospital ownership.

Hensley-Quinn said frustrated state officials have come to her years after their states repealed certificate of need laws, saying that even with a licensure process, they don't have insight into the financial state of their health systems or facilities, or how they're managed. Certificate of need laws force companies seeking a new foothold in the state to submit voluminous applications. Once the laws are gone, few regulations force transparency. That leaves states unaware when a health system contracts with private equity to provide hospital services, for example.
"Without CON, without ownership reporting, and without an entity that monitors transactions or providers in that way, there's no way for you to know," Hensley-Quinn said.
Tennessee's certificate of need law

Tennessee lawmakers had pushed to change the state's certificate of need law for years but didn't pass sweeping legislation until it faced losing out on federal funding. Like all states, Tennessee is set to receive an equal share of half of the Rural Health Transformation Program's grants, while the other $25 billion in funding is contingent on other factors, including states' policy commitments.

In 2024, the state's hospital association opposed a repeal effort in a letter penned by 12 hospital and health system leaders, many serving rural areas, though that more limited legislation passed anyway.

A repeal would harm vulnerable patients by driving up costs and thinning existing hospital staff, said Martin Chaney, CEO of Maury Regional Health, a system in rural Middle Tennessee south of Nashville. Ending the law would create rural healthcare deserts, Chaney wrote in the letter, because hospitals would choose to expand in areas that were already the most profitable, where residents had a range of health insurance providers.

"The premise that eliminating CON regulations will expand health care opportunities by increasing competition is not true for ALL Tennesseans," Chaney wrote. "Instead, it would result in cherry-picking and increasing the gap in access to medical care in rural areas."

A month later, TriStar Health — owned by the largest hospital company in the U.S., for-profit HCA Healthcare — applied for a certificate of need to build a hospital just 20 minutes north of Maury Regional Medical Center. Nashville-based HCA received approval despite brief opposition from Maury Regional Health, the system led by Chaney.
HCA did not respond to requests for comment.

Local leaders are divided on what the new hospital would do to healthcare in the region. "Competition is good," Maury County Commissioner Kevin Markham told KFF Health News. Markham, like many in favor of the new hospital, said that patients should have options when it comes to choosing where they get hospital care.

But leaders of smaller hospital systems in Tennessee are worried. Judy Herbert, a Williamson County commissioner and board member at Williamson Health, another health system in the area, said ending certificate of need laws will prompt hospital closures. Big hospital systems will become the default for expensive procedures and dominate rural markets, while smaller hospitals that provided those procedures before will lose so much money, they'll be forced to shutter or sell, Herbert reasoned, echoing the concerns of other advocates of the laws.

"Many challenges have emerged that place increasing pressure on healthcare organizations, especially independent nonprofits like Williamson Health," that health system's leadership said in an open letter in July 2025, citing Tennessee's intentions around certificates of need.

In late July, Williamson Health's board voted to sell its network of clinics, diagnostic centers, and a more than 330-bed hospital in a $900 million deal with Ascension St. Thomas, part of one of the largest healthcare systems in the nation.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Federal actions around voting system expand weeks ahead of midterms
summary: With early voting for the midterms underway, federal actions around the U.S. voting system are expanding. Election officials explain their response, and the Justice Department says "there should be no interruption" with the results.
story: With midterm elections just two weeks away, there are concerns that the federal government's pressure on election officials is breeding distrust in the system.

Federal agents have seized ballots, and voting machines have been examined. The Justice Department is locked in legal battles with states across the country over information about individual voters and this past week threatened to prosecute California election officials if they knowingly count mail-in ballots from 20,000 people the Trump administration says are "likely noncitizens."
It's a kind of interference Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, a Republican in a deeply red state, said she's never seen before.

"In the past two elections that I oversaw as lieutenant governor, the threats were all external: non-state actors, cyber security threats and other things," she said. "But now we also have threats coming from within our own government."
Federal government actions on elections

In the U.S., elections are local. They're run by towns and counties and states. It's stated in Article I of the Constitution. Congress makes laws regulating elections, but the president doesn't have a role in running them.
Still, during his second term Mr. Trump has signed two executive orders around voting: one requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and another on mail-in ballots.

The administration's latest move came Thursday, when the Justice Department sued California, claiming it was mailing ballots to more than 20,000 likely noncitizens. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said the federal government was threatening the right of thousands of Californians to vote without providing any detail about how they identified those individuals, and she questioned the accuracy of the data.

The Justice Department's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber said in a statement.
"Noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections," head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon told 60 Minutes. "So the question is simply how many of them there are."
Demands for voter rolls
Last year the Justice Department asked nearly every state in the country for their full and complete voter rolls, including confidential voter information.

"They wanted things that we typically are required by law to keep private: social security numbers, full dates of birth, driver's license numbers," said Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, who is responsible for Utah's elections.

Henderson told 60 Minutes she wasn't given good answers about why the federal government wanted the information, and she was concerned about what would be done with the data. She refused to turn them over.

Officials in 29 other states — Democratic and Republican — have also refused to comply with the government's demands. The Justice Department has sued all of them. The Trump administration says access to voter rolls will help purge the lists of immigrant voters who are not entitled to vote. The administration has alleged, without providing evidence, that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote. And a White House spokesperson has said that noncitizens "continue to register and vote in federal elections."

Noncitizen voting does happen, but it's extremely rare. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said this summer that thousands of noncitizens were mistakenly registered in her state due to a software glitch. About 340 of them actually voted.
Since the beginning of Mr. Trump's second term, the Justice Department has charged more than 100 noncitizens with voting illegally.
Henderson said she found just 52 questionable voters on the rolls out of more than 2 million registered voters in Utah.
DHS Secretary Mullin this summer said that any election official who knowingly allows noncitizens to vote could be prosecuted, or even sent to prison."
"We're not going to prison. No. It's silly," Henderson said.
Last month, in writing, the Justice Department told Henderson she was under investigation.

"I have to tell myself it doesn't matter what the consequences are, as long as I feel like I'm doing what's right," she said. "I think this is an important thing for me to do, holding these guard rails, holding the line. Someone has to."
Henderson believes there can still be honest and fair elections. The question for her is whether the losing candidate will accept the results.

"We are seeing a trend of candidates who lose races now refusing to concede, saying it was rigged, saying it wasn't fair, even when it isn't close," she said. "Candidates who lose can do so much good by graciously conceding. That will instill confidence in the public."
"I never imagined that we would be raided by the FBI"
In January, armed federal agents seized ballots from a local facility in Fulton County, Georgia.
"In my wildest dreams, I never imagined that we would be raided by the FBI," Fulton County Commissioner Dana Barrett, a Democrat, told 60 Minutes.

The agents had a criminal search warrant that Georgia's secretary of state described as being full of "baseless and repackaged claims," but it enabled them to seize ballots and other election materials from the 2020 election, which Mr. Trump has repeatedly claimed he won. Federal agents in Fulton County packed up more than 600 boxes of election records. Then director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, watched as boxes of ballots were loaded onto trucks.
Barrett has no idea where the ballots are now. She believes the seizure was "political theater aimed at undermining the 2026 and 2028 elections."
"I think it was all part of this concerted effort that's happening nationwide to undermine faith in elections," Barrett said.

Three months ago, the FBI temporarily reassigned 260 analysts to work on a "priority investigation" into the Georgia materials, according to an internal FBI email obtained by 60 Minutes. So far, nothing has come of the investigation. There have been dozens of probes into the 2020 election in Fulton County, but none have moved the needle.
"People see all of these investigations and FBI raids and subpoenas and they say, 'Something must be wrong there. Why should I believe the results?'"
The Justice Department responds

Dhillon, the head of the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department, said the administration is aggressively pursuing new investigations and they are looking at "thousands" of possible cases of noncitizen voting.
"We've been in office for less than two years. We've had investigations ongoing for over a year and it takes time," Dhillon said.

Dhillon said there have been irregularities during prior elections, and that a record number of election observers and monitors – more than 1,000 of them – would be at the polls during midterms as a way to increase voter confidence.
Recent surveys show that only about half of Americans expect the midterms to be free and fair.
Dhillon called concerns that Mr. Trump might challenge midterm results "paranoia." If a noncitizen votes, that individual vote would be challenged, she said, not the entire election.

"I don't know what is going to happen," Dhillon told 60 Minutes, "but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states."

title: CBS News poll: Talarico-Paxton Senate race is a Texas toss-up
summary: Turnout will be key as Texans voice cost of living concerns in Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico.
story: The Texas Senate race is tight — essentially tied — and now all about...turnout.

Republican Ken Paxton benefits from the state's overall Republican leanings, while Democrat James Talarico is boosted by voters' economic concerns and higher perceptions of personal character to serve as senator.

Talarico's standing is helped by more Democrats saying they'll definitely vote. That leaves the dynamic in the closing weeks very much up for grabs. If more Republicans decide to vote, it could certainly change.
The bulk of Paxton's voters are backing him either because he's the GOP nominee or to oppose Talarico, and because they want to support President Trump.
Where Talarico does well

Some of the economic headwinds facing Republicans nationally are showing up here. The cost of living is the top issue for Texas voters, and most say they've been negatively affected by higher prices. Among these voters, Talarico enjoys a sizable lead over Paxton.
And more see Talarico as having the right character to serve as senator.
Personal qualities matter far more to Talarico's backers than to Paxton's.
Talarico gets 5% of those who identify as Republicans.
On a wider scale, he draws 9% of people who — regardless of their own party affiliation — say they never vote for Democrats, but will this time.
Where Paxton does well

But some things are different in Texas than in the country overall: The Trump administration's deportation program gets more support in Texas, compared to the most recent CBS News national poll, and that advantages Paxton.
And outside the economic considerations, Republicans say they feel Talarico represents policies that are a threat to their culture and way of life.
(Democrats, for their part, feel the same about Paxton.)
A lot of Paxton's backing from Republicans is an effort to support Trump.
And in a state where few voters describe themselves as liberal, Talarico is viewed as "very liberal" by nearly half. When they describe Talarico this way, they're voting for Paxton.
Demographics on vote

Texas just has a lot more Republicans than Democrats. That means Talarico needs to do overwhelmingly well with independents and get some vote shift among GOPers, or activate enough new voters to offset that.
He also needs strong turnout from younger voters, who today say they back him in large percentages. Historically, younger voters don't typically turn out at as high a rate as older voters do.

Latino voters in Texas swung toward Trump in 2024, but most are now backing Democrat Talarico. Latinos are more likely than voters overall to say higher prices have been a hardship or difficult, and most of them do not think Paxton has the right personal character to serve as a senator.
The race for governor
Incumbent Greg Abbott has an edge over Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the race for governor.
Abbott also receives the backing of 7% of Talarico voters.

This CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted with a representative sample of 1,492 registered voters in Texas  interviewed between October 8-16, 2026. The sample was weighted according to gender, age, race and education based on  U.S. Census data, as well as to 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error is ± 3.4 points for the sample of registered voters, and ± 3.5 points for likely voters.

title: 7 highlights from JD Vance's CBS News town hall
summary: In an hour-long town hall hosted by CBS News, Vice President JD Vance argued the Trump administration's handling of the economy and Iran will pay dividends in the future.
story: In an hour-long town hall hosted by CBS News, Vice President JD Vance argued the Trump administration's handling of the economy and Iran strategy will pay dividends in the future.

He was also pressed on the Trump administration's controversial immigration tactics, widespread discontent about the cost of living and his own political future during "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance," which aired Saturday evening and was hosted by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil.

Vance took questions from voters in Michigan, a swing state that helped propel Vance and President Trump to victory in 2024 — and is the host of a tight Senate race that could help determine which party wins control of the upper chamber in next month's midterm elections.
Vance says he hasn't decided if he'll run for president

If he decides to run for president in 2028, the vice president is widely viewed as an early frontrunner in the Republican primaries and a possible heir to Mr. Trump's political movement. Mr. Trump has called Vance his "most likely" GOP successor and has joked about a potential contest between Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Asked by Dokoupil if there's any chance he won't run, Vance said: "Of course there's a chance."
"The way that I think about life, big life decisions — my wife will tell you this — is I'm a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it," said Vance, adding that he'll "have to think about it."
He also noted that he and his wife, Usha Vance, have four young children, and the second lady "has never loved politics," though "she loves public service."
On economy, Vance says "we're turning the ship around" but it will take time
Several town hall attendees asked Vance about cost-of-living issues.

The topic weighs heavily in the midterms, and has demonstrated it's a liability for Republicans based on CBS News polling. Voter dissatisfaction with inflation and the state of the economy under the Biden administration helped bring Mr. Trump and Vance to power, but polls indicate that most voters are still unhappy with the economy and hold the Trump administration responsible.
Sandy Johnson said the family entertainment center she owns is "barely making ends meet," and asked when she can expect changes "so that the normal American has money to spend on small businesses."
The vice president argued it could take some time.

"What broke the United States, as much as I might like to criticize Joe Biden, but it was a bipartisan, multi-generational failure to under-invest in American workers, to under-invest in American manufacturing, to ship all of our good jobs overseas," Vance said. "If all the good jobs are overseas, then people here in Michigan can't spend money at your family business."
He pointed to promises of new foreign investment in the United States, and growth plans by the three major Detroit-area automakers, General Motors, Ford and Chrysler parent Stellantis.

"We are turning the tide on this," Vance said, referring to the decline in U.S. manufacturing. "And I think there are all these things I pointed to that show signs of progress. But Sandy, I'll be the first person to tell you that, just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around."

Since Mr. Trump returned to office last year, the unemployment rate has remained low, but inflation has remained stubbornly higher than the Federal Reserve's 2%-per-year target, eating into Americans' wages. The number of manufacturing jobs has also remained roughly flat.

Asked by Dokoupil about Mr. Trump's assessment of an "A+" economy, Vance said the president was referring to new investments, "but he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first before you can employ the workers working in those factories."
Vance later said: "I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around."
Iran and energy: "I recognize that gas prices are too high right now"
One of the biggest pressure points on Americans' wallets is the Iran war, which has kept oil prices high even as the U.S. and Iran have refrained from active fighting in recent weeks.

Keshon Wheatley, a barber from Detroit, told Vance that he voted for Mr. Trump in 2020 and 2024, in large part because he gave the president credit for low gas prices during his first term. Now, gas prices are far higher — and he said he plans to vote for Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, not Republican Mike Rogers.
Vance pointed to Iran's attacks on oil tankers.

"We've never had a situation like this, where you have effectively the largest state sponsor of terrorism that's trying to completely choke off world energy supply," the vice president said, arguing that "if we just … left, and we let the Iranians control shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, what that would mean is you would pay a lot more for gasoline."

Asked how long it will take for prices to ease, Vance said, "When this conflict is over, we are going to see gas prices come down." He said oil is still being exported from the Middle East because of efforts by the U.S. military to allow ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

On the competitive Michigan Senate race, he argued El-Sayed — a frequent critic of the Iran war — has not offered a solution to the problem, and gave Rogers credit for calling for the war to end. "He's been remarkably independent about this," Vance said of Rogers.
Dokoupil asked Vance why the U.S. hasn't decisively won the Iran war, which has dragged on for longer than Mr. Trump initially expected.
Vance argued that "in some ways we have won decisively," but "the enemy gets a vote here."

The vice president — who participated in negotiations with Iran over the summer — defended the president's Iran strategy, and said the Trump administration is looking for a "final firm commitment from the Iranians that they're not going to rebuild their nuclear program."
Man whose wife died in Iranian strike decries "fundamental failures"
The Iran war has also imposed human costs, with 21 U.S. service members killed and hundreds injured since the conflict began in late February.

In the war's early hours, six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed in an Iranian strike on a site in Kuwait, including Master Sgt. Nicole Amor. Her husband, Joey Amor, asked Vance about reports that the facility in Kuwait was not adequately secured.

"Though the Iranian drone was the weapon that killed my wife, there were a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures that led up to that," Amor said, asking Vance "how this administration is gonna start holding those leaders accountable."
Vance said he didn't doubt there were failures, but "sometimes information doesn't filter up to me." He vowed to "take every single failure extremely seriously."

He also noted that cheap drones have changed warfare, and "we have changed a lot of our tactics to try to suppress that drone fire, to try to protect our troops to make it so that more people don't have to pay the ultimate sacrifice."
Vance also said: "I know that there are some issues with, for example … where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake and that we could do better on. And we have changed that."
Nun presses Vance on immigration tactics
Sister Nancy Sylvester, a member of the Sister Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, asked Vance about the Trump administration's approach to immigration enforcement.

She asked Vance, a fellow Catholic, "how you would justify [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactics] to people of faith," and "what policies would you advocate to try to promote more compassionate and [respectful] behavior toward our immigrant sisters and brothers."

Vance responded, "We're trying to strike a balance between: How do we do law enforcement, but how do we also do it humanely, and how do we not do so little law enforcement that you actually empower some of the worst people in the world."

Vance later said most ICE agents are "amazing people who are patriots," but some of them "make mistakes" or "really screw up." He added that "obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up."

Asked if any major mistakes by ICE come to mind, Vance responded that "there are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE."

Another town hall attendee pressed Vance on some of the administration's rhetoric around immigration, including Vance's own comments that likened some holders of employment-based H-1B visas to "foreign indentured servants."
Vance responded, "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me."
He said his comments were "not a criticism of the H-1B holder."

"That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker, bring somebody else in, and knows that person, if they complain, if they get too uppity at work, if they have a disagreement with their boss, they couldn't just lose their job, … they can be shipped back to their country of origin," Vance said. "And I think that gives employers way too much power."

He said, "My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant." But he said he is seeking "to make it so that we can have a country with some baseline of social cohesion and sense of community, because what happens when too many people come to the United States, even if they're very good people, … [is] it changes the country in very profound ways."
"D.C. is a corrupt town," but Vance says no evidence Trump is participating in it
Dokoupil asked Vance about polling that indicates many voters are concerned about corruption and believe Mr. Trump is prioritizing his own personal business interests while in office.
Vance said, "I've never seen anything like that from the president."
"Yes, D.C. is a corrupt town," Vance said, but "I have not seen a single shred of evidence that he participates or sanctions in that corruption."

Dokoupil also asked about a string of recent reports, including Mr. Trump's cryptocurrency earnings and U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's ouster over allegations that she asked a person seeking help from the Trump administration to wire her $100,000. Guilfoyle has denied all wrongdoing. Mr. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest.
Vance responded: "If somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences."
The vice president also said he will "follow the law" if a Democratic Congress launches investigations and subpoenas the Trump administration.
Data centers need to be "good community citizens"
A major point of tension in many communities across the country is the explosion in data center development, as the artificial intelligence boom leads to insatiable demand for computing power.

Mr. Trump has enthusiastically backed the AI industry, casting it as an engine of economic growth and a key area of competition with China. He has also argued data center construction can be beneficial to local communities, bringing jobs and investments in crucial technology. But many voters have raised concerns about noise, disruption and pressure on the electrical grid, leading to calls for development to slow down.

Vance took a question from one Michigan resident who lives across the street from a data center and said the constant buzzing has made "opening our windows to let in a breeze … a luxury that we could no longer enjoy."

The vice president said "data centers can be good" and can also "cause real problems." He said his view is that data centers should be "good community citizens," offering more tax revenue to local governments. The data centers should also not lead to higher residential utility bills, Vance said.
"Some of the economic benefits they're generating, they can't just go to a few tech billionaires," he said. "It has to go to the community writ large."

title: Japan launches ambitious robotic mission to Martian moon Phobos
summary: Soil samples collected by the MMX probe will shed light on the mysterious origin of the red planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos.
story: Japan launched an ambitious $350 million mission to Mars on Monday to study the red planet's two moons in unprecedented detail, dropping a small rover on the largest — Phobos — before the mothership touches down to robotically collect soil samples for return to Earth.

The primary goal of the Martian Moons Exploration mission, or MMX, is to determine whether Phobos and the smaller moon Deimos were created by the impact of a large body early in the solar system's history or whether the two are asteroids that once passed close enough to Mars to be captured by the red planet's gravity.

The Martian moons are much smaller than Earth's, with Phobos measuring just 17 miles across at its widest while Deimos is less than half that size. Both are irregularly shaped and similar in appearance to asteroids. But size and shape alone are not enough to answer the question of their origin.

"One of the most intriguing questions about Phobos and Deimos is simply why these two little moons are there in the first place," said Thomas Statler, who helped oversee development of two NASA instruments aboard the MMX spacecraft.

"In some ways, they resemble asteroids from the outer part of the asteroid belt ... but there (are) other lines of evidence pointing to these moons being remnants of a giant impact early in Mars' history."
The collected samples, expected to be returned to Earth in 2031, should answer that question one way or the other.

"By going to the Martian moons, studying them up close and bringing samples back to Earth, we'll be able to determine whether Phobos material is more consistent with an asteroid composition or with debris created by a collision involving Mars," Statler said.

The mission got underway at 3:41 p.m. EDT (4:41 a.m. Japan time) with the sky-lighting launch of a Japanese H3 rocket from the picturesque Tanegashima Space Center operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA.

Four solid-propellant strap-on boosters and two hydrogen-fueled first stage engines powered the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before the H3's second stage took over to continue the climb to space.
One hour and 11 minutes after liftoff, following two firings of the upper stage engine, the 9,900-pound MMX probe was released to fly on its own.
If all goes well, the spacecraft will brake into orbit around the red planet in September 2027 on a trajectory that will allow it to circle the planet in lockstep with Phobos.

MMX will spend three years in that orbit, training a battery of instruments on Phobos and its surrounding environment, studying its chemical and mineral composition, assessing its possible use as a staging base for future astronauts and dropping a small rover, supplied by the German and French space agencies, onto the moon's surface in early 2029.

The 55-pound rover is not equipped with braking rockets or anything else to slow its descent. Given the gravity of Phobos is just 1/1,000th as strong as Earth's, the rover is expected to bounce down on the surface, tumbling gently to a stop.

It is designed to right itself regardless of how it ends up after coming to rest and then to begin its surface exploration. It is equipped with cameras for navigation and to study the soil as it rolls about, an instrument to fire laser beams into the ground to determine what minerals might be present and another that will monitor soil temperatures.

About a year after the rover's landing, in the 2030 timeframe, the MMX spacecraft itself will touch down on Phobos once and possibly twice to collect a tiny amount of soil using two devices, one built by JAXA and the other supplied by NASA.
The official mission requirement is to capture at least 10 grams, or less than half an ounce, of material. Depending on the nature of the soil, however, the sample size could be larger.

The MMX then will lift off and, after wrapping up remote observations of Deimos, head back to Earth, putting the Phobos samples into an aerodynamic, heat-resistant capsule that will re-enter the atmosphere over Australia, where a recovery team will be standing by.
The samples will be studied by an international team of researchers.
"There's a lot of adrenaline, a lot of excitement, and a lot of wow," said Statler. "MMX will be the first spacecraft ever to return to Earth from the Mars system. That says a lot."

But "the most exciting thing of all," he said, "will be watching the sample return capsule re-enter Earth's atmosphere and opening that capsule and seeing those materials for the first time. There is absolutely no lack of excitement and adrenaline on this mission."

title: As AI dominates conversations, here are key terms to know
summary: Artificial intelligence and the conversations around it are rapidly evolving. These terms can help to understand the developments.
story: As artificial intelligence — and the conversation surrounding it — rapidly evolves, keeping up with the language being used to describe it has become essential to understanding its impacts.
Here are some key terms to know:
Abliteration

Abliteration (a portmanteau of the words ablation, meaning to remove a part of something, and obliteration) is a process where an AI model's safety guardrails and refusal mechanisms are removed. Once an AI model is abliterated, it will not refuse requests, including harmful ones.

The patterns that a model learns during safety training to identify harmful requests can be found in a model's weights, or the billions of numerical parameters that represent its knowledge. Models that are open-weight, meaning the weights are public and can be modified, are vulnerable to abliteration.
AI agent

An AI agent can carry out tasks with some degree of autonomy on a user's behalf. Users can interact with an AI agent like they would a chatbot, but as Meta — which recently released its AI agent, "Muse" — puts it: Unlike a traditional chatbot, AI agents can complete multiple steps of a task without requiring input at each stage.
AI agents use external tools such as web browsers and apps so that they can perform tasks, including sending an email, booking a reservation or managing a user's calendar.
AI agents have been popular in Silicon Valley for years and are now bursting into the mainstream with consumer-friendly AI agents like Meta's "Muse" and OpenAI's "Dots."

Since AI agents are tasked with completing the goals assigned to them by the user, there have been rogue incidents where agents, in pursuit of a goal, behave in unexpected ways in order to achieve it. A recent report from nonprofit research lab Transluce identifies cases where AI agents targeted U.S. government websites using "aggressive techniques to access publicly available data."
Alignment

When an AI model is described as aligned, it behaves in line with human goals and values. As a model undergoes safety training, it is fine-tuned to follow instructions and generate responsible outputs. OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki defines alignment as "getting the AI to 'try to do the right thing by human standards'" and wrote that it is "the core problem in AI research."

When AI is misaligned, it might behave unexpectedly. In September, OpenAI released a framework for reporting misalignment and said that identifying and sharing these cases can help show where safeguards need strengthening. Anthropic says its alignment team trains models to remain "helpful, honest and harmless" and shares its findings with the public.
There is debate among researchers about how to ensure alignment, or if it is even possible to do so.
Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
Some researchers believe that when an AI system has reached the same level of learning, reasoning and cognitive performance as a human, it will have achieved artificial general intelligence.
Stanford University calls the term "controversial," pointing to the fact that "human-level intelligence" can mean different things to different people and is a subject of debate by AI experts.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is among those who believe AGI is here already, saying on a podcast, "I think we've achieved AGI." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in 2025 that AGI is "not a super useful term," echoing experts who believe it only serves to confuse.
Artificial superintelligence (ASI)

If AI systems surpass even the most advanced humans in every cognitive domain, they will be considered artificial superintelligence. This hypothetical scenario has sparked debate among researchers, AI experts and politicians.

Some industry leaders and researchers have warned about the existential risks of the pursuit of superintelligence, with the concern that an AI that powerful could evolve beyond human control. The CEO of Microsoft AI Mustafa Suleyman called superintelligence an "anti-goal" because it "doesn't feel like a positive vision of the future."

Other technology leaders, such as Mark Zuckerberg, are generally in favor of the notion of superintelligent AI. Zuckerberg argued that developing superintelligence and distributing it widely could lead to "a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential, pursue their interests, and improve their lives and the world more than ever before."
Distillation
Distillation is a process where a smaller AI model is trained, usually, on a larger, stronger one so that it behaves similarly.

In an announcement on detecting and preventing distillation attacks, Anthropic said that while distillation is a legitimate method used by frontier labs, which distill their own models to create smaller, more cost-effective versions, it can also be used to snatch capabilities from competing labs whose models are more powerful. Companies might do this because it is faster and cheaper than developing their own.

The NSA and FBI warned in September that China-based AI companies "are engaging in aggressive, industrial-scale distillation activities" to extract restricted functionalities from U.S. frontier models.
Gradual disempowerment

Gradual disempowerment is a phrase coined by AI safety researchers that describes a path where AI displaces all, or most, of human labor and decision-making. In this scenario, AI agents or AI-enabled robots are superior to humans at nearly all tasks and human creativity, cognition and agency erode away.
Jailbreak
Jailbreaking is an attempt to bypass or "trick" an AI model's guardrails typically through prompting. Researchers jailbreak systems to identify vulnerabilities.

Jailbreaks can vary in terms of their severity, according to Anthropic. "Sometimes they only unblock minor undesirable behaviors, and sometimes they unblock a wide range of harmful outputs, making a model much more dangerous," the company wrote in July.
When a model is jailbroken, it may answer questions that could cause harm, such as designing a chemical weapon or creating illegal images.
Open models
When a model is "open," some of its internal mechanics are publicly available.

A model can be "open weight," meaning that its weights, which represent a model's knowledge, are public and can be copied or modified by anyone. Some examples of open-weight models include Beijing-based Moonshot's Kimi model series and Meta's Llama models.

While the ability to tamper with a model's weights can lead to the weakening of its safety or ethical guardrails, it can also be beneficial. Researchers are able to examine the weights, fine-tune them and identify vulnerabilities that can lead to strengthening. They are also less restricted when it comes to, perhaps, using the model for hard science or cyberattack defense.

A model can also be "open source," which is when its code is publicly available. That can be in addition to its weights being open. When a model is open source, anyone can see how it was built and can go in and change it.

Open models tend to be cheaper, or even free to use, and can be hosted on the users' own hardware. They've been embraced in China, which some researchers say is closing the AI capability gap between China and the U.S. The open-weight marketplace also appears to be expanding in the U.S. with Meta and Apple announcing in October a rare collaboration to bring open-weight models to Apple desktops.

Some open models are mere months behind proprietary, or closed, ones in terms of capability, though there is some evidence that the reason they remain close behind is because they are trained using American proprietary models. According to MIT, open models achieve about 90% of the performance of closed models upon release.
Proprietary models
The AI models American consumers commonly interact with, such as Anthropic's Claude Opus, OpenAI's GPT-5 and Google's Gemini 2.5, are closed, proprietary models.
When a model is "closed," its provider keeps elements of a model's inner workings — such as its weights, source code and underlying infrastructure — private.
These models tend to be more expensive to use than ones that have open weights.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
Recursive self-improvement describes when an AI model can improve itself or build its successor.

Anthropic says this has not yet been achieved, but that it could "come sooner than most institutions are prepared for," and OpenAI last month shared a detailed report on progress toward RSI, saying the company aims to build an automated AI researcher that, under human supervision, can "further progress on deep learning and alignment, enabling iterative improvements."

At a recent hearing on AI safety, held by the New York City Council, all three AI whistleblowers who appeared spoke about RSI. Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who publicly resigned from Anthropic over the summer, said that automatic AI research has become the primary goal of AI companies. Daniel Kokotajlo, who resigned from OpenAI two years ago, said that AI companies should not be allowed to pursue RSI, but that if they do, the process should be slowed. Alex Turner, a former researcher at Google DeepMind, said RSI could "quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension," calling it an "extremely dangerous thing."
Red team

Red teaming is a cybersecurity method where a team is tasked with simulating an adversarial attack in order to test a system's defenses and see how it will respond. Red teaming of AI models is also used to test how well a model is aligned, or behaving in line with human goals and values.
Sandbox
A sandbox is a controlled, secure environment where AI tools can be tested. It's a place to learn how an AI agent or model might behave before releasing it to consumers.

OpenAI has documented cases where its AI agents have escaped their sandbox during testing and hacked into the servers of Hugging Face. The models, OpenAI said, were so "hyperfocused on finding a solution" to a cybersecurity challenge that they went to extreme lengths to achieve it.
Anthropic has also disclosed sandbox escapes where Claude models broke out in order to complete a task.

title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
summary: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
story: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.
Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.
Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.
When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."
Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."
Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.
"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.
His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."
"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.
How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.
It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.
"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."
Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.
"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."
Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.
He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.
Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.
"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.
She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be hardest to stop
summary: The time to prepare for "gradual disempowerment" is now, according to researchers. One calls it "a civilization-scale problem."
story: It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.

But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."
It's not just a threat to jobs. They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.

One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.
And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.
"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.
Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks, which could be accelerated by capable AI.
"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."
What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?
The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.
At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems, doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture.

We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.

It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.

To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.

But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.

But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.

Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.
Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.

The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?
With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.

"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.
"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"
A risk to democratic governance

It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military, for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.

If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle, its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.

"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.
States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?
"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.

Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.
If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.

"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.
"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."
How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?
Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions."
"We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."

The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy.
"This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write.

One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs, it helps to know that in granular detail.

But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged.

"This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."

Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it.
Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task.

"You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening."

Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong.

But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute.

"There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."

If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness.

"We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."
But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture.
"All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."
