title: Air Force member dies in rappelling incident at UT San Antonio football game
summary: A service member was injured and later died after falling while rappelling from the ceiling of the University of Texas at San Antonio football stadium on Saturday.
story: A member of the U.S. Air Force was injured and later died after he fell while rappelling from the ceiling of the Alamodome stadium in San Antonio, Texas, on Saturday, ahead of a University of Texas at San Antonio football game.

The incident took place during a pregame ceremony, before the official kickoff of UTSA's annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game against Navy, CBS affiliate KENS reported. The service member landed near the middle of the field after falling, a KENS photographer said.

Nellis Air Force Base Public Affairs issued a statement saying that the service member — identified as Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, Joint Base San Antonio, Texas — was injured at the stadium and died at a local hospital. CBS News has reached out to Nellis AFB for additional comment.
Originally from Fort Stewart, Georgia, Patterson had served in the Air Force for 15 years, the base said Sunday night.

"This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing," Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander, said in a statement Sunday night. "Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian's family, loved ones, and fellow Airmen as we navigate this profound loss together."

Patterson was one of four military service members who were scheduled to participate in a rappelling demonstration before Saturday's game. According to an Air Force website, they were part of a team of specialists who embed with Army and Marine units and help to direct air and artillery strikes from forward ground locations.
Part of their training includes learning to rapidly drop by rope, sometimes from helicopters that are 100 feet or more above the ground.

A video of the fall that was posted on social media showed Patterson, in combat fatigues, quickly descending to the ground feet first. The fall occurred with fans in the stands and a band assembled nearby on the field. He was treated on the field for several minutes and taken away on a gurney.
The incident is under investigation.

The game between the UTSA Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen still took place on Saturday. The American Conference said in a statement Sunday night that the decision to play the game was made before the airman's death had been confirmed.

"In accordance with conference bylaws and with the support of both participating member institutions, the conference made the decision to continue the game," the statement read in part. "Respect for the family's privacy and adherence to the military's notification process guided the decision to mitigate speculation about the service member's medical status and avoid additional distress for his family."

The conference also noted it was "heartbroken" about the death and said, "We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, teammates and members of the 57th Wing who had the privilege of serving with him. We honor his service and join the military community in mourning his loss."
After the game, the university issued a statement saying it was "deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight's football game."

"Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues," the statement said. "We recognize that members of our campus community may be emotionally affected by this incident and are activating wellbeing services to support our faculty, staff and students."
Taylor Eighmy, the university's president, also spoke out in the wake of the accident.

"What was intended to be a day of camaraderie, tradition and celebration has been marked by profound sadness," Eighmy said. "I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member's family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy."

In a separate statement, Lisa Campos, the vice president for intercollegiate athletics at UT San Antonio, added: "Moments like these remind us that we are all part of something much greater than a game."
After the game, which UTSA won 38-34, UTSA coach Jeff Traylor told reporters that the accident was "heartbreaking" and "tragic."

He said the team could see the effect that it had on the crowd of over 23,000 people as soon as players arrived on the field for the game, although Traylor had only been told there had been an "incident" that would delay the start of the game by about 10 minutes.
"You could tell the energy was just gone," he said. "It just really puts things in perspective. It really does."

title: Feds probing suspicious letters to election officials, lawmakers
summary: Federal investigators said they are looking into suspicious letters containing unknown substances that were mailed to state election officials and congressional offices.
story: Washington — Federal investigators said they are looking into "suspicious" letters mailed to state election officials and congressional offices, some of which contained unknown substances.

Several Democratic senators' and House members' offices were sent the letters in recent days, many of which were intercepted before they were delivered. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's office was one of those targeted, CBS News has learned. At least three Senate Republicans were also sent letters.

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the "suspicious mailings," according to Brendan Donahue, the deputy chief inspector at the USPIS. Donahue told reporters earlier that some letters have contained an unknown substance and that they were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including "secretary of state offices and the related election offices."

"We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable," Donahue said. "Our partners, including the FBI and we at the Postal Inspection Service, will bring all of our resources to bear on these investigations."

The Senate sergeant at arms also issued a notice to congressional staff informing them of the investigation. The message, which was obtained by CBS News, said congressional offices were among those who received the suspicious letters.

A spokesperson for Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester told CBS News that a state office received a suspicious letter that contained a white powder. The letter was not opened in the office, the spokesperson said.

A letter meant for New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand was found at the senator's office in New York City and postal inspectors were on the scene to investigate, an aide for the senator said. A letter intended for one of Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks' former state offices was intercepted by the Postal Service, her office said Friday.
A spokesman for Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut said his office was "sent a letter with a suspicious substance."

"Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement," said Josh Sorbe, a spokesman for Murphy. "Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger."
A letter was also sent to Sen. Alex Padilla's office, according to a spokesperson for the California Democrat.
"We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS," the spokesperson said.
A suspicious letter was sent to the office of Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, according to a spokesperson, who said the office was "working with law enforcement."
On Friday, Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Pete Ricketts of Nebraska reported receiving suspicious letters.

Ricketts said his office in Omaha was sent a letter with a "powdery substance" that matched the description of other suspicious packages, and law enforcement "confirmed the substance was not harmful."
Rounds said his office in Sioux Falls was evacuated after it received suspicious mail.

Republican Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin said his office in Milwaukee received a "suspicious envelope" on Monday, with a return address that "matched the description of letters sent to other congressional and state offices across the nation."

Six workers in Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres' office in the Bronx were exposed to a white powder found in a letter on Friday. The substance was determined to be harmless. Torres said the address on the envelope indicated it was from San Antonio, Texas, and his team has turned it over to the FBI for further investigation.

Democratic Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia on Saturday confirmed the FBI contacted his office to report that investigators had intercepted mail containing a suspicious substance addressed to his district office.
"I am grateful to law enforcement for their efforts to keep my staff safe. Threats and attempts at intimidation are unacceptable and must not be tolerated," Scott said on social media.

Colorado Democratic Rep. Joe Neguse said Monday a "threatening letter with suspicious substances" was delivered to his office in Boulder. He added that "there is no continued threat to public safety in the area."
Another Colorado Democrat, Rep. Jason Crow, said his office received a letter with a "suspicious substance" on Monday.

The House sergeant at arms sent a notice to the lower chamber's offices on Thursday stating that no House members were known to have been targeted, a message that came before the discovery of powder at Torres' office.

Federal officials are working to identify the responsible parties and have intercepted some of the letters, Donahue said. Donahue declined to provide an exact number of incidents or discuss possible connections, citing the ongoing investigation. He added that investigators would bring their full resources to bear on the cases.
The development comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections. Federal investigators also probed a series of suspicious letters ahead of the 2024 elections.
In addition to the congressional offices, top election officials in at least eight states have reported that their offices were sent suspicious packages in recent days.

Delaware's Department of Elections said in a post on X that it "received and opened a letter which was discovered to contain a white powdery substance" on Thursday. "Staff members followed security and USPS instructions on handling suspicious mail," the post said.
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said Tuesday that an employee in her office's Elections Division opened a package and found a white powder.
"Law enforcement responded to today's incident and conducted tests that found no evidence of harmful substances," she wrote on Facebook, adding that no one was injured.
The Oklahoma State Election Board said it received an envelope containing "suspicious" white powder Tuesday morning, and its office was evacuated.
Paul Ziriax, secretary of the election board, said no one was hurt as a result of the incident, and law enforcement is investigating.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said it received a "suspicious mail piece" on Wednesday, but "field testing confirmed no hazardous material was detected."

The secretaries of state in Pennsylvania, Maryland, New Hampshire, Ohio and Mississippi said their offices were also sent suspicious mail, but the deliveries were intercepted by the U.S. Postal Service or law enforcement before they arrived.

title: Boy among 2 killed after truck drives onto Wichita soccer field
summary: A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed during a soccer game at Stryker Soccer Complex in Wichita, Kansas, according to police.
story: Two people were killed, and 11 were injured after a truck drove onto a soccer field Saturday in Wichita, Kansas, authorities said.

A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed during a soccer game at Stryker Soccer Complex, said Aaron Moses, a captain and executive officer with the Wichita Police Department. The boy was identified Sunday as Cole Adrian and the man as Nicholas Schafer, both of whom are from McPherson, Kansas, but they were not related, according to police.
Eleven people were transported to local hospitals with injuries that were not life-threatening, ranging in age from 5 years old to 68 years old, Moses said at a news conference.

The driver, a 34-year-old woman, was taken into custody and had been cooperative with the investigation, Moses said. Two juveniles were also inside the vehicle at the time, Moses said. It's unclear if the incident was intentional.

An investigation into the incident was ongoing, police said. No charges have been filed, and the driver was later released pending the results of toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of the vehicle, police said Sunday.
The city of Wichita said in a statement that all events at the soccer complex have been canceled until further notice.

"Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita," Mayor Lily Wu said during a news conference on Saturday. "Families came to Stryker Soccer Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon watching their children play soccer. No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold."
David Griekspoor was there watching his nephew play. He and his family sprang into action to help, and they are all safe.

"The families that were on that field, that had to dive out of the way, who lost loved ones, who have kids or family members in the hospital... it was just a hard sight to see," he said.  For many in the community, there are now more questions than answers.   "I know they are doing further investigations ... but for her to be free when so many people went through so much ... it just doesn't make sense," Griekspoor said about the driver.
In a statement on social media Sunday, U.S. Soccer said it was "heartbroken" by the tragedy and offered its condolences to the families impacted.

"The entire U.S. Soccer family stands with the soccer communities in Wichita and across Kansas during this incredibly difficult time," the statement said. "We will work closely with Wichita Youth Soccer to understand how we can best support the community in the days and weeks ahead."

title: Ex-OpenAI worker who allegedly planted bug contacted Saudi royal
summary: The wife and infant son of the ex-OpenAI engineer left the U.S. for Saudi Arabia in October with business-class tickets purchased by a Saudi military official, prosecutors allege.
story: A former OpenAI engineer who allegedly installed a sophisticated listening device in an executive conference room was in close contact with a member of the Saudi royal family and was planning to leave the U.S. for Riyadh when authorities arrested him, federal prosecutors said Sunday in a court memorandum.

Abdulrahman Alfozan is accused of tapping artificial intelligence tools to help him develop encrypted recording devices and identify meeting rooms used by OpenAI executives, government officials and business partners.
The Saudi national earned an annual paycheck of $385,000 at OpenAI and received a $2.2 million equity grant when he first joined the company in July 2025.

In an 11-page filing, prosecutors wrote that investigators recovered evidence suggesting Alfozan may have planned to place even more devices inside OpenAI offices. Prosecutors also revealed that the suspect engaged in WhatsApp messages with an unidentified Saudi royal who repeatedly encouraged him to return to the kingdom and join a Saudi AI initiative.

The filing also shows photographs of other potential surveillance locations, internal searches concerning meetings between OpenAI and Saudi government officials, and notes suggesting he planned to take back the devices before leaving the company.

Investigators allege that on Sept. 28 Alfozan installed a "surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days."
Prosecutors allege that he "modified the device to prevent data transfer between it and the television into which it was inserted" and "had also encrypted the content stored on the device's microSD."

In the days before the device was installed, investigators claim that Alfozan used an AI chatbot account belonging to his wife to research how to customize the recording device, including how to: "build a continuous audio recorder," "captur[e] microphone audio and save compressed WAV recordings to an SD card," "improve audio and live listening," "develop … speech-triggered recording," "add browser access and controls" including "live listening," and "encrypt the SD card" and "decrypt and recover recordings from the removed card."

Meetings in that executive conference room, according to prosecutors, "frequently involve discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships."

According to the filing, investigators determined that in the "days surrounding the time period that the device was installed, OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room," alleging the "defendant's conduct could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."
Prosecutors also disclosed that his cellphone contained photographs of at least one other concealed recorder as well as electronic equipment in other OpenAI meeting rooms.
Prosecutors allege that throughout 2025 and 2026, Alfozan "was in frequent communication via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family, including as recently as October 5, 2026."
The Saudi royal, according to prosecutors, told Alfozan that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and enticed him to join it.
"Saudi needs you more than [sic] the US!" the member wrote, part of a campaign to recruit the defendant. Alfozan agreed but said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested.
The suspect was arrested Oct. 9, three days before he was scheduled to depart San Francisco with his wife and infant son on a one-way flight to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Instead, his wife and 3-month-old son left the country the following day on business-class tickets purchased by a Saudi military official, prosecutors allege. Before his arrest, the defendant had been scheduled to take two months of parental leave beginning in October 2026.
Alfozan, who has no prior criminal record, according to the filing, became a U.S. permanent resident in September 2020 and applied for citizenship thereafter. OpenAI fired him after his arrest.
At a detention hearing Monday, U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex Tse denied a request by Alfozan's lawyers to release him to home confinement.

The government argued that Alfozan should be detained pending his trial, alleging that his wealth, connections and apparent assistance from Saudi government officials put him at risk of fleeing the country.
He is due back in court next month.

title: 1 person killed in shooting near Columbus, Ohio mosque
summary: A fatal shooting outside a mosque in Columbus, Ohio, was not an attack on the building, police said.
story: One person was killed in a shooting near a mosque in Columbus, Ohio, on Monday afternoon, but the shooting was not connected to the mosque or those who were inside, police said.
"We want to make it clear this was not an attack on the mosque," said Sgt. James Fuqua.
The Columbus Division of Police said they received multiple calls of shots fired in the area shortly after 2 p.m.

"This incident occurred in the parking lot of an apartment complex adjacent to a mosque," the police statement said. "While we are still in the preliminary stages of the investigation as to the details regarding this shooting, this was not a targeted attack on the mosque, nor did this incident occur at the mosque."
Officers for the Columbus Division of Police responded to the report of a shooting around 2:10 p.m. in the 2200 block of Albert Avenue. https://t.co/QaxuY5euBf

The federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said earlier Monday in a post on social media that agents were responding to a report of a shooting at the mosque, which is northeast of downtown Columbus. The area includes a nearby cluster of two-story apartment buildings.

An ATF spokesperson said preliminary information indicated people were leaving a funeral at the mosque at the time. The spokesperson said ATF special agents are assisting Columbus police with the ongoing investigation.

title: Elon Musk pledges to give a SpaceX share to every U.S. child
summary: The SpaceX CEO wrote on social media on Monday that the gift "will be the first of many."
story: Elon Musk said in a social media post on Monday that he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to each child in the U.S., writing that the gift "will be the first of many."

Musk didn't specify how the shares would be distributed or other details of how the pledge might be fulfilled. The offer arrived a day after artificial intelligence company Anthropic announced that it will commit 5% of its shares to a new "public benefit" fund.
Anthropic said it will contribute an additional 2% of shares at its board's discretion for every 50% increase in the company's value, above a set threshold.
Shares of SpaceX, which will report quarterly earnings on Tuesday, rose $3.46, or 2.7%, to $149.49 in Monday morning trading.

The SpaceX CEO is the company's largest shareholder with a 10.5% stake, according to financial data firm FactSet. His stake included 4.8 billion shares of SpaceX when the company went public earlier this year, an event that briefly made Musk the world's first trillionaire.
There are about 73 million children in the U.S., according to Census Bureau data.
Musk, the world's richest person, is currently worth about $904 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Anthropic made its pledge to commit a portion of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which it described as "a new entity," at a time when AI researchers from leading labs are warning of doomsday scenarios with potentially catastrophic outcomes that extend far beyond job losses.

Anthropic said the company has a two-pronged mission, with its research providing both a public benefit component and for-profit value. The new fund will give it more flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or gifts to specific populations, the company added.

Anthropic also called out AI's impact on workers, acknowledging that tech advances could "cause instability" for many employees, and noted that it has already committed $200 million to analyzing and addressing AI's effects on parts of the labor force.
"Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good," Anthropic said.

President Trump wrote on social media that SpaceX shares would be donated through the recently created Trump Accounts program. The accounts, under new rules laid out by the Treasury, allow donors to deliver stock to the accounts without paying capital-gains taxes.
Mr. Trump thanked Musk for his "incredible generosity" and called the planned donation "exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS."

Michael Piwowar, executive director of Georgetown McDonough's Psaros Center for Financial Markets and Policy, called Trump Accounts the "perfect vehicle" through which Musk could deliver SpaceX shares to recipients.
"One of their great features, in addition to $1,000 seed money, is the ability of philanthropists to make philanthropic donations to a class of individuals," he said.
The Treasury Department is automatically enrolling up to 60 million children in the Trump Accounts program.
Piwowar added that with Musk's donation, "American children will immediately be invested in the American dream."

The tax-deferred accounts, created under Mr. Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill tax and spending bill for U.S. citizens born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a $1,000 seed donation from the government.

title: Iran touts closest ever ties with Russia, contradicting Trump

story: What to know about the Iran war today:

Iran's foreign minister said Tuesday that Tehran's ties with Russia had never been so close, after President Trump said Moscow was "doing very little, if anything, to help" Iran amid the war in the Middle East. title: U.S. ramps up warnings to Americans in Middle East after Houthi strikes
summary: U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of warnings to Americans amid attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia.
story: U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.

The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.

"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."

The State Department has maintained restrictions on diplomatic operations across parts of the region since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran in February. State Department officials have said the restrictions are intended to be temporary and allow embassies to adjust staffing as security conditions evolve.
Under a longstanding "no double standard" policy, embassies are required to share security threat information with private American citizens when the same risks apply to U.S. diplomatic personnel.

The latest alerts follow a surge in Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including repeated strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco. The Oct. 10 airport attack killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi authorities.
The attacks continued Tuesday, with the Saudi-led coalition reporting it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh as well as a drone near the capital.

The escalating attacks have raised questions about the effectiveness of the Trump administration's approach to the conflict. While the administration has provided intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia, President Trump has thus far declined repeated requests from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for direct U.S. military intervention. He has left open the possibility of joining in airstrikes but has not announced a decision.
"We may," Mr. Trump said on Oct. 10, after the deadly attack on Riyadh's airport. "We're going to look at it."

The Houthis have continued to make territorial gains in Yemen, where a Houthi attack killed two teenage girls in Taiz on Tuesday. That came a day after a strike on a government military camp killed 73 recruits and wounded more than 200.

In an interview Tuesday with CBS News, Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to the minister of foreign affairs of the government of Yemen, warned that the Houthis would continue expanding their attacks unless confronted. He argued that Yemen's military campaign was intended to protect the wider region as well as its own population.
"We are fighting on behalf of everyone, because the threat and risk of the Houthis will expand," Noman said.

He added that Yemen's government was seeking expanded U.S. and international assistance, including greater intelligence sharing, air defenses and support for its coast guard, but was not asking Washington to deploy ground troops.

The requests come as the Trump administration faces competing demands for air defense weapons. Speaking to reporters in India on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that countries including Saudi Arabia and Israel are seeking additional American-made missile interceptors, even as Ukraine presses for more supplies.
"Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said. "It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field."

title: 2 men rearrested for alleged spying for Iran in U.K. air base incident
summary: Police said a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national were arrested under the National Security Act.
story: British police said Tuesday they have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service over the suspected plot at a U.S.-run air base in England last month.
Counter Terrorism Policing said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.
The men were earlier arrested but had been bailed pending more investigation.
Police are investigating a suspected terror plot on Sept. 27 against the U.S.-run base at RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year's war.

Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford.
Five other men who were also arrested earlier remain on bail. No one has yet been charged.
Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K., said detectives are looking at "many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation."

"This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," he said in a statement.
"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it," he added.

Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. But the Iranian Embassy in London said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Air Force removed all of its bombers from the air base following the security incident.

title: Egypt weighs sending troops to Saudi Arabia in war with Iran-backed rebels
summary: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil infrastructure.
story: Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting airports and oil infrastructure.
Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.
"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.

On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.

The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."

Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.

"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.
Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.

The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."
Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.
"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."
However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.
"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."

Ragheb argued that the United States' refusal to attack the Houthis in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.
Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.
"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

title: Ukraine's military evacuates wounded soldier with aerial drone
summary: Ukraine's military says a soldier reportedly trapped by Russian fire on the front line for more than a year was evacuated by an aerial drone.
story: Ukraine's military says it carried out a front-line medical evacuation by aerial drone —   an apparent world-first for the drone-savvy nation — as Russia's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark.
The Ukrainian Ground Forces' 92nd Assault Brigade said Monday that it had evacuated a wounded soldier from the front line using a heavy-lift aerial drone.

For almost 500 days, soldier Konstantyn Vlasenko of the 30th Separate Brigade was stuck in a position out of reach for Ukrainian ground forces or robots due to dense mining and heavy Russian drone activity, according to Ukrainian news outlets, including some linked with the military.
The reports said Vlasenko was wounded by a Russian drone earlier this year while trapped, forcing him to carry out partial self-amputations of both of his legs as he hoped for a rescue.

A Ukrainian-made Gurzuf Defence heavy hexacopter, originally configured as an attack drone to drop bombs on Russian positions, was used for the rescue operation —   provided to the military free of charge, according to the statement from the 92nd Brigade.
Specialists worked with the company to modify the unmanned aircraft to carry a person without flipping or swinging them, and the new configuration was tested before the rescue was planned.

Four different Ukrainian brigades were involved in the complex operation, which took seven days to prepare, though the actual rescue only took about an hour and 15 minutes. In that time, the drone flew almost 40 miles, with Ukrainian units using other drones to distract the Russian military, the brigade said.

Gurzuf Defence co-founder Pavlo Feldbloom told CBS News the company "never set out to create a platform designed exclusively for evacuation; instead, we developed a heavy-duty, modular, multi-mission platform."
He said the company understood, however, that a drone capable of carrying such a payload should also be capable of carrying out rescue missions.
"At the same time, we do not believe that aerial evacuation will become a routine, large-scale practice," he said, as the "risks to a wounded person in the air are simply too high."
"Aerial transport is the last resort —   an option to be used only when there is no other way to save a person's life," Feldbloom said.

Before the aerial evacuation, there was an attempt to rescue Konstantyn using a ground drone, another technique pioneered by Ukrainian forces during the war, but it was destroyed on its way to him, according to the Ukrainian Armed Forces 2nd Mechanized Battalion.
When Vlasenko landed, he described his evacuation flight as calm and said he was relieved to be back on friendly ground.

title: Shark kills woman swimming off popular beach in South Africa
summary: Local media reported the woman was a regular swimmer and had been swimming with a group when the attack occurred.
story: A woman died after being mauled by a shark while swimming off a popular beach on South Africa's southeastern coast on Tuesday, witnesses and authorities said.
Fatal shark attacks are uncommon worldwide but South Africa has a history of deadly encounters along its long coastline.
Tuesday's attack was at Orient Beach in KuGompo City, previously known as East London.
Police said they were called to the scene at around 7:00 am local time, where they found the body of a 65-year-old woman with "open wounds."

Local media reported the woman was a regular swimmer and had been swimming with a group when the attack occurred. A local community group said other swimmers had spotted a shark's tail and fin. The group said the woman sustained "severe injuries to the right side of her arm and leg."

"We all realized she'd been bitten by a shark, and she was in a very bad way," a witness told public broadcaster SABC. "The bites were very severe, but there were only two, one on her thigh and one on her upper arm."
After the attack, the municipality closed nearby beaches and urged the public to stay out of the water.
"It has been confirmed that a shark attack occurred at Orient Beach this morning, and this resulted in a tragic incident," the local municipality  said in a statement.
The incident comes about one month after a man was killed by a shark in front of beachgoers as he swam off a Western Australian city shore.

There were 65 unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025, up from 47 the previous year, including nine fatalities, according to the University of Florida's International Shark Attack File. There was one unprovoked attack in South Africa last year, which was fatal. By contrast, there were 25 unprovoked attacks in the U.S. (one fatal) and 21 unprovoked attacks in Australia (five fatal).
In 2022, there were two fatal shark attacks in South Africa, including a 39-year-old woman who was on vacation with her husband and young child when she was killed.

Researchers say encounters can be influenced by a range of factors, including growing coastal populations, increased use of marine waters, environmental changes and shifts in the distribution of sharks and their prey.

title: Man charged in "targeted" attack on Australian lawmaker Helen Haines
summary: Australian police charged a man on Tuesday over what they alleged was a "targeted" attack with a vehicle on independent lawmaker Helen Haines.
story: Australian police charged a man on Tuesday over what they alleged was a "targeted" attack with a vehicle on independent lawmaker Helen Haines.

Haines has reportedly lost one of her legs in the aftermath of the incident on Monday afternoon, in which a car rammed into her multiple times as she stood near the trunk of her own parked vehicle in the southeastern city of Wangaratta, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

Authorities said the 65-year-old was getting something from the back of her car when her alleged attacker drove past in a Toyota Land Cruiser. He allegedly turned the car around before veering into Haines, pinning her against her own vehicle and then reversing before ramming into her again, according to local authorities and Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke.

Brendan Nugent, from nearby Tarrawingee, was charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official, police said in a statement on Tuesday.
Police have said little about the suspect's potential motive, but they have characterized the incident as a "deliberate" act of violence.
Political violence is historically uncommon across Australia, though data show threats have grown in recent years.
Suspect to face court on Wednesday

Nugent has been in police custody since shortly after Haines was injured and a crowd of bystanders subdued him. He will appear in a Wangaratta court on Wednesday, when he could potentially be released on bail.
His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement Tuesday describing Haines as a "deeply respected, valued and much-loved member of our local community."
"Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable," the father said, adding that he would cooperate with police.
"Absolutely devastated"
Wangaratta Mayor Irene Grant said a somber mood had settled over the town of about 30,000 people, a regional hub about 250 kilometers, or 155 miles, northeast of state capital Melbourne.

"Helen was well-respected. She was diligent and hard working," Grant told AFP. "What has happened to Helen has caused the community to step back in utter disbelief. We can't believe it, people are horrified by what has happened."
Locals, meanwhile, are struggling to comprehend why anyone would wish harm on the well-liked Haines.
Florist Jess Woodrow said Haines was a friendly face who would pop into the store when she was not tied up in the capital Canberra.

"We are absolutely devastated to hear what has happened. Helen was a beautiful person. She didn't have a bad bone in her body," Woodrow told AFP. "It's the last thing you would think would happen here."

Haines entered parliament as an independent lawmaker in 2019, representing the sprawling seat of Indi. Her popularity led to her holding the seat in the 2025 election, with a hefty margin of more than 18,000 votes.

Haines was a vocal champion for greater climate action, better rural healthcare, and help for struggling small businesses, while the First Peoples' Assembly of Victoria said Haines was a "staunch supporter" of Indigenous rights as well. But it was her work to hold politicians to account that perhaps earned Haines the most respect both inside and outside parliament.

"Helen Haines is characterized by her kindness, her compassion, her diligence, her intelligence," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. "She's someone who is such a strong advocate and is widely respected right across the political spectrum because the way that she advocates is very respectful."

title: Zelenskyy says if Trump can't stop Putin, help Ukraine do it
summary: Ukraine's leader calls on Trump to allow delivery of interceptor missiles already purchased by European allies if the U.S. "cannot rein Putin in."
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview published Tuesday that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself, as the war of words between the two leaders continues to escalate.

"If you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy told the Italian newspaper Corriere Della Sera, referring to Russia's autocratic President Vladimir Putin.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said later Tuesday that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."
The exchange came as Zelenskyy prepared to meet U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, with his fellow envoy, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, expected to join remotely.

Zelenskyy has accused the Trump administration this week of delaying shipments of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, as well as constraining Starlink satellite data that is vital to Ukrainian forces' ability to intercept incoming Russian attack drones.

Ukraine has nearly run out of the U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors used to take down Russian ballistic missiles, and Zelenskyy has long pleaded for more. This week he said the U.S. was delaying delivery of Patriots already purchased by European nations for Ukraine.
Rubio, on a visit to India, said "every other country in the world" also wanted Patriots.

"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," he said. "It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field. So, when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying."

The meeting comes as daily Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities continue claiming civilian lives, and as relations between Kyiv and Washington appear more strained than they have been since Zelenskyy's tumultuous February 2025 meeting in the Oval Office.

The Ukrainian president said Monday that his country had suffered another night of Russian strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners." At least four people were killed in the capital in the latest attacks, Kyiv officials said Tuesday.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Finnish President Alexander Stubb would also join the talks in Oslo, with "the aim to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," according to a statement from the prime minister's office.
Starshield and Patriots

Mr. Trump on Friday waived some sanctions against Russia, reducing penalties for its energy sales in a bid to ease rising U.S. gas prices caused by the ongoing war with Iran —   a policy Zelenskyy says could embolden Moscow to step up its four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine.
Mr. Trump has criticized Zelenskyy for saying he would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation for the latest Russian onslaught.
Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield —   the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite network —   to intercept Russian drones.

The Trump administration has denied ordering Starshield restrictions. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday that there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

In recent days, Mr. Trump has intensified his public criticism of Zelenskyy, saying in a Truth Social post that the Ukrainian leader "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," and telling reporters, "maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate."

Mr. Trump has never publicly acknowledged that Russia started the war against its neighbor, which initially began in 2014, and has at times blamed Zelenskyy for the full-scale invasion ordered by Putin on Feb. 24, 2022.

Ahead of his Tuesday meeting with Mr. Trump's envoys, Zelenskyy said he had a "substantive conversation" with Rubio the previous day in which he stressed that Starshield "needs to be restored" and ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives."

Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers via video call on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries. He said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hadn't signed off on the shipment.

Multiple European countries were waiting for U.S. approval to transfer their own Patriot interceptors, he added, saying he believed "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."

Rubio said Tuesday that it ⁠could be accurate that a batch ‌of interceptors purchased for Ukraine ⁠had not been delivered, but he told reporters: "I think the important takeaway for ⁠you is that there has not been some ‌deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."

Rubio also said Mr. Trump was "frustrated because, first of all, he doesn't like to be blamed for things that aren't true, including accusations that somehow he had ordered intelligence sharing to be cut off. And that's not true. He's said that repeatedly."
"I think the president, more than anything, is responding to the insinuation that somehow he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine —   which is not fair and not true," he added.
In his interview with the Italian newspaper, published hours earlier, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had built its relationship with Washington "on honesty, fairness, and, most importantly, transparency."

"When you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States," Zelenskyy told the paper, adding: "We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today."

"The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them," he said. "Let's believe that America really wants to, but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back —   that is neither honest nor fair — but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure."
Trump-Xi-Putin summit on Ukraine?
U.S.-led efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict have stalled in recent months, with Washington more focused on its war with Iran.
Mr. Trump recently said he was ready to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next month for talks that could include discussion of the Ukraine war.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has confirmed that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this week that any such meeting on his country's fate, without Ukraine at the table, would "only encourage Putin to continue this war."

title: Israel detains 40 ultra-Orthodox men accused of draft dodging
summary: At least 40 ultra-Orthodox Jewish men were arrested at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport on suspicion of attempting to evade the country's military draft.
story: Tel Aviv — At least 40 ultra-Orthodox Jewish men were arrested upon arriving Tuesday morning at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport on suspicion of attempting to evade the country's military draft, the Israel Defense Forces said.

"The aforementioned individuals, who passed through the border crossing at Ben Gurion Airport, are subject to mandatory military service and will be tried in accordance with the law," the IDF said in a statement.

The mass-arrest by military police was unusual in its scale, and it came amid a national reckoning over whether the ultra-Orthodox should have to serve in the military like the rest of Israel's Jewish citizens.

The ultra-Orthodox have traditionally been exempt from military service, but in 2024, Israel's Supreme Court ruled that in the absence of any law legalizing the exemption, the military must start drafting them.

Since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel and the subsequent multi-front war, the issue of equality of service has been thrust to the forefront of political debate ahead of Israel's looming national elections on Oct. 27.
Many Israelis who serve in the military, particularly in the reserves, have complained of having to take on an unfair amount of the security burden for the state.

Ultra-Orthodox or Haredi Jews make up around 13% of Israel's population, but that number is growing faster than any other group in the country. They are expected to represent close to 25% of the population by 2050, according to projections by Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics.
Rather than serve in the military, most ultra-Orthodox men study full-time in religious seminaries.

Ultra-Orthodox political leaders have demanded a law to formalize the group's broad exemption from the draft, but one that would also determine a percentage of ultra-Orthodox men and women who would be subject to compulsory service.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has relied directly, since the last national elections in 2022, on the support of ultra-Orthodox parties to remain in power, and he has had to walk a tight line between their demands and those of other supporters demanding equality of service.

In an interview Tuesday morning with the ultra-Orthodox radio station Kol Barama, Netanyahu said he opposed the arrests of ultra-Orthodox draft evaders, arguing that it harmed efforts to enlist them without coercion.

title: Voters reject separation of Alberta from Canada in referendum
summary: The vote was not a referendum on independence from Canada, but it would have begun a process towards possible separation.
story: Voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, results showed early Tuesday, delivering a victory for Prime Minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity amid President Trump's trade war and annexation threats.
The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.
With more than 1 million votes counted, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation.
"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.

Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. More than 1.35 million Albertans, or 43% of eligible voters, cast advance or special ballots. Albertans were deciding whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could have led to a second vote on separation.

Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.
Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said Albertans have long been mistreated by Ottawa.
"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us and not return anything."
Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation.
"I think it'll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta," she said.
Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than health care.
Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that will not disappear.
Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. "Vote like Canada's future depends on it because it does," he told a rally Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.

title: Hegseth meets Netanyahu ahead of elections, possible Iran war restart
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel just over a week before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stands for elections, and as President Trump floats restarting the Iran war.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
A second source involved in the matter in Israel confirmed Tuesday morning that Netanyahu met Hegseth.

The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.

Hegseth confirmed in an X post that he was in U.S. Central Command's area of responsibility on Monday, sharing a photo of himself addressing American service members who he said were "on a historic mission." He did not specify his location or mention Israel.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit. CBS News has reached out to the Israeli government for comment.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.

Israeli and U.S. forces jointly launched strikes against Iran in late February, and the two allies worked closely with each other early in the war. The U.S. also struck three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during a broader conflict between Israel and Iran.

Iran and the U.S. have largely refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, but Mr. Trump has said openly that he is still weighing whether to cut a deal with Iran's leadership or "annihilate" the country — a decision he says could come after the November midterm elections.

Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, faces his own political uncertainty a week from Tuesday. The coalition led by his right-wing Likud party is seeking to remain in power, but it faces several more centrist challengers, including one party run by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu told Israeli media last week he is not planning to launch renewed strikes against Iran before the Oct. 27 elections, saying, "it is not convenient for us."
Mr. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, calling him "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."

The U.S. president has maintained a close relationship with Netanyahu, though he has put pressure on Israel at times. Over the spring and summer, the Trump administration urged Israel to ease up on striking Lebanon, home to Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.
The administration has also encouraged Israel to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank and cut a longer-term deal with Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Last month, Trump envoy Jared Kushner suggested the upcoming Israeli elections may have delayed progress in Gaza, saying at a conference in Kyiv: "They just have a crazy election, and that makes them a little irrational in certain regards."

                                  Charlie  D'Agata and 
                                                  
                                  Eleanor  Watson

title: Zelenskyy says it's Putin who wants an endless war, not him
summary: Ukraine's leader rejects Trump's accusations, says Putin is refusing peace, not him, and the U.S. military is delaying "vital supplies."
story: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Monday that his country had been subjected to another night of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners."

Zelenskyy has accused the U.S. of limiting intelligence, and possibly other assistance to Ukraine amid renewed tension with President Trump, who accused the Ukrainian leader over the weekend of not wanting to end the war. Mr. Trump has significantly softened the U.S. government's policy toward Russia, easing sanctions to allow Russian energy sales  in a bid to ease U.S. gas prices.
Zelenskyy says the moves risk emboldening Moscow and enabling it to continue and intensify its four-and-a-half-year, full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The target of the most recent strikes was energy and other infrastructure, Zelenskyy said, adding that a medical clinic, school, metro station and "ordinary residential buildings" were also hit.

Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite technology, to intercept Russian drones. The network is crucial to Ukrainian forces as it enables them to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones and other weapons.
The Trump administration has denied making any changes to the intelligence it shares with Ukraine, or deliberately slowing down Starshield data.

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday, "There has been no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

Asked Saturday if the U.S. government was responsible for the change in Starlink service in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate … we have nothing to do with that."

"The United States — nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored. It's back to where it was before," he said, without elaborating on what he meant by "it sort of happened."

Denys Sienik, Ukraine's chargé d'affaires and current top diplomat in the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or Musk's SpaceX to inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."

"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X, adding that there had also been "delays in certain types of vital supplies at the level of the U.S. Department of War."
He did not expound on his assertion that the Pentagon was delaying shipments of supplies.

The Ukrainian leader issued the statement amid an increasingly terse exchange of accusations with Mr. Trump who, over the weekend, accused Zelenskyy of not wanting the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion to end.
In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump said Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."

"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump argued.

The U.S. president has over the last month walked back sanctions on Russia — that had support from a majority of Republicans and Democrats —   that were intended to increase financial pressure on Moscow over its assault on Ukraine.
"Ukraine never wanted this war," Zelenskyy said in another statement shared Monday on social media. "We took positively literally EVERY attempt of partners to end this war with dignity."

Just over a week ago Mr. Trump declared in a social media post that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," which would mean a halt to attacks on the other country's energy infrastructure. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to any such deal, and within hours Ukrainian authorities reported new Russian attacks on refineries.
Zelenskyy said "again and again Russia's answers" to efforts at diplomacy were new attacks.

"Putin does not want the end of this war, or even any de-escalation steps," he said, adding: "It is very important to call things by their names. Call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine protect lives. When the supply of missiles to Ukrainian air defense is blocked, and Russia receives a weakening or postponement of sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality from partners. In reality, the war continues, and continues only because of Russian strikes — the Russian desire to prolong this war."
The Kremlin, meanwhile, has attempted to frame Russia as a willing partner in peace efforts.

Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Moscow values U.S. mediation efforts, but that reaching agreements without the participation of representatives from Kyiv is impossible. There have been direct talks, mediated by the U.S., between Ukraine and Russia, but so far the meetings have yielded little more than prisoner swaps, not ceasefires.

The Wall Street Journal first reported Sunday evening that Putin had proposed a meeting between U.S., Chinese and Russian officials to discuss solutions to the Ukraine war, but without a seat for Ukraine at the negotiating table. The newspaper said he proposed the idea for a summit during a call with Mr. Trump on Oct. 9.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Monday in a post on X that "a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war."

title: France vows to crack down after protests spiral out of control
summary: French officials implemented local curfews Monday and said an "ultra-left movement" was behind widespread violence and vandalism amid anti-government protests.
story: Paris — French officials implemented local curfews Monday as the nation reeled from a weekend of violence. Widespread anti-government protests in many large cities descended into riots, with damage to historic properties and thousands of arrests.

A curfew issued by Paris police on Monday will be in effect for the Place de la République and the Les Halles neighborhood. The curfew will be in effect from 11 p.m. local time Monday until 6 a.m. Tuesday. Gatherings in Paris after 8 p.m. were also banned, CBS News' partner network BBC News reported.
In Nice, a curfew was in effect from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., the city's mayor announced. A curfew covering that same time frame was also in effect for Lyon, according to the BBC.

In hard-hit Marseille, France's second-largest city, all large gatherings were banned Monday in the wake of the violence, which started weeks ago as protests by young people furious over the state of their schools, but quickly snowballed into national demonstrations over the rising cost of living and declining public services.

The 19th-century town hall in the city of Limoges was burned to the ground on Saturday by masked rioters who hijacked marches across France, looting stores, torching cars and buildings and clashing with police as the protests turned violent.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested, France's Justice Ministry said.
The U.S. State Department issued an advisory Monday urging Americans to "avoid the areas of the demonstrations."
In an address Sunday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron, vowed that "those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable."

Speaking Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed at least some of the violence on "an ultra-left movement intent on orchestrating profound disorder in the country leading up to the presidential election" in April.

He said police "had lost control" during the unrest, and as the Yellow Vests protest movement, which organized the weekend rallies that turned violent, called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday, he called for regional authorities to impose "partial" and "localized" curfews to protect businesses.
"I'm absolutely determined to restore public order," Lecornu said, adding that the government was ready to impose a national state of emergency, "if needed."

Speaking of the alleged agitators, Lecornu said there was "⁠an entire network that could be mobilized to challenge the presidential election schedule and the very holding of the presidential election," adding that the government was committed to protecting the country's democratic process.

⁠"There is no way we will allow violent minorities to impose an agenda of violence and, quite obviously, prevent us from holding this election," he said, acknowledging that the protests by high school students over classroom conditions were legitimate, but adding that "the freedom to demonstrate is being undermined."

While French officials have not suggested any link between the unrest and immigration, President Trump claimed one in a brief social media post on Monday, saying: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"
Damage to landmarks

Capital city Paris has seen the worst of the unrest, and residents woke up Monday to streets littered with debris and burned vehicles. But severe damage was inflicted across the country, with centuries of heritage being damaged or destroyed by flames.

Video captured the moment the clock tower of Limoges' historic town hall, in southwest France — a landmark that had stood for nearly 150 years, surviving both World Wars — was engulfed in flames and came toppling down.

The tourist office in the eastern city of Lyon stood for years in one of France's most famous, beautiful city squares. But vandals, many of them masked, rampaged around the building and set it on fire, too.
The city hall in Marseille, on the Mediterranean coast, which dates back to the 1600s, was also stormed and vandalized with graffiti.
On Monday, hundreds of protesters gathered outside Paris' iconic Louvre Museum in support of the school students who initiated the demonstrations more than a month ago.
What protesters say they want

The protests began as demonstrations by high school students about a month ago, with thousands taking to the streets peacefully to vent frustration over crumbling schools, overpacked classes and teacher shortages.
But it grew into a nationwide outpouring of anger over the soaring cost of living — salaries that aren't keeping up with inflation, and crumbling public services.

More than 500,000 people took to the streets on Saturday, when the unrest peaked. But as the government alludes to, there have also been opportunists —   people and groups looting, vandalizing and attacking police as they try to control the crowds.

"There are so many reasons," Kamil Alahyan, 18, told French news agency AFP. "The politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been raking in more and more wealth over the last 10 years … everyone has a different reason."

Anae, a 24-year-old student in Grenoble, told AFP she had completed her studies but now has "no income. I've got no money. I don't necessarily have a secure future. Our planet is burning. And we've got a government that's making a joke out of us!"
