title: Transcript: Rep. Mike Turner on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 18, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Mike Turner, Republican of Ohio, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Mike Turner, Republican of Ohio, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner. Good morning, and thanks for being here in person. A lot to get to with you, but let's start on politics. Ohio has been reliably Republican, but you've got a competitive gubernatorial race and Senate race in Minnesota, in Iowa, in Michigan, and in Maine. Republicans have been positioning themselves as independent of the president on some issues. Take a listen.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]
MICHELLE TAFOYA: When Trump is right, I'll work with him. When he's wrong, I'll stand up for Minnesota.
ASHLEY HINSON: We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it.
MIKE ROGERS: Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now.
SEN. SUSAN COLLINS: I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: I know you've been endorsed by President Trump. You did appear at a rally with him, but do you feel it would help to create some distance, like they did?

REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, as you know, I don't run with the president. I don't run from the president. It's one of the reasons why you have me on this show because of the fact that- that I have my- my own agenda, and I think what's important, as your pollster has- has indicated, he's in- he's talking of- of trends. What's most important, as he ended his presentation, as Anthony said, this is about who gets out to vote, and everybody needs to get out and vote. You know, Margaret, my very first race, I won by 244 votes out of 44,000. It's really, really important as to who gets out and votes. So, my message would be to everyone, is to get out and vote. And also, when they go to the polls, they need to make certain that they vote in every race. It's amazing the number of drop-offs that people have as they go down the ballot. People need to vote in every race, and they need to get out and vote.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But clearly, those candidates felt they needed to say that. Fox had a poll this week showing six in 10 respondents were extremely concerned about government corruption. AP had one that said six in 10 adults believe Trump is illegally profiting from the presidency or at least doing something unethical. Your local paper, the Columbus Dispatch, wrote it could not endorse the Republican Senate candidate because of the "abject failure," this is a quote- "of Republicans in Congress to stop visible corruption and abuse of power by the Trump administration." You referred to Republicans as almost entirely spineless. How do you counter those perceptions? Do you feel you need to?
REP. TURNER: No, first off, that- Columbus is not my local- local paper, and- and the--
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're Dayton, but--
REP. TURNER: Right, yes, I'm- I'm- I'm Dayton--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --but it is still talking about the Senate race and talking about the perception that Congress has not pushed back on the president.

REP. TURNER: Right. Well, I think- I think Congress has pushed back, and certainly I have pushed back. And in- in my community, I'm seen as part of the integral economic development team- the local economic development team of my community. And the- the aspect of what people are doing or are not doing with respect to this administration is, I think an individual candidate's issue, and people vote for individual candidates. They don't vote for a team. They don't vote for- for a slate, and- and I think that's why individual candidates are talking about their individual records as- as I do. People look in my community, they see me as a job creator. They see me as someone- if- Margaret, if you came into my community and we took a drive along my community, and I showed you my accomplishments, you'd see things at, you know, my local base where we've doubled the jobs both inside and outside the fence, the VA where we've created senior housing, and like- my opponent wouldn't be able to get out of the driveway of her house. Those are the kind of things that people look to for the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But the president is central here. The president is telling people, vote like he is on the ballot.
REP. TURNER: Well, that's- that's- that's the president. That's not the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He thinks he's doing candidates like you, some- some good when he says things like that and comes out and rallies in Ohio.

REP. TURNER: Well, he came to a rally in my community, as the- as he said in the community when he was there campaigning for the top of the ticket. When he came to my community, he actually came when he was speaking of my record that he was committing to sign legislation to restore the Delphi salary pensioners who had their pensions taken away under the Obama administration.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, that hasn't happened yet.

REP. TURNER: He committed to sign that legislation to restore those pensions that I had been working on for over a decade. That makes over 5,000 people in my community restore their pensions. I've been working on paychecks and pensions, and that's the type of thing that makes a difference in my community.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well- well, let's talk about some of those things, which, because that hasn't passed yet, some of those things could get gunked up in the lame-duck because of what I'm about to ask you about and that is--
[CROSSTALK]
REP. TURNER: --that the president has committed to sign.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, if it can get to his desk. I want to ask you about Elon Musk's SpaceX technology, Starlink. Ukraine uses it for communication, they use it to control their drones. Secretary Rubio said no one at the White House ordered it to be slowed down this week so that drones couldn't use it. But effectively, that was the outcome. Here is how Secretary Rubio explained it last night.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]

SEC. MARCO RUBIO: We had nothing to do with it. I don't- I don't- the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened. But my understanding is it's been restored.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is "it sort of happened" sufficient explanation for you and others on the Armed Services Committee?

REP. TURNER: Absolutely not. I mean, this is something where there needs to be an investigation. There needs to be a congressional investigation. I mean, this is one of those things where- where we see that- that policies occur where sometimes there's- there's breaks in- in weapon systems that are supposed to be sent to Ukraine that doesn't happen, where monies are- are- don't arrive, where intelligence gets broken, where then later that we have- find, you know, unnamed people in the Pentagon perhaps break it. There needs to be an investigation. We need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things. And even today, you know, the Institute for the Study of War reports today--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
REP. TURNER: --and Zelenskyy reports that, you know, perhaps it's spotty. There are areas where that it's restored--
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's been straddled back.
REP. TURNER: --and there are areas where perhaps it is not. People's lives are at risk, and this- this is within Ukraine. This is areas where they're trying to defend themselves.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
REP. TURNER: This is essential to the United States support of Ukraine in defending real aggressive attacks by Russia within Ukraine, and this needs to be restored.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But Elon Musk, who owns this company, and Starlink is a commercial enterprise. Elon Musk publicly opposes President Zelenskyy. He posted on social media he doesn't want Starlink used for offensive military action. I know Secretary Rubio said it had been restored, but--
REP. TURNER: But this is within Ukraine. This is defending Ukraine against aggression within Ukraine.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Exactly, but it is just- they're all pointing at each other, saying no, DOD is in charge. No, Elon Musk's in charge. I don't know, it just sort of happened.
REP. TURNER: But the policy decision has been made that- that Starshield will be utilized for the purposes of Ukraine defending itself against Russian aggression--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Starshield.
REP. TURNER: Starshield.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which is the U.S. military contract.

REP. TURNER: Within its territory, and it has, by everybody's reports, been broken in- in its ability to be able to be accessed. And there should be an investigation as to why, and it should be completely restored.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The president- there were a series of actions, not just the diesel waivers. These actions in regard to Ukraine's ability to defend itself, and then you saw him waive or at least pause for a period of time the sanctions that you voted should be in place under the Lindsey Graham bill. They were supposed to punish buyers of Russian oil. He said, "Don't implement them."
REP. TURNER: Well, there's- there's two--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Will you encourage him to reverse course?
REP. TURNER: Okay, there's two separate things here. The- the sanctions under the Lindsey Graham bill this weekend there was a deadline for the president--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Today.

REP. TURNER: --to either waive or to impose sanctions upon- there are three categories: the individuals in the Russian government, Russia itself, and individuals doing business, governments doing business with Russia.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. TURNER: The president had those three categories- impose them, or waive them, or waive them in part. I would encourage the president to do so. That bill being in place is- and the president has signed it- is important. It's a legacy of Lindsey Graham. It's important that's in place. The president now has that authority. He has waived it. He has in that waiver that he signed, a continuing opportunity to now- and the- Secretary Rubio has confirmed, to continue daily--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
REP. TURNER: --the opportunity to waive in part or not waive in part. In other words, to- to institute those sanctions, I would encourage him to do so.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Does that mean you would withhold your vote for some of his agenda items in the lame-duck, as we've had other representatives, Don Bacon, Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike McCaul* suggest they would do?

REP. TURNER: Well, I think it depends as we go through the- this- this process of discussion as to what this- I don't- I don't think there's any, you know, brinksmanship that needs to have to occur on this. I think there are discussions need to occur on these- these waivers. Some of those waivers should not be absolute because, for example, you know, the- the biggest offender of this, and Zelenskyy needs to come to the table loudly. The EU is the fourth largest offender of purchasing--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REP. TURNER: --energy from Russia, and the- France is one of them. A quarter of a billion dollars, they purchased of energy from--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REP. TURNER: --Russia, just in August.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, we have to leave it there. Congressman, thank you.
REP. TURNER: Thank you.
MARGARET BRENNAN:  We'll be right back, one minute. Stay with us.

*Editor's Note: McCaul clarified to CBS News after the interview that the president's actions on Ukraine are impacting Republicans' decisions, but he has not made a decision to withhold his vote on the president's agenda items during the lame-duck after the November midterms in protest.

title: Japan launches ambitious robotic mission to Martian moon Phobos
summary: Soil samples collected by the MMX probe will shed light on the mysterious origin of the red planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos.
story: Japan launched an ambitious $350 million mission to Mars on Monday to study the red planet's two moons in unprecedented detail, dropping a small rover on the largest — Phobos — before the mothership touches down to robotically collect soil samples for return to Earth.

The primary goal of the Martian Moons Exploration mission, or MMX, is to determine whether Phobos and the smaller moon Deimos were created by the impact of a large body early in the solar system's history or whether the two are asteroids that once passed close enough to Mars to be captured by the red planet's gravity.

The Martian moons are much smaller than Earth's, with Phobos measuring just 17 miles across at its widest while Deimos is less than half that size. Both are irregularly shaped and similar in appearance to asteroids. But size and shape alone are not enough to answer the question of their origin.

"One of the most intriguing questions about Phobos and Deimos is simply why these two little moons are there in the first place," said Thomas Statler, who helped oversee development of two NASA instruments aboard the MMX spacecraft.

"In some ways, they resemble asteroids from the outer part of the asteroid belt ... but there (are) other lines of evidence pointing to these moons being remnants of a giant impact early in Mars' history."
The collected samples, expected to be returned to Earth in 2031, should answer that question one way or the other.

"By going to the Martian moons, studying them up close and bringing samples back to Earth, we'll be able to determine whether Phobos material is more consistent with an asteroid composition or with debris created by a collision involving Mars," Statler said.

The mission got underway at 3:41 p.m. EDT (4:41 a.m. Japan time) with the sky-lighting launch of a Japanese H3 rocket from the picturesque Tanegashima Space Center operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA.

Four solid-propellant strap-on boosters and two hydrogen-fueled first stage engines powered the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before the H3's second stage took over to continue the climb to space.
One hour and 11 minutes after liftoff, following two firings of the upper stage engine, the 9,900-pound MMX probe was released to fly on its own.
If all goes well, the spacecraft will brake into orbit around the red planet in September 2027 on a trajectory that will allow it to circle the planet in lockstep with Phobos.

MMX will spend three years in that orbit, training a battery of instruments on Phobos and its surrounding environment, studying its chemical and mineral composition, assessing its possible use as a staging base for future astronauts and dropping a small rover, supplied by the German and French space agencies, onto the moon's surface in early 2029.

The 55-pound rover is not equipped with braking rockets or anything else to slow its descent. Given the gravity of Phobos is just 1/1,000th as strong as Earth's, the rover is expected to bounce down on the surface, tumbling gently to a stop.

It is designed to right itself regardless of how it ends up after coming to rest and then to begin its surface exploration. It is equipped with cameras for navigation and to study the soil as it rolls about, an instrument to fire laser beams into the ground to determine what minerals might be present and another that will monitor soil temperatures.

About a year after the rover's landing, in the 2030 timeframe, the MMX spacecraft itself will touch down on Phobos once and possibly twice to collect a tiny amount of soil using two devices, one built by JAXA and the other supplied by NASA.
The official mission requirement is to capture at least 10 grams, or less than half an ounce, of material. Depending on the nature of the soil, however, the sample size could be larger.

The MMX then will lift off and, after wrapping up remote observations of Deimos, head back to Earth, putting the Phobos samples into an aerodynamic, heat-resistant capsule that will re-enter the atmosphere over Australia, where a recovery team will be standing by.
The samples will be studied by an international team of researchers.
"There's a lot of adrenaline, a lot of excitement, and a lot of wow," said Statler. "MMX will be the first spacecraft ever to return to Earth from the Mars system. That says a lot."

But "the most exciting thing of all," he said, "will be watching the sample return capsule re-enter Earth's atmosphere and opening that capsule and seeing those materials for the first time. There is absolutely no lack of excitement and adrenaline on this mission."

title: Starvation cult leader found guilty of murder of 190 children
summary: Paul Mackenzie is alleged to have incited his acolytes to starve to death in order to "meet Jesus."
story: A self-proclaimed Kenyan preacher and his associates were found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in an infamous starvation cult by a Mombasa court on Monday.
"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," the judge said.
Hundreds of bodies have been discovered since 2023 at the cult base inland from the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi, in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."
Paul Mackenzie is alleged to have incited his acolytes to starve to death in order to "meet Jesus."
Mackenzie and his associates pleaded not guilty to 191 counts of murder in 2024. He has also denied charges of manslaughter and terrorism in separate cases.

The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions welcomed the "momentous" verdict, with director Renson Ingonga telling reporters: "Getting a conviction of such counts...is not something that comes that easily."
In the three years since the grisly discovery, more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400.
Mackenzie looked impassive as he arrived at Mombasa Law Courts on Monday with 29 other accused, who descended from a barred-window bus handcuffed in pairs.
Relatives of the victims were also in court, many making their way to Mombasa from rural communities along the coast.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, in Shakahola.
"This day, to me, is a very, very important day," he told AFP before the session started.
"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he said, expressing anger over the initial government inaction.
There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.

The prosecution alleges that Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women and then men.
The children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said, based on postmortems and police reports.
Mackenzie's lawyers said the case was "largely founded on circumstantial evidence, hearsay accounts and inconclusive forensic findings."
Case exposed
Mackenzie was arrested in April 2023, after a rights group tipped off authorities and some followers were rescued.
The subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of shallow graves, with a soaring death toll that required a pause in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.
The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights said in 2024 that the death toll was 429. Some victims are still unidentified.
In January, Mackenzie was charged over another 52 bodies found at a nearby village.
The self-styled pastor has a history of extremism and evaded law enforcement for years.
He established the Good News International Church in 2003, and set up branches in Nairobi and along Kenya's coast that attracted thousands of devotees, though he claimed it closed in 2019.

Followers have told their families and officials they believed Mackenzie when he preached that starvation was the path to salvation. He allegedly split members into smaller groups assigned biblical names. It's believed these smaller groups died together and were buried together in mass graves.
State pathologists have said many of the exhumed victims died of starvation, but some showed signs of strangulation.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2017 over charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.

Investigators have said Mackenzie was a taxi driver in the early 2000s, before he created the Good News International Ministry. Locals have said he quickly drew followers with fiery sermons at his church on the coast in Malindi, then from across Kenya with his online presence.

Several surviving members of the group have told family members that what he preached would often come true, citing as an example his prediction that "a great virus" would come, just before COVID-19 hit the country. As people struggled during the pandemic, financially and medically, Mackenzie preached about leaving the difficulties of life behind and "turning to salvation."

Sarah  Carter

title: Europe's surging populist right reshapes establishment politics
summary: A wave of anti-immigration populism is bringing new parties to the fore in many European nations, at the expense of the entrenched center-right.
story: London — From the upper floors of Millbank Tower, a skyscraper overlooking the River Thames in London, the U.K. Houses of Parliament are just a few hundred yards away. For decades, the building housed the headquarters of Britain's Conservative Party, one of the world's oldest political parties.

Today, it is home to Reform UK, the right-wing populist party led by Nigel Farage that is hoping to — and by some measures may already have —   replace the Conservatives as the dominant force on the British right.

The change of occupants reflects a wider political upheaval sweeping some of Europe's biggest democracies. In France, Marine Le Pen's right-wing National Rally has overtaken much of the traditional right ahead of the next year's presidential election.

In Germany, the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has made historic electoral gains, challenging the center-right Christian Democrats. There are similar trends in Italy, Spain, Sweden and other corners of the continent.

While the histories and ambitions of the movements in all these countries differ, collectively, their rise is forcing many of Europe's established conservative parties to make a choice: either adopt some of the populist right's increasingly hard-line positions on immigration and national identity and cooperate with them, or risk losing voters to them altogether.

"The larger issue is the general great realignment of politics towards identity and nationalism being the main axis of debate, not the economy," Steve Baker, a former British Conservative government minister, told CBS News.

The European Commission forecasts EU economic growth of just 1.1% in 2026, down from 1.5% in 2025. Baker, who pointed to President Trump's election in the United States as evidence of the same wider trend, believes the shift reflects a deeper frustration with political and economic institutions.
"The world does not work for far too many people, and almost no one is able to explain why," he said. "In that environment ... someone gets the blame."
Increasingly, he warned, that blame is being directed at ethnic and cultural minorities.
Britain's battle for the right
In Britain, the Conservative Party is fighting for its political survival after its 14-year hold on power was brought to an end with a crushing electoral defeat in 2024.

Reform UK, led by Farage, has capitalized on and encouraged anger over immigration, accusing successive Conservative governments of breaking promises to reduce immigrant arrivals as net migration reached a record of nearly a million in the party's final years in power. A September poll found that 44% of Britons considered immigration one of the most important issues facing the nation.

But the battle for Britain's political right is increasingly about more than immigration numbers. It has become a debate over British identity, ethnicity and who can call themselves English, with research finding support for ethnicity-based definitions of citizenship increasing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, whose parents are Nigerian, has challenged those on the right who seek to define Englishness through ancestry alone, after London-born senior Reform UK politician Suella Braverman —   who is of Indian descent —   said she does not consider herself English, because "Englishness is an ethnicity."

"I don't want to live in a country run by people who ... debate whether my mixed-race children are English," Badenoch said at the Conservative Party conference in October. "We must not let these people take us backwards."

Baker, who represented the Wycombe constituency in southeast England as Conservative Member of Parliament, told CBS News that voter concerns about immigration and demographic change cannot simply be dismissed.

He said in some local areas of his constituency, "the minority white population remaining will often express discontent that the area in which they live now looks radically different to when they moved in, and people do object to that," he said. Census data does support his assertion that in some local areas of Wycombe, white residents have become minorities, though not in the constituency as a whole.
Baker added that he opposes the turn to ethnicity in Britain's current political debates.
"None of us were talking about ethno-nationalism a few years ago," he said. "I recoil in absolute horror to see this conversation going mainstream."
After polling at around 28% in May, Reform U.K.'s support has recently fallen to 22% in some surveys as the party deals with internal controversies and financial scandals.
Farage and Reform are also facing pressure from parties further to the right.

Restore Britain, led by former Reform lawmaker Rupert Lowe and publicly backed by billionaire Elon Musk, is targeting voters who believe Farage's party isn't pushing hard enough on immigration, Islam and national identity.
One poll put Restore's support as high as 9%, suggesting the battle for Britain's conservative hearts and minds is far from settled.
Germany's political firewall under pressure

In Germany, the direction of right wing political movements is especially fraught given its history as the birthplace of the Nazi party. Since World War II, all of Germany's established parties have maintained what's become known as a political firewall against far-right extremists, refusing to enter governing coalitions with any party associated with nationalist, anti-democratic rhetoric or with links to extremist movements.

That firewall, or brandmauer in German, has stood against the AfD, which has been designated an extremist group by some regional authorities due to the associations and rhetoric of figures within the party.

The AfD openly uses the term and espouses "remigration," a notion anti-hate groups say has been employed by extreme right-wing activists to advocate the expulsion of all immigrants and, in some cases, non-white European citizens.

The party insists its own definition is different, describing remigration as "all measures and incentives for the lawful and legally compliant return of foreigners who are required to leave the country to their homeland."

The AfD explicitly rejects the removal of German citizens on the basis of their ancestry, stating "all Germans are part of our nation, regardless of origin, ancestry, worldview, or religious affiliation.".
But German security authorities have documented links between AfD figures and extremist activists who advocate for a broader, ethnicity-defined concept of remigration.
The AfD's recent gains in local and regional elections is putting the firewall under pressure.

In September, the AfD won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its support from the previous election. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which had previously led the state government, finished a distant second with 17.2% of the vote.

The AfD has built its strongest base in eastern Germany, seizing on lingering resentment over the unification of the country's Cold War-era East and West, economic inequality and a widespread distrust of political institutions. But its support now extends well beyond those traditional strongholds.

The AfD's rise has also been fueled by dissatisfaction with Germany's handling of the 2015–2016 European migration crisis. The country, under former Chancellor Angela Merkel and amid broad sympathy for people being displaced by Syria's civil war, welcomed about 890,000 asylum seekers in 2015 alone, more than any other European nation.
A decade later, in the 2025 federal election, the AfD won approximately 32% of the vote in eastern states and 18% in western Germany, becoming the country's second-largest party nationally.

AfD politician Tomasz Froelich told CBS News the party has attracted voters from across the political spectrum, especially "working-class voters, skilled workers in industrial occupations who fear for their economic future, and small business owners who are not financially secure."
Froelich predicted the major parties that have led Germany for decades would eventually fail to maintain the firewall keeping his own out of power.
"If the AfD continues to rise towards 35% nationally ... and comes to represent more than one third of voters, this approach will sooner or later become impossible to sustain," he said.

While electoral popularity alone may not compel other parties to cooperate with a movement they consider a threat to Germany's constitutional order, the AfD argues it has already forced its mainstream rivals to change their own policies.

"Calls for rigorous border controls, a cap on migration or a stronger emphasis on national interests were long portrayed as politically unacceptable," Mary Khan, another AfD politician, told CBS News. "Today, many of these positions are being openly discussed even within the CDU, and far beyond."

In January 2025, Merz, then the leader of the opposition Christian Democrats and now the German chancellor, faced a major backlash after backing a parliamentary motion calling for tougher immigration controls that passed with the support of AfD lawmakers. The vote prompted nationwide protests and criticism from former chancellor Merkel. A subsequent attempt to pass an immigration bill into law failed, with 12 conservative lawmakers declining to back it.

The AfD stands out in Europe as its positions have alienated some of its potential allies on Europe's nationalist right. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has cited fundamental differences with the AfD over Russia's war on Ukraine, while France's National Rally broke with the German party in 2024 after a leading AfD candidate made remarks appearing to downplay the crimes of the Nazis' notorious SS paramilitary force.
From political outsider to presidential contender

Few European politicians illustrate the transformation of the continent's right wing more clearly than France's Marine Le Pen. An early October survey found Le Pen would likely garner between 31% and 36% of first-round votes in a national election, leading her nearest rival by at least 11 percentage points. France's next presidential election will be held in April.

For years, Le Pen has worked to distance her National Rally (RN) party, formerly the National Front, from the extremist reputation it held from the time of its inception at the hands of her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen.

His antisemitic statements made the National Front politically toxic to much of the French electorate. His daughter has changed the party's name, moderated some of its positions and sought to persuade voters it is capable of governing France. The strategy, known as dédiabolisation (de-demonization), has helped National Rally shed its political outsider skin and become one of the country's most powerful electoral forces.
It has consigned France's traditional conservative party, Les Républicains, to near irrelevance, with national support around only 9% according to recent polling.
Stéphane Azihari, a French essayist who writes for the newspaper Le Figaro, said Le Pen has succeeded by appealing to voters who feel abandoned by both the traditional right and left.

"She has simultaneously filled the void left by a right wing that's greatly disappointed voters on immigration and security, while also capturing working-class voters from the left," he told CBS News. "The primary driver of RN voting remains, of course, the fear of non-European immigration, and Muslim immigration in particular."
France has a long tradition of democratic secularism, but political debate in the country has increasingly focused on perceptions of immigration and Islam as threats.

A 2024 poll found that 77% of National Rally voters considered immigration an important factor in their voting, while research published by the Brookings Institution in 2020 found that 73% believed Islam was incompatible with French society.
Around 10% of adults in France between the ages of 18 and 59 identify as Muslim, according to official statistics, the highest proportion in western Europe.

Azihari argued that concerns about Islamist terrorism, particularly following the deadly 2015 attacks on the Charlie Hebdo newspaper and the Bataclan concert hall in Paris, have helped normalize National Rally's positions on immigration and security.
"The center's inability to effectively address security and immigration concerns explains much of the National Rally's progression," he said.

President Emmanuel Macron, who cannot seek a third consecutive term in 2027, has also backed more restrictive immigration measures during his presidency. But adopting tougher positions has not necessarily diminished the National Rally's appeal.
Across Europe, established parties face a similar dilemma: Embrace tougher positions on immigration and national identity and cooperate with populist rivals, or risk losing more voters.
According to one survey of party support across 31 European nations from earlier this year, almost a quarter of voters say they now support far-right parties.

Even if those populist parties fail to win control of governments on the continent, their influence is already being felt, and the question now is how far to the right they will pull other parties that have long rejected their legitimacy.

title: Expedition to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane comes up empty
summary: The researchers said what they had hoped was the plane was "likely a collection of large trees" that had washed away, leaving a "single Y-shaped segment."
story: A mysterious object discovered near a remote Pacific island is not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's missing plane, researchers said after an expedition to the site, dealing another setback to efforts to solve one of aviation's greatest mysteries nearly 90 years after the pilot disappeared.

"Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro confirmed that the visual anomaly first seen in satellite imagery in 2020 was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit," the researchers said. "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment," which they said is what they had initially hoped was the plane.

The researchers said the reflective surface of the anomaly, which had led them to believe it could be metal, was the result of a carbonate veneer, noting other items found nearby were "similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand."

On Oct. 14, a 17-member expedition team led by Purdue University's Steve Schultz and the Archaeological Legacy Institute's Richard Pettigrew launched an expedition to investigate a mysterious object that in aerial photos appeared to resemble possible wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane.

Severe weather kept the research team aboard their ship for three of the five days allotted for the search, while limited fuel and supplies prevented them from extending the expedition. The search area was so remote, it took the team five days at sea to reach it.

The expedition focused on a lagoon off Nikumaroro, where researchers examined the Taraia Object, an anomaly spotted by a Navy veteran in satellite imagery during the COVID pandemic. Although visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938, the object went unnoticed until 2020. Pettigrew said before reaching it that they believed it could be metal rather than a tree, but further investigation was needed to confirm its identity.

"Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," Pettigrew said Sunday. "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible. Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished."

The team had developed plans to photograph and film the lagoon and Taraia Object before using magnetometers and sonar equipment to survey the area. Researchers then planned to retrieve the object for identification. The Archaeology Channel documented the expedition through short video updates on its Heritage Broadcasting Service streaming platform.
The research team previously said in a news release that there was "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.

Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared on July 2, 1937, roughly 22,000 miles into their trip. Earhart was attempting to become the first female pilot to circle the world, and the first pilot to do so around the equator, Earth's widest point.
Recently, President Trump ordered the declassification of records related to Earhart.

Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were headed when they disappeared during their attempted flight around the world.

Pettigrew believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and survived there for some time. He points to relics dating to the 1930s and to human remains discovered on the island, which were later lost as possible evidence. However, several competing theories about the aviator's disappearance have emerged over the decades, many of which lack conclusive evidence.

Researchers have spent decades searching for Earhart's plane, hoping its discovery could shed light on her disappearance. In 2024, an expedition team captured a sonar image of what appeared to be an aircraft on the ocean floor, but the object was later identified as a rock formation.

title: U.S. lauds Israel for arresting 10 over West Bank settler attacks
summary: Israeli police say they arrested 10 people over alleged Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians and a U.S. journalist as more attacks on Palestinians are reported.
story: Tel Aviv — Israeli police announced on Monday the arrest of 10 people suspected to have taken part in recent violent attacks on Palestinians, an American photojournalist and European diplomats in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

The arrests come amid an avalanche of criticism, including from some senior U.S. officials, directed at Israel over repeated violent attacks by groups of mostly young Israeli settlers targeting Palestinians and others in the West Bank.
The announcement of the arrests came as more violence against Palestinians in the occupied territory was reported Monday.

Israeli police said officers working in conjunction with the Shin Bet domestic security and intelligence agency conducted a pre-dawn raid in the West Bank to locate individuals suspected of involvement in the violence and of violating a military commander's order declaring a closed military zone.
The arrests, dubbed Operation Olive Leaf by the police, came in the wake of multiple reported attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians as they worked on the annual olive harvest.
"Items linking the suspects to the alleged offenses were seized, and several vehicles were confiscated," the police said in a statement after the arrests.

On Friday, several Palestinians and Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine were injured when a group of masked Israeli men attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to videos, eyewitnesses and Palestinian authorities.

On Saturday, European officials and the Israeli military said a diplomatic convoy with representatives from France, Belgium and Poland was assaulted by masked individuals near the Palestinian village of Taybeh.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, in a social media post on Monday, called the arrests "a very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat Heidi Levine an unarmed journalist."
Over the weekend, Huckabee called the attack on Levine an "act of terror carried out by masked cowards."
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also condemned the attack on Levine Saturday, saying President Trump didn't want to see a crisis in the West Bank.
"We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff," Rubio said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office, in a statement on Saturday, urged people to exercise caution before drawing conclusions about the reported attacks on the European diplomats.

Netanyahu's office noted that video published online of the incident appeared to show masked individuals confronting a diplomatic vehicle and others showed a smashed car window and someone lying on the ground, but it said those images alone did "not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility."

Israel's military said the diplomatic convoy was not coordinated with the defense forces, and that such coordination would've provided more safety, but it did not deny that the convoy came under attack by settlers.

On Monday, new attacks on Palestinians by Israel settlers were reported by WAFA, the official media arm of the Palestinian Authority, which governs most Palestinians in the West Bank but has limited control over security in the occupied territory.

Two Palestinians were injured in the villages of Turmus Ayya and Deir Abu Mash'al, northwest of Ramallah, amid attempts by individuals to set homes on fire by torching vehicles in front of the buildings, WAFA reported.

On Sunday night, Israel's military said several Israeli civilians entered the Palestinian village of Wadi a-Rahim in the West Bank, sprayed graffiti and set fire to a storage shed. The military said it had begun dismantling an illegal Israeli settler outpost in the area.
Violence by Israeli settlers targeting Palestinians in the West Bank has surged in recent years.

Statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office show that it started ramping up after Netanyahu took office in 2022 at the head of Israel's most far-right-wing coalition government in modern history in late 2022.

The attacks have intensified in the wake of the war in Gaza, and amid strong support from some members of Netanyahu's cabinet for settlement expansion, and even for the West Bank to be completely annexed by Israel.

title: Trump says Zelenskyy doesn't want to end Russia's war on Ukraine
summary: As Ukraine and Russia continue trading strikes, Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war sparked by Putin's ongoing full-scale invasion.
story: President Trump said Sunday that he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," and he accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the conflict sparked four and a half years ago by Russia's full-scale invasion.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Mr. Trump criticized Zelenskyy for targeting Russian diesel refineries and said, "he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."

"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump wrote.

The comments come amid a deepening rift between Mr. Trump and Zelenskyy, with the U.S. president criticizing his Ukrainian counterpart for attacking Russian oil infrastructure — a tactic Ukrainian forces have focused on in recent months in a bid to deprive Putin's forces of both cash and fuel to continue their brutal offensive.

Mr. Trump said Sunday that he had decided to hold off on implementing new sanctions against Russia because he doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."

Mr. Trump asserted on Truth Social that "great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations," adding that, regarding the additional sanctions, "I can sign it later, or any time that I want!"
Zelenskyy earlier said that while he trusted Mr. Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a "historic mistake" for Washington.

"People want to forget what's going on. But we can't give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth," Zelenskyy said. "We can't compare me and Putin. He's aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He's a terrorist, and that's why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position."

Speaking Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions against Russia, which Mr. Trump has already done to enable Russian diesel exports, would strengthen Putin's war effort. He also said U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being "blocked for some period of time."

Asked Sunday about reports, including by CBS News, that the U.S. may have intentionally withheld early warnings from Ukraine last week of deadly Russian missile strikes, and Zelenskyy's assertion that data sharing was blocked for a period of time, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate."
"We have nothing to do with that," said Rubio.

Regarding separate but linked claims from Ukrainian officials that crucial satellite data from Elon Musk's Starlink network had been constrained last week, inhibiting Ukraine's offensive and defensive drone operations, Rubio said, "The United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored. It's back to where it was before."

Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as "next steps in diplomacy."

Ukraine and Russia continued trading strikes over the weekend. Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday it had intercepted more than 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.

At least one person was killed and five others wounded in an attack on St. Petersburg that also sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchi oil depot, according to local government authorities.
A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion but could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.

title: Falling crucifix kills priest during livestreamed Mass in Ecuador
summary: "Father, Father! Call an ambulance!" people at the church could be heard shouting just before a livestreamed broadcast cuts out.
story: A Catholic priest died Saturday when a wooden crucifix fell from a wall and crushed him against the pulpit during a livestreamed Mass in the Ecuadorian city of Guayaquil.
Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died Saturday, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil announced.
"Father, Father! Call an ambulance!" people at Our Lady of Perpetual Help church could be heard shouting just before a livestreamed broadcast cuts out.

The Mass was livestreamed on the priest's Facebook page where he has over 4,600 followers. The video shows Sánchez facing the congregation as a large crucifix hanging on a wall behind him falls onto the back of his head. He falls to the ground and does not get back up.
The graphic footage of the accident went viral Sunday on social media and was widely carried by news outlets.
In a social media post, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil said Sánchez "has departed to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory."
The archdiocese mourned the death of the priest in a statement and expressed its "solidarity, affection and love" for his family and friends.
Local authorities have not commented on the incident.
Sánchez belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic religious order founded in 1732 with a presence in 80 countries.

The Associated  Press
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine still can't intercept drones due to Starlink issues, Zelenskyy says
summary: The Ukrainian president said Starlink issues are hampering his country's defensive efforts against Russian drones.
story: Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump.

"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."

Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory.

"Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems."

"Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, when asked about the situation Saturday on the tarmac of Joint Base Andrews, said, "Starshield is a defense product, a military product, and as I said … that is something that we have,  the military, United States military, uses. It's not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that's under conversation. It's under discussion right now about how they would want to use it."

Pushed on whether the U.S. government was responsible for the service outage in Ukraine, Rubio responded, "No," and alleged that Ukraine's military has never had access to Starshield, but has only been using Starlink.

"I don't know what Zelenskyy said, I'm not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate," Rubio said. "We had nothing to do with that. I don't, the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored, it's back to what it was before."

Rubio went on: "Starshield is a contract with the U.S. military, it has nothing to do with Ukraine. I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield, they do not have Starshield now. They've asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment. Those are two different products."

Denys Sienik, the chargé d'affaires of Ukraine to the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or SpaceX regarding its inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."
Sienik said "based on the data currently available to us, we cannot confirm that these capabilities have been fully restored."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either.

"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."

Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating"

Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.

Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters.

"President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News on Saturday in response to a question about lifting the sanctions. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."

Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire.

In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.
On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted: "Time for Zelensky to go."

title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS and is now 'back at square one'
summary: Christina Applegate fought back tears discussing her MS misdiagnosis, saying the news brought confusion, depression and no relief from symptoms.
story: Christina Applegate thanked her friends and family for taking care of her, especially her daughter, who she called "the most important" person.
Christina Applegate is back at "square one" after doctors told her she does not have multiple sclerosis.
The 54-year-old actress, who was diagnosed with MS in 2021, addressed the surprising development Tuesday on her "MeSsy" podcast with Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

"This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one," Applegate said while fighting back tears. "It’s hard to say that [my doctor] came into my room, and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.’"
KATHIE LEE GIFFORD ADMITS SHE 'WANTED TO DIE' AFTER MISDIAGNOSIS AND MULTIPLE SURGERIES FOR CHRONIC PAIN
Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS. (Getty Images for Critics Choice Association)
"What does that moment feel like?" Sigler asked.
"I was, like, not happy at all," Applegate admitted. "Everybody else was so happy … You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I’m better."
"I haven’t gotten better, Jamie!" she continued. "If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways. So I’m back at square one that I don’t know what’s going on with me."
Applegate said her doctors are now working to determine what has caused her ongoing health problems and why she was diagnosed with MS in the first place.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Applegate was initially diagnosed with MS in 2021. (John Shearer)
"There’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS," she said. "So this is not a rare occurrence. It’s clear now that they’re finding something different. Something else is going on."
The actress also admitted that the news left her feeling confused and as if she had "let everybody down."
MICHAEL J. FOX SAYS GOING PUBLIC WITH PARKINSON'S WAS 'HELL' ON WIFE TRACY POLLAN

"It’s this weird feeling of like … I became this — you and I, the poster children for MS," Applegate told Sigler. "And all that I did, everything I was doing. I had a reason. I had a f---ing reason as to why my day sucked every day."
"And now I don’t have a reason, and it’s very unnerving, and it’s really confusing for me," she added.
Applegate also opened up about the toll her chronic pain and mobility issues have taken on her mental health and career.

"I’ve gone through a great depression because of it," she said through tears. "But you know, I lost everything. I lost my job. I lost — sorry. What do you say to someone who’s been living with this for six years? God, I’m so sorry, I get really emotional because it stopped my life."
The actress has been open about her health struggles over the past five years. (Valerie Macon)
Applegate clarified that the change in her diagnosis has not changed her physical condition.

"I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office," she said. "I can’t walk from the car to the room. I’m still in this. Nothing magical happened when she said, ‘You don’t have MS.’ Nothing magical happened."
Doctor Marwa Kaisey, associate professor with the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center department of neurology, said that MS misdiagnoses are actually "fairly common."

"We don’t have one single test for MS. It’s not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says, ‘Yes. You have it.’ ‘No. You don’t.’ It’s a list of criteria," Dr. Kaisey said on the podcast. "Almost one in five of these people who’d been told they had MS, some for decades, didn’t actually have it. And a majority of them were on medication to treat their MS," she added.
Applegate first revealed her MS diagnosis on X in 2021.

"Hi friends. A few months ago I was diagnosed with MS," she wrote at the time. "It’s been a strange journey. But I have been so supported by people that I know who also have this condition."
"It’s been a tough road," she continued. "But as we all know, the road keeps going. Unless some a--hole blocks it."
Christina Applegate said her health issues have been hard on daughter Sadie Grace LeNoble. (Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images)
The actress has been candid about how her health struggles have affected her life, including her ability to parent her 15-year-old daughter, Sadie, whom she shares with husband Martyn LeNoble.

"I want to take her [to school and activities]; it’s my favorite thing to do," Applegate previously told People. "It’s the only time we have together by ourselves. I tell myself, ‘Just get her there safely and get home so you can get back into bed.’ And that’s what I do."

Applegate said her physical limitations have also made her more determined to be honest about her life.
Christina Applegate rose to fame on "Married… With Children." (Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images; John Shearer/Getty Images)
"My life isn’t wrapped up with a bow," she said. "People’s lives, sorry for lack of a better term, f---ing suck sometimes. So I’m being as honest and raw as I possibly can."
During a previous episode of her "MeSsy" podcast, Applegate discussed how her health struggles have affected Sadie.
"She didn’t know this. It was like losing the mom she had to this f---ing thing," Applegate said. "And the more she’s gotten older now, I think the more it’s hurting her."
"Mommy can’t do all the things that she used to be able to do, and I see it in her eyes," she added. "I see it."

title: Larry David saw OJ Simpson the day of Nicole Brown Simpson's 1994 murder: book
summary: Larry David's authorized biography reveals he crossed paths with O.J. Simpson on the day Nicole Brown Simpson was killed.
story: 'Outnumbered' reacts to a New York Times report detailing allegations that a longtime criminal informant may have helped O.J. Simpson attempt to cover up the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
Larry David eerily crossed paths with O.J. Simpson on the day Nicole Brown Simpson was brutally murdered in 1994.

David, the co-creator of "Seinfeld" and creator/star of "Curb Your Enthusiasm," discussed the chilling moment in his newly released authorized biography, "Emperor Of Nothing: The Making of Larry David." The book was written by Blake J. Harris.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
The cover of Larry David's authorized biography "Emperor of Nothing." (Dey Street Books)

On the morning of June 12, 1994, David was eating breakfast at the exclusive Riviera Country Club in Los Angeles alongside his then-wife Laurie, newborn daughter Cazzie and fellow comedy writer Alan Zweibel. Zweibel's wife, Robin, was also at the table.
FORMER OJ SIMPSON ATTORNEY, LONGTIME FRIEND BOTH SUPPORT POSSIBILITY OF ACCOMPLICE IN 1994 MURDERS
Zweibel said that he will never forget that breakfast with Larry, or the date, "because that night O.J. Simpson killed Nicole [Brown Simpson] and Ron Goldman."
"[We] saw him in the dining room the day of the murder!" David said.
O.J. Simpson was accused of murdering his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, in 1994. He was acquitted in 1995. (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)
In the biography, Zweibel explained that he not only saw Simpson, but interacted with him twice that same day.
"We were having breakfast and all of a sudden I hear somebody say my name: ‘Zwa-bell.’ I turn around. It’s O.J. Simpson," Zweibel said.
"[We] saw him in the dining room the day of the murder!" David said.
He went on to explain how he knew Simpson. "I knew O.J. because I went to the University of Buffalo while he was playing for the [Buffalo] Bills," Zweibel began.

"He was like a god. And when he came to host ‘SNL’ [in 1978], I remember saying to Lorne, ‘This is my hero.’ So I spent a lot of time with O.J. that week. I wrote a lot for that show. And then in subsequent years, we had a mutual friend on Rockingham, and we all had kids around the same age, so we’d see each other at birthday parties and s--- like that," he continued.
Writer and producer Alan Zweibel recalled seeing Simpson twice the day Nicole was murdered. (WireImage)
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Zweibel said that he also saw Simpson later that afternoon at his daughter's middle school dance recital.
"Our daughters were [both performing]. And on our way out, I again hear a familiar voice," he said.
"S---," O.J. said to Zweibel. "Twice in the same day!"
"Hey, Juice!" Zweibel replied.
O.J. Simpson sits in Superior Court in Los Angeles in 1994 during an open court session. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Zweibel explained in the biography that he called Simpson by his famous nickname and told him that he had nothing new to share since he had already seen him earlier that day.
O.J. SIMPSON JOKES ABOUT ‘BLOODY BRONCO,’ BOASTS OF ITS ‘GREAT ESCAPABILITY’ IN DISTURBING RESURFACED VIDEO
"Though, of course, [in retrospect] what I should have said was ‘Stay home tonight! Order in! Don’t go out!'" he said.
Simpson and Nicole married in 1985 and had two children, Sydney and Justin. They separated in 1992, and Brown filed for divorce after seven years of marriage.
Ron Goldman was murdered with O.J. Simpson's ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson on June 12, 1994. (Lee Celano/WireImage)
In 1994, Brown and Goldman, her friend, were killed. Simpson was tried for their murders and acquitted in October 1995.

On Oct. 18, The New York Times reported that a mob-linked drug trafficker with ties to Simpson secretly became a jailhouse snitch and claimed to have information about efforts to dispose of evidence, potentially including a murder weapon that was never recovered.

The outlet said that Joseph Ippolito, a former cigarette boat racer, drug trafficker and restaurateur who knew Simpson, had told federal prosecutors he had information on the murder weapon. One has never been recovered.
Larry David recalled seeing O.J. Simpson at the Riviera Country Club in Los Angeles the day Nicole and Ron were murdered. (Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Elsewhere in David's biography, he discussed the famous decades before "Seinfeld" when he was a NYC comedian. David was infamous among NYC comedians for walking offstage mid-set, refusing to perform if someone looked at their watch, yelling at paying crowds and needing bouncers to protect him from a "mountain" of a heckler he almost fought.
WATCH: OJ Simpson may have had mob accomplice, new report says

"I didn't react well to adversity, so I would just walk off," David said. "I was young. I had a bad temper. And my stuff wasn't very commercial. I couldn't really give [the audience] what they wanted. [Before each set] there was a better chance that I'd bomb than do well. And I just couldn't handle being terrible."

He continued, "Basically, if the audience didn't like me, I didn't see the need for me to continue torturing them, or them to torture me. So, I'd just leave. I guess the best way to describe me onstage was 'unprofessional.'"
David discussed his run-ins with hecklers and wrote that he was always smart about the fights he would have with audience members.
Larry David rose to fame as a comedian in New York City in the 1970s. (Getty Images)

"I did have some fights with the audience, [but] they were really more arguments—I'd say something to them and then they'd say something back. I was never stupid about it, though. I always made sure I had the bouncers behind me any time I said anything," he said.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Before his career took off, David shared in his biography that he was voted "Least Likely to Accomplish Anything" by his peers in high school. He had a long list of bizarre pre-fame jobs — from carrying a bag of irregular bras down Broadway to driving a half-blind woman in a limo — all while violently rejecting his mother’s desperate pleas for him to become a postal worker.
"She wanted me to be a mailman. She wanted me to work for the post office. She was always begging me to take the civil service test," David said of his mother's pleas.
Larry David's mother wanted him to be a postal service worker. (Araya Doheny/Getty Images for HBO)
"Just take the test!! Take the test! What do you have to lose?" he recalled her saying to him.
But the comedian had a very logical reason why he didn't pursue postal work as his profession.

"I think I could have done the 'rain' and the 'snow.' But the hail would have done me in, you know? I'm not gonna be delivering in hail," David said. "I would have gone to the supervisor, 'I'm sorry, I can't deliver in hail. I know you got the big motto up there. But I'm not doing hail!'"
"Emperor Of Nothing: The Making of Larry David" releases on Oct. 20.
