title: Your phone may reveal doctor, church and pharmacy visits
summary: Your phone's location data can expose visits to doctors, pharmacies and places of worship. The FTC took action against data brokers selling this data.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson lays out how to limit what health apps used by insurance companies can track about you, the user.

Nobody needs to follow you to know where you went this week. The phone in your pocket can already keep a record of your movements. And parts of that information can end up in the hands of other companies.

Your pharmacy. Your cardiologist. The church you attend on Sunday morning. The support group you'd rather nobody knew about. None of it necessarily comes from hacking. It can come from ordinary apps you installed yourself and the permissions you gave them. Here's how your movements can get out, who buys location data and the settings that can limit how much gets shared.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.
WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE
A smartphone can share location and other device data that may reveal sensitive details about where you go. (Tero Vesalainen/Getty Images)
Your phone can carry an advertising identifier

Smartphones can use advertising identifiers that help advertisers and developers measure ads and activity. On Apple devices, the system advertising identifier is known as the IDFA. Android devices can use Google's advertising ID.

Advertising identifiers can help connect activity across apps when apps and advertising systems are permitted to use them. Combined with location data and other signals, those identifiers can help companies build a much more detailed trail of where a device has been.

And a trail stops being anonymous fast. A device that sleeps at your address every night and turns up at a dialysis center every Tuesday and Thursday isn't much of a mystery to anyone who can connect those locations with other identifying information.
The apps hand it off, and it keeps moving

An app asks for your location. Often for a fair reason, like providing a local forecast or showing the nearest pharmacy. What many people don't realize is that apps can include advertising and analytics software from outside companies. Depending on the app, its permissions and its privacy practices, that technology may collect or receive information about your device and location. Location information can also become part of the digital advertising ecosystem, where information about a device can pass among multiple companies. Once location data leaves your phone, controlling where it goes next becomes much harder.
Federal regulators have already gone after this

This isn't a theory about what could happen. The government spent years fighting one such case in court. On May 4, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission announced a settlement that bars the data broker Kochava and its subsidiary, Collective Data Solutions, from selling, sharing or disclosing sensitive location data without people's affirmative express consent, subject to the terms of the order. The FTC alleged Kochava sold location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices that could track people to health facilities, places of worship and other sensitive locations. Kochava did not admit wrongdoing. Kochava wasn't alone. In December 2024, the FTC took action against two more location data companies, Gravy Analytics and Mobilewalla, over allegations involving the sale of sensitive location data.
Then one of them got robbed

In January 2025, Gravy Analytics was breached. A hacker posted what they claimed was 17 terabytes of stolen data on a Russian cybercrime forum. Security researchers examining a sample found more than 30 million location points, including phones at the White House, the Kremlin and military bases around the world. The data reportedly came from everyday apps, including games and dating apps. Think about what that means. A company collects movements. Regulators take action over how sensitive location data gets handled. Then criminals allegedly obtain a massive collection of data anyway.
What your movements actually tell a stranger
Strip out the technical language. A few weeks of location data can potentially reveal:

Which clinic you go to and how often you go backWhich house of worship you attend and whether you still doWhether anyone else appears to live at your addressWhat hours your home may sit emptyWhich relatives you visit and on what day
Which clinic you go to and how often you go back
Which house of worship you attend and whether you still do
Whether anyone else appears to live at your address
What hours your home may sit empty
Which relatives you visit and on what day

Those last few can turn a privacy problem into a safety concern. A device that regularly leaves a home at the same time and returns two hours later can reveal patterns about when someone may be away. Location information can also make a scam call more convincing. "I'm calling from the billing office at the clinic on Oak Street about your visit last week" is much harder to dismiss when the clinic and timing happen to be correct. And with Medicare Open Enrollment beginning October 15, a caller who seems to know your doctor or pharmacy may sound more convincing than a random scammer.
'But I never share my location'

If you've ever tapped "Allow" on a weather app, a store app or a game, you may have shared it. You might have granted that permission years ago and forgotten about it. Even apps without precise location permission may be able to estimate your general area through information such as your internet connection. You can't make yourself invisible, but you can make your movements harder to track.
What you can do about it

You can't stop your phone from knowing where you are and still use every location-based feature. But you can limit which apps get that information and reduce some of the identifiers used for advertising and tracking. None of this takes technical skill, and you can tackle one part at a time.
Start here: limit advertising tracking
Advertising identifiers aren't the only way companies can recognize a device, but limiting them can remove one tool used to connect activity for advertising purposes.
First, control whether apps can request permission to track you across other companies' apps and websites:
Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap TrackingTurn off Allow Apps to Request to Track
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Tracking
Turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track
When this setting is off, apps that request permission to track are treated as though you selected Ask App Not to Track. They cannot access Apple's system advertising identifier, known as the IDFA.
Apple also has a separate setting for ads that Apple itself delivers:
Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap Apple AdvertisingTurn off Personalized Ads
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Apple Advertising
Turn off Personalized Ads
This second setting limits how Apple personalizes the ads it delivers in services such as the App Store, Apple News and Stocks. It is separate from the app-tracking control above.
THE SCAMMER AT YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE MAY ALREADY KNOW WHO YOU ARE
Social media apps collect more data than many users realize, from clicks and contacts to location history. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
To check your advertising ID controls:
Open SettingsTap Security and privacyScroll down and tap More privacy settingsOpen AdsTap Delete advertising ID if that option appearsConfirm your choice
Open Settings
Tap Security and privacy
Scroll down and tap More privacy settings
Open Ads
Tap Delete advertising ID if that option appears
Confirm your choice
Depending on your Galaxy model and software configuration, you may also find Google's advertising controls through Settings > Google > All services > Ads.
Deleting the advertising ID prevents apps from accessing that particular Google advertising identifier. It does not prevent every form of advertising, analytics or device identification.
Open SettingsTap Security & PrivacyTap Privacy controlsTap AdsTap Delete advertising IDConfirm your choice
Open Settings
Tap Security & Privacy
Tap Privacy controls
Tap Ads
Tap Delete advertising ID
Confirm your choice

Google says deleting the advertising ID removes that identifier. Apps that try to access it receive a string of zeros instead. Apps can still have their own privacy and advertising settings, so this does not eliminate every form of tracking.
Next: tighten location permissions
Now look at which apps can see where you are and whether they really need that access.

Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap Location ServicesScroll through the list of appsTap an app you want to reviewChoose the appropriate access, such as Never, Ask Next Time or When I Share or While Using the AppIf the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Precise Location
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Location Services
Scroll through the list of apps
Tap an app you want to review
Choose the appropriate access, such as Never, Ask Next Time or When I Share or While Using the App
If the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Precise Location
You don't have to turn Location Services off completely. Doing so can interfere with useful features. Instead, focus on apps that have more access than they need.

Open SettingsTap LocationTap App permissions or App location permissionsReview the apps that can access your locationTap an app you want to changeSelect the appropriate option, such as Don't allow, Ask every time or Allow only while using the appIf the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Use precise location
Open Settings
Tap Location
Tap App permissions or App location permissions
Review the apps that can access your location
Tap an app you want to change
Select the appropriate option, such as Don't allow, Ask every time or Allow only while using the app
If the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Use precise location
Pay particular attention to apps allowed to access your location all the time. Weather, shopping and similar apps often don't need continuous background access.
YOUR HOME IS EMPTY. DO BURGLARS ALREADY KNOW?
Data broker listings often include sensitive details like your address, phone number and relatives, making removal a critical first step. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Open SettingsTap LocationTap App location permissionsReview the apps under categories such as Allowed all the time, Allowed only while in use, Ask every time or allow when I share and Not allowedTap an app you want to changeChoose the level of location access it actually needsTurn off Use precise location when an approximate location is enough
Open Settings
Tap Location
Tap App location permissions
Review the apps under categories such as Allowed all the time, Allowed only while in use, Ask every time or allow when I share and Not allowed
Tap an app you want to change
Choose the level of location access it actually needs
Turn off Use precise location when an approximate location is enough
A weather app, for example, usually doesn't need to know exactly where you're standing. Navigation is one situation where precise location makes much more sense.
Then: clear out what you're not using

Delete dormant apps. Every unused app is another set of permissions and data practices you may have forgotten about. If you haven't opened an app since last year and no longer need it, consider deleting it.
Finally: do it for your parents too

If you have older relatives, their phones are worth checking next. They may be carrying years of old app permissions, and scammers frequently target older adults. Sit down with them for 10 minutes the next time you visit. Review location permissions, advertising controls and apps they no longer use.
The half your phone settings can't reach

Changing these settings can reduce future collection and sharing, but it doesn't erase information that companies may have already collected. And here's the piece many people miss. A location trail by itself may consist largely of coordinates and device information. It becomes much more revealing when someone can connect those movements with a name, home address, phone number or relatives. Some of that identifying information can come from people-search and data broker sites that publish or sell personal details. You can run a quick free scan to see what a scammer would see if they looked you up right now. If it shows details you never agreed to publish, you'll be able to take action and get them removed.

This is where I strongly recommend using a personal data removal service. These services can automatically send removal requests to hundreds of data brokers, including people-search websites, on your behalf. They can also keep monitoring and resubmitting requests when your information reappears, which is important because data can return even after it has been removed. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

Your phone can reveal far more about your life than you may realize. Location data can expose visits to doctors, pharmacies, places of worship and other sensitive locations, especially when it gets combined with advertising identifiers and other information about you. The FTC's actions against location data brokers show this is not a hypothetical privacy problem. And the Gravy Analytics breach showed what can happen when enormous collections of location information fall into the wrong hands. I would start by reviewing which apps have access to your location and removing access from anything that doesn't truly need it. Then limit app tracking on your iPhone or delete your advertising ID on Android if that option is available. These changes won't make you invisible, but they can reduce the amount of information available to build a detailed trail of where you go. And don't forget the phones belonging to parents or older relatives. Years of forgotten app permissions can leave far more information exposed than they realize.

title: NY cop calls for police protections after protester he arrested showed up to his house, harassed his family
summary: Louis Civello says a protester he arrested tracked down his home address and showed up with a billboard truck to terrorize his family in Suffolk County.
story: NYPD officers rally at New York City Hall, urging the passage of anti-doxxing legislation to protect law enforcement from public harassment and threats. NYPD DEA Union President Scott Munro highlights the severe risks officers face, with personal information and home addresses being exposed, impacting their families' safety. Munro explains the bill aims to mirror Florida's "Halo" law, enforcing a 15-foot buffer zone.

Louis Civello, a Suffolk County police officer and president of the Suffolk County Police Benevolent Association, detailed Tuesday a prior incident in which a protester he once arrested tracked him down and waited outside his home.

"We are at an inflection point. This job is harder than ever before," Civello said during a New York State Public Safety Alliance event advocating for stronger legal protections for law enforcement officers and other local officials.
Civello recounted an incident in early 2026 in which he arrested a protester who showed up at his office for trespassing.
EXCLUSIVE: LA ICE DIRECTOR REVEALS OFFICERS FOLLOWED HOME, HARASSED AS POLICE FAIL TO HELP IN SANCTUARY CITY
"Well, that wasn't enough for this individual," Civello said.
"He then decided he was going to find my address, came to my home with a billboard truck. That's how much money these people are making. They can buy billboard trucks," Civello continued.
DAVID MARCUS: WHY THE GOVERNMENT MUST PROTECT OUR NEIGHBORHOODS FROM VIOLENT PROTESTS
Louis Civello, president of the Suffolk County Police Benevolent Association, speaks during a New York State Public Safety Alliance event on Oct. 20, 2026. (WNYW)

"Now, there's only one reason to come to my house, right? I'm a public figure. Everyone knows where my building is in Suffolk County. There are seven police precincts in Suffolk County that you can protest in front of if you so choose. You only come to my home to terrorize my family, to get at me via my wife and my children," Civello said.
He then explained that the harassment his family endured from the provocateur was far from an isolated incident, but rather the norm.
DEADLY CARTELS KNOW WHERE OUR BORDER AGENTS LIVE. WE HAVE TO PROTECT THEIR FAMILIES
He used the moment as an example of why he believed New York state needed to enact stronger protections for police officers, particularly as it pertains to privacy.
A Suffolk County, New York police vehicle sits at the scene of an investigation in Medford, N.Y., on Dec. 28, 2022. (Newsday via Getty Images)
"The laws are woefully inadequate, and they're gonna get worse if we don't work to fix them," he said.
CHURCH PROTESTERS COULD FACE TOUGHER PENALTIES UNDER RARE BIPARTISAN CRACKDOWN

"Right now, no law against it. No law against coming to my house. So if you are a rapist, and I as a police officer arrest you, you can sit at the edge of my driveway and greet my wife as she comes home. No law against it. No law is publishing my address. If you want to look me up, look any police officer up, look any of us up, it's a few clicks of a mouse," he continued.

Civello called for an anti-doxxing law, and also questioned why New York doesn't have a "Halo Law," the popular moniker assigned to a newly enacted Florida statute that protects first responders from harassment after they give an individual a warning.
PHILADELPHIA POLICE OFFICER KILLED, PARTNER SHOT 12 TIMES IN AMBUSH; SUSPECT FOUND HIDING IN TREE
"Why don't have an anti-doxxing law? Why don't we have laws that make sense?" Civello asked.
Civello was not the only law enforcement officer calling for stronger protections.
AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND
"All we're asking for is fifteen foot," Scott Munro, the president of the Detectives' Endowment Association, said. "Fifteen foot, that's all we're asking for, for safety reasons."

Munro also highlighted the broader coalition the New York State Public Safety Alliance had cobbled together in an effort to protect public employees from civilian violence. The group, Munro relayed, included 99 unions. complete with firefighters, traffic agents, sanitation enforcement agents, environmental police, bus drivers and more.
BRUCE BLAKEMAN HAMMERS DEM GOV HOCHUL, MAMDANI OVER SUBWAY SAFETY DURING NYC CAMPAIGN RIDE
Scott Munro, the president of the Detectives' Endowment Association, speaks during a New York Public Safety Alliance event on Oct. 20, 2026. (WNYW)
"You're gonna say 'why MTA?'" Munro said, "it's because they're assaulted every day, they're in their faces every day," he continued.

title: Madison Brooks rape suspect's attorney held in contempt for using her name to try to ban pink in courtroom

story: Madison Brooks was a student at LSU when she was allegedly gang raped then killed in Louisiana. title: Elderly Miss man killed with own gun in random home invasion as sheriff questions possible religious motive

story: Union County Sheriff Jimmy Edwards spoke about a deadly Mississippi home invasion in which an elderly man was killed with his own gun and explained why a possible religious motive is being questioned.
An elderly Mississippi man was fatally shot with his own gun while fighting an alleged burglar inside his home, and his wife managed to escape, authorities said.
Union County Sheriff Jimmy Edwards told Fox News Digital that Eric Basco broke into Bobby McGill’s home around 4 a.m. Thursday while McGill and his wife were asleep.
McGill, 81, struggled with Basco, who got hold of McGill’s gun and fatally shot him multiple times, Edwards said.
MISSISSIPPI TEEN ALLEGEDLY KILLED ELDERLY COUPLE IN THEIR HOME BEFORE FIRING ON DEPUTIES IN STANDOFF

Bobby McGill, right, pictured with his wife, Peggy, was fatally shot with his own gun during a home invasion in Mississippi. Peggy escaped the attack and called 911, authorities said. (Haley McGill/Facebook)

"It appears that there was a struggle that had ensued between the assailant and the homeowner. And he had a pistol that he kept in his chest there at the foot of his bed," Edwards said. "It looks like to us that what we're piecing together, is that he may have tried to get that pistol and the individual was fighting him, and they had a fight and the guy got the pistol and shot Mr. Bobby multiple times."
McGill's wife, Peggy, was able to escape the home safely and called 911 to report that someone "came into their house and attacked her husband," Edwards said.

story: Edward Brown, a Boston school security official, faces rape charges after a woman was allegedly attacked inside the Massachusetts State Police barracks on Martha's Vineyard.

A school security official at an elite Boston school has been charged with the rape of a woman visiting from Ireland after police say they found her naked on the side of the road outside the Massachusetts State Police barracks on Martha's Vineyard.
The suspect was allegedly a guest at the barracks visiting a state trooper friend from college, prosecutors said in court at his arraignment.
Edward Brown, 27, pleaded not guilty in connection with the alleged Aug. 15 attack, which prosecutors said took place inside the barracks.
He allegedly met the victim at The Ritz, a bar in Oak Bluffs — the upscale waterfront community where former President Barack Obama owns a home.

Brown had allegedly been staying at the barracks as a guest of a trooper stationed there for the summer. Prosecutors identified the trooper as Ryan Costello and said they found Brown with help from a bouncer at The Ritz, the bar where the victim allegedly met her attacker.

The bouncer didn't know his name but knew he was friends with state troopers and had a photo. Oak Bluffs police sent the picture to Costello on Aug. 29, two weeks after the alleged assault, Scalice said. He identified the man shown as Brown and said they'd been friends since college.

Once detectives identified a suspect and obtained a search warrant for Brown's Uber account, detectives also found a ride from about a half hour before the 911 calls.

"Officers interviewed the Uber driver who confirmed picking up a Black male matching the defendant's description and a very young looking White female and driving them to the State Police barracks," Scalice said. Brown is listed in jail records as 5 feet, 11 inches tall and 260 pounds. Prosecutors said that they learned from Boston police that he had been the subject of four police reports from two ex-girlfriends claiming he had been harassing them between March and August of this year.

title: UNC settles Trump admin probes into alleged campus antisemitism, race-based admissions
summary: The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill settled 18 Trump administration probes over alleged campus antisemitism and race-based admissions
story: Avi Gordon, executive director of Alums for Campus Fairness, outlines five factors shaping Jewish life on college campuses, including antisemitic incidents, university responses and anti-Israel activism.

The Trump administration reached a settlement with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill that will close 18 active federal investigations and a separate Justice Department compliance review involving alleged antisemitism and race discrimination at the university.

The voluntary settlement agreement does not require a monetary payment, and the university does not admit to any wrongdoing or liability. The deal, which will remain effective until the end of 2028, allows UNC to maintain its eligibility for federal funding.

Under the agreement, UNC will appoint an internal "Merit & Civil Rights Administrator" and establish a "Title VI Coordinator" position in its compliance office to address complaints about antisemitism and race-based discrimination.

The university said Elizabeth Hall, associate vice chancellor for university compliance, was appointed to serve in both roles in addition to her existing duties. She will be the point of contact for the Justice Department and oversee UNC's reporting obligations.
DOJ SUES UCLA OVER ALLEGED ‘JUDENREIN’ CONDITIONS DURING ANTI-ISRAEL ENCAMPMENT
The Trump administration reached a settlement with UNC that will close 18 active Education Department investigations and a separate Justice Department compliance review. (Eros Hoagland/Getty Images)

"This announcement reinforces our commitment to the fair and equal treatment of everyone at Carolina," UNC Chancellor Lee H. Roberts said in a statement. "For at least a decade, through different presidential administrations, U.S. universities have faced heightened public scrutiny across a range of issues. We’re proud to resolve those issues at Carolina in a way that protects our mission and affirms the civil rights of everyone in our community."
The agreement also requires UNC to provide mandatory antisemitism training to students, faculty and staff.

UNC will also prohibit face masks used to conceal an individual's identity, subject to certain exceptions, as part of the deal, which said student groups "shall be subject to discipline for antisemitic discriminatory conduct."

President Donald Trump and administration officials have accused pro-Palestinian protesters of antisemitism. But protesters, including some Jewish groups, contend that opposing Israel's military offensive in Gaza is not antisemitic and that support for Palestinian rights does not indicate support for extremism.

The settlement agreement also said UNC will adopt what the Justice Department called a "color-blind admissions system," barring the university from using race or altering its admissions process to change the racial composition of its student body. However, it does not prevent UNC from considering how applicants overcame adversity at a personal level, and the university may consider aspects of family background, such as poverty, if those considerations are applied consistently.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS
The agreement requires UNC to provide mandatory antisemitism training to students, faculty and staff. (Jonathan Drake/Reuters)
UNC must also maintain race-blind policies governing student benefits, scholarships, financial aid and programming, according to the agreement.
The administration has argued that policies favoring certain racial groups over others violate federal anti-discrimination law.
The deal said UNC will send any antisemitism and race discrimination complaints it has received to the DOJ and the Department of Education on a quarterly basis.

As part of the agreement, the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights will close 18 active investigations into UNC, while the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division will close a separate 18-month compliance review opened in April 2025.

"Title VI requires that all students — regardless of their ancestry or race — receive equal treatment under the law at federally funded colleges and universities," Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon said in a statement.
UNC will prohibit face masks used to conceal an individual's identity as part of the settlement. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"Higher ed policies and practices that tolerate antisemitism or favor certain racial groups over others frustrate our color-blind justice system. The Civil Rights Division commends UNC for its cooperation in meeting its obligations under federal law without the need for litigation; we hope other institutions will take note and do the same," she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In 2023, the Supreme Court rejected affirmative action at colleges as it struck down ​race-based admissions programs at UNC and Harvard.

The administration has targeted universities across the country with probes and threats to pull federal funding in response to pro-Palestinian protests on campus, diversity initiatives and transgender policies.

The federal government has also settled with some other schools, including Columbia University, which last year agreed to pay more than $200 million to resolve federal probes, and Brown University, which agreed to provide $50 million over 10 years to Rhode Island workforce-development organizations as part of its settlement.
Harvard, which has been a primary target of the administration's threats, has not yet made a deal.
Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Firefighters save historic 'Godfather' church from raging NYC warehouse blaze
summary: A fire at a vacant warehouse threatened the Staten Island church featured in "The Godfather," but the iconic building was saved from the blaze.
story: A massive four-alarm fire tore through a vacant Staten Island warehouse, injuring a firefighter but sparing a historic church featured in the 1972 classic "The Godfather." (via FDNY)
Firefighters saved a historic New York City church, notable for its appearance in "The Godfather," as a four-alarm fire tore through a nearby vacant warehouse.

More than 200 firefighters and EMS personnel rushed to Mount Loretto in Staten Island after the blaze began to spread inside an empty warehouse at around 5:45 p.m. on Saturday, FDNY Chief of Operations Kevin Woods said at a press conference that evening.
"There is heavy, heavy damage to this structure, the roof did collapse, and right now we’re maintaining a collapse zone around that structure," Woods said.
NYC 5-ALARM FIRE INJURES AT LEAST 17 FIREFIGHTERS, OTHERS AS BLAZE DAMAGES MULTIPLE APARTMENT BUILDINGS
The blaze broke out in an empty warehouse at around 5:45 p.m. on Saturday. (FDNY)

"Upon arrival, units encountered heavy fire throughout the building and immediately went into a defensive operation," Woods said. "We set up multiple large-caliber stream tower ladders and handlines."

The warehouse at 6581 Hylan Boulevard has been vacant for five years, but it is located near several other structures on the Mount Loretto grounds, including two schools and the historic Old Church of St. Joachim and St. Anne, which was famously featured in exterior shots of the baptism scene of the 1972 film "The Godfather."
FIRE BREAKS OUT AT HISTORIC BROADWAY THEATER THAT HOSTS 'THE BOOK OF MORMON' IN NEW YORK CITY
The warehouse has been vacant for five years, but it is located near several other structures on the Mount Loretto grounds. (FDNY)
The ornate Catholic Church was largely destroyed by a fire in 1973, though its façade survived, and it was rebuilt three years later.
Firefighters managed to control the blaze on Saturday and stop it from spreading to the other buildings. The fire was under control at around 8:30 p.m.
"It’s very windy out here tonight. Our units did a great job with many of the flying embers, preventing additional structures from going on fire," Woods said.
Firefighters managed to control the blaze on Saturday and stop it from spreading to the other buildings. (FDNY)

title: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro
summary: A no-bond Florida arrest warrant charges Raúl Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown.
story: Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., discusses the indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro on murder and conspiracy charges tied to the 1996 shoot-down of two civilian aircraft that killed four American pilots on ‘Sunday Night in America.’

Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder stemming from the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown, according to a warrant obtained by Fox News Digital.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose office reopened the state's investigation into Castro after he took office, secured the new arrest warrant. Gov. Ron DeSantis is expected to address the development at a press conference Monday morning.The no-bond warrant, issued in Miami-Dade County, directs law enforcement to immediately arrest Castro and says a judge found probable cause to believe he conspired to commit first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of four men aboard the unarmed civilian aircraft.The warrant marks a new front in efforts to hold Castro accountable for the Feb. 24, 1996, attack, which has long reverberated through South Florida's Cuban-American community. Castro already faces a separate federal prosecution over the shootdown.
HAVANA REGIME IN SUSPENSE AFTER CASTRO INDICTMENT WITH TRUMP PRESSURE ON, SAYS CUBAN-BORN GOP REP.
Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. (AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa)

"The investigation revealed evidence of a conspiracy to kill persons aboard BTTR aircraft. The deaths of Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña, and Armando Alejandre Jr. were the object of that conspiracy," the warrant reads.

According to the warrant, investigators allege that in 1996, the Castro regime's foreign intelligence service's plan to shoot down Brothers to the Rescue aircraft and kill their occupants traveled through the chain of command, with Raúl Castro and his brother, former Cuban leader Fidel Castro, as the final decision-makers.
Raúl and Fidel Castro attend a parade Dec. 2, 1996, in Havana, Cuba. (Sven Creutzmann/Mambo Photography/Getty Images)

"They have violated the airspace, the waters of the Republic. I made it clear that this had to be decentralized if we wanted it to do its job, and five generals were given the authority. I used to say: Try to shoot them down over our territory. But they would come into Havana and leave," Raúl Castro, now 95, said in a recorded statement months after the incident, recounting orders he gave to senior military leaders before the shootdown, according to the warrant.

"Of course, with a missile shot like that, plane against plane, what comes down is a ball of fire, and it is going to fall on top of the city. So I said: Fine, shoot them down at sea when they show up, and those who have the authority are not to consult anyone," he added in his statement.
RAÚL CASTRO MAKES FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE SINCE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION CHARGED HIM WITH MURDER

The Attorney General’s Office of Statewide Prosecution will assume jurisdiction over the multi-circuit criminal conspiracy case against Raúl Castro. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Brothers to the Rescue is a Miami-based organization that flew unarmed civilian aircraft to search for Cuban migrants stranded or lost at sea. By the mid-1990s, the group had also become involved in anti-Castro political activity, including dropping pro-democracy leaflets over Cuba.
The Cuban government has rejected the U.S. prosecution of Castro, maintaining that Brothers to the Rescue repeatedly violated Cuban airspace and that Cuba acted in defense of its sovereignty.

The warrant indicates that Florida authorities are seeking full extradition of Raúl Castro if he is arrested outside the Sunshine State, authorizing authorities to pursue his return to Florida to face the felony charge if he is arrested in another U.S. jurisdiction.
The attorney general’s Office of Statewide Prosecution will assume jurisdiction over the multi-circuit criminal conspiracy case against Castro.

title: Arizona man accused of plotting mass casualty attack on religious site with 'cookbook' tied to OKC bombing
summary: Prosecutors accused an Arizona man of keeping the Oklahoma City bombing-linked "Anarchist Cookbook" as his "Bible" while allegedly plotting a religious site attack.
story: An 18-year-old Minnesota man is accused of plotting an ISIS-inspired attack on the Mall of America after reportedly being monitored by the FBI for two years, as counterterrorism expert Ryan Mauro warns that so-called lone wolves may be connected to broader extremist networks.

An Arizona man who allegedly plotted a mass casualty attack on a Jewish or Muslim house of worship is being accused by prosecutors of possessing an infamous bomb-making manual linked to the Oklahoma City bomber.
Matthew Bjornholt, 27, faces a felony count of making a terrorist threat in connection with his alleged plot to attack a religious site.
Prosecutors in Maricopa County said Bjornholt laid out a chilling blueprint for violence that involved guns, explosives and an accomplice tasked with gunning down survivors.
During an initial court appearance on Friday, prosecutor Stephen Garcia sought a $500,000 cash bond, calling Bjornholt an imminent danger to the community, according to FOX 10.
TRANS NEO-NAZI ACCUSED OF PLOTTING HINDU TEMPLE MASSACRE, WILL RECEIVE HORMONE TREATMENT IN JAIL: OFFICIALS
Matthew Bjornholt, 27, faces a felony count of making a terrorist threat in connection with his alleged plot to attack a religious site. (Maricopa County Jail)

Bjornholt allegedly outlined detailed plans to attack a religious site, according to Garcia, who also claimed the suspect kept a copy of "The Anarchist Cookbook," a manual containing bomb-making instructions linked to Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh.
Garcia alleged that Bjornholt referred to the book as his "Bible."
The alleged plot included plans to detonate bombs before an accomplice of Bjornholt's would begin "picking off people" with firearms, according to prosecutors.
Investigators later seized three guns and ammunition from Bjornholt’s home.

Bjornholt’s defense attorney, Chad Schell, pushed back against the allegations, claiming that the charges are based solely on unverified hearsay from a disgruntled former acquaintance, according to FOX 10.
Schell told the court that the tip came from a "homeless alcoholic" whom Bjornholt had briefly let crash on his couch before kicking him out late last month.
PENNSYLVANIA MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING ISIS ATTACK ARRESTED WITH RIFLE AND 190 ROUNDS OF AMMUNITION: DOJ

Prosecutors in Maricopa County said Bjornholt laid out a chilling blueprint for violence that involved guns, explosives and an accomplice tasked with gunning down survivors. (Maricopa County Sheriff's Office)

Schell said federal authorities had already investigated the claims weeks ago. Schell said the FBI executed a search warrant at Bjornholt’s home on Sept. 29 and that Bjornholt voluntarily provided investigators with his electronic devices and passwords.

According to Schell, federal investigators found no evidence of terrorism or bomb-making materials and did not pursue federal charges before county authorities took over the case a couple of weeks later.

"There is no evidence he's a danger to the community. What is the evidence that he's a danger to the community? Some hearsay statements from some dude — that my client kicked out of his house two days before September 29," Schell told the court.

"Again, the FBI served a search warrant, got all of his electronic devices. He gave them access, gave him his passwords to those devices. They went through all of those electronic devices. They didn't see anything about terrorism. And FBI cut him loose," he continued.

Schell also argued that the three seized guns were lawfully possessed, adding that Bjornholt's civil rights were restored after completing a previous sentence on a drug charge stemming from a closed first-degree murder case. According to Schell, the murder charge against Bjornholt was dropped because of a lack of evidence.
The ammunition found inside the home, Schell said, was no more than standard magazine loads.
"The Anarchist Cookbook," a manual containing bomb-making instructions that has been linked to Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office and FBI Phoenix for comment.

Despite prosecutors citing Bjornholt's criminal history in arguing for a larger bond, the judge said the state's preliminary evidence relied heavily on hearsay and set Bjornholt's bond at $100,000, according to FOX 10.
The judge nevertheless found enough probable cause to move the case forward.
It remains unclear whether specific houses of worship were targeted in the alleged plot or whether there was a specific accomplice.
Bjornholt is scheduled to return to court on Oct. 22 for a status conference and then later for a preliminary hearing on Oct. 26.

Ten people were taken to Ascension Via Christi and Wesley Medical Center with injuries police described Sunday as noncritical. The injured children included a 5-year-old girl, a 5-year-old boy, two 8-year-old boys and a 9-year-old girl.
The five injured adults ranged in age from 28 to 68. An additional woman, 61, was hospitalized for medical complications unrelated to traumatic injuries, bringing the total number transported to 11.
Sporting Wichita Academy said the tragedy had shaken a soccer community built around families and teammates, thanking first responders, medical workers and bystanders who stepped in to help.

"Soccer is more than a game. It is a community. It is families in the stands, teammates standing beside one another, and people who come together through a shared love of the game," the academy wrote on Facebook. "Today, that community is hurting, and we must lean on one another more than ever."
Two people, including a 6-year-old boy, were killed after a pickup truck drove through a youth soccer game at the Striker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (REUTERS)
As investigators search for answers, a restaurant is stepping in to help grieving families and those with loved ones in the hospital.
Meddys pledged to donate 20% of all revenue from its Wichita and Salina locations from Oct. 18 through Oct. 24 to families affected by the tragedy.
The business also offered free meals to the immediate families of those injured for as long as their loved ones remain hospitalized.
"With so much to carry right now, figuring out your next meal should not have to be one more worry," Meddys wrote on Facebook.

The restaurant partnered with local nonprofit Kingdom Athletics Mission to receive and distribute donations to the affected McPherson families after people outside the area asked how they could help. Meddys said the nonprofit would manage both GoFundMe donations and the business’ contributions.
"Wichita is our home. These are our neighbors. In moments like this, we take care of one another," the business wrote.
PANTHERS GREAT JONATHAN STEWART EXPLAINS WHY YOUTH SPORTS MATTER FAR BEYOND THE FIELD
Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan also offered condolences to the families Sunday.

"What should have been a day of children playing soccer and families spending time together ended in tragedy," he said. "We are also thinking about those who were injured, their loved ones and everyone who witnessed what happened. We know this tragedy has affected many people throughout our community, and we want those families to know they are not alone."

The deadly crash also halted the Kansas State High School Activities Association’s inaugural girls flag football state championship, which was taking place on an adjacent field. The association suspended play and said games would not resume that weekend.
At Saturday’s news conference, Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said the driver had a valid license, no outstanding arrest warrants and was cooperating with investigators.
Sullivan underscored the unanswered question confronting investigators.
"We know what happened, but now we’re working very hard to find out why it happened," he said Saturday.

Police are asking anyone with information about the crash to call investigators at 316-268-4407. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Crime Stoppers at 316-267-2111.
Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller and Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.

title: Brother of possible OJ Simpson accomplice claims he returned with bloody hands on night of murders: report
summary: Joey Ippolito, a mob-connected figure, returned with apparent blood on his hands the night Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were killed, his brother told The New York Times.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A convicted drug trafficker with ties to the mafia may have helped O.J. Simpson cover up the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, according to a bombshell New York Times investigation that uncovered secret federal records and allegations that the man returned from the night of the killings with blood on his hands.

Joseph "Joey" Ippolito, a mob-connected associate of Simpson and his longtime friend Al Cowlings, allegedly returned to a Los Angeles apartment around midnight on June 12, 1994, carrying a mysterious bag containing a heavy object, his brother Sam Ippolito told the Times in an account that has raised questions, as well as some doubts.

The investigation also uncovered previously sealed federal court records revealing that Ippolito had provided authorities with information about Simpson's alleged disposal of the murder weapon, which was never recovered.
MARK FUHRMAN, DETECTIVE AT CENTER OF OJ SIMPSON MURDER TRIAL, DEAD AT 74
O. J. Simpson sits in Superior Court in Los Angeles in 1994 during an open court session. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Sam Ippolito claimed his brother appeared to have blood on his hands after leaving the apartment hours earlier to help a friend. Joey allegedly stuffed his clothes into the bag and instructed Sam to dispose of it while he showered.
Sam Ippolito told the newspaper he tossed the bag into a dumpster near a construction site along Doheny Drive in Los Angeles.
He also claimed to have overheard Joey telling Cowlings over the phone that he had been "helping" Simpson that night.

Joey Ippolito, a convicted drug trafficker who escaped from a Florida prison in May 1994, became a federal informant after his arrest in August 1995, while Simpson's nationally televised murder trial was nearing its conclusion.

A December 1996 federal prosecution memorandum, recently unsealed at the newspaper's request, described Ippolito as a valuable source who possessed information about Simpson's alleged efforts to dispose of the murder weapon and his attempted flight from authorities.
Johnnie Cochran, Robert Kardashian, Barry Scheck, F. Lee Bailey, Shapiro and Alan Dershowitz comprised OJ Simpson's dream team. (Sam Mircovich/AFP)

Then-federal prosecutor David Kelley described Ippolito in the letter as a "remarkable source of information" whose cooperation had proven valuable to investigators. When the newspaper spoke to Kelley recently, he said that he did not believe Joey Ippolito was involved in the killings.
BILLS SUPERFAN DEFENDS OJ SIMPSON'S FOOTBALL LEGACY AFTER TEAM LEAVES JUICE OFF ITS WALL OF FAME
The Times reported that the records show that information from Joey Ippolito was shared with Los Angeles prosecutors during Simpson's murder trial, although he was never called to testify.
Former prosecutor Marcia Clark told the Times she had no knowledge of Joey Ippolito and maintained that she would have been informed if he had provided credible or relevant evidence.
Nicole Brown Simpson and O.J. Simpson married on Feb. 2, 1985. (Gary Leonard/Corbis via Getty Images)
The account from Joey Ippolito's brother has come under scrutiny.

After maintaining his allegations for months, Sam Ippolito reportedly sought compensation from the Times and later attempted to retract his statements, claiming he could no longer distinguish what was real from what was not.
Friends and relatives of Joey Ippolito, who died in 2006, have also disputed suggestions that he participated in the murders.
Cowlings did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment by the time of its article's publication.
The newly uncovered information raises fresh questions about whether Simpson had help on the night Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were stabbed to death outside her Los Angeles home.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Simpson was acquitted of their murders in 1995 but was later found liable for their deaths in a civil trial. He died in April 2024 at age 76.
The Los Angeles Police Department confirmed to the Times that the decades-old double-murder case remains an open investigation.

title: WATCH: Virginia cops crawl through burning house to save man trapped in fire
summary: Body-worn camera footage captures four Culpeper, Virginia, police officers crawling through heavy smoke to drag an unresponsive man to safety.
story: Police officers in Culpeper, Virginia, rescued a man who was unconscious in a burning house. (Culpeper Police Department)
As police officers raced up to a wooden house in the town of Culpeper, Virginia on the evening of Oct. 3, heavy smoke billowed out of the windows.
Residents who lived in separate apartments in the house stood outside, according to the Culpeper Police Department.
But one man hadn’t come out, they told police. They worried that he might be inside.
Culpeper Police Department officers enter a burning home to save a man from the fire. (Culpeper Police Department)
MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE
Officer Ashley Sain didn’t wait. She rushed toward the house and went in without protective gear and began checking doors, searching for anyone who might still be inside.
Moments later, Officer Neal Coffey joined her.
SHERIFF'S DEPUTY SAVES MAN FROM FIERY WRECK AFTER HIGH-SPEED CHASE ENDS IN CRASH
Body-worn camera footage shows one officer running up stairs, past "No Smoking" signs with red lettering posted on the walls.
On the second floor, the duo found a door that was locked from the inside. Smoke slipped through through cracks above and below.
MARINE VETERAN AND BOSTON FIREFIGHTER DIES AFTER RESCUE EFFORTS AT MASSIVE HOUSE BLAZE
"Police department, if you’re in here!" Sain shouted over shrieking smoke alarms.
Police officers and firefighters responded to a house fire in Culpeper, Virginia, on Oct. 3, 2026. (Culpeper Police Department)
Meanwhile, Coffey quickly opened the lock with a pocket-size tool and cautiously swung open the door, calling out, "Police department!"
HISTORIC NYC CHURCH ENGULFED IN 5-ALARM BLAZE; 6 FIREFIGHTERS INJURED BATTLING STUBBORN FLAMES
But there was no answer.
Heavy black smoke poured from the bedroom. The officers could see flames.
MASSIVE FIRE ENGULFS APARTMENT COMPLEX UNDER CONSTRUCTION, FORCES EVACUATIONS IN SOUTH BEND
"Police department!" Sain shouted again. "Anybody inside?"
By that time, Sgt. David Cole and Officer Michael Beel had made it to the second floor, as well.
HEART-STOPPING VIDEO SHOWS OFFICERS USE UNLIKELY TOOL TO SAVE FAMILY TRAPPED IN FLOODWATERS
Body-worn camera footage shows Coffey crawling on his hands and knees, then flat on the wooden plank floor, searching the room with a flashlight.
"I can’t see!" he shouted with a tone of increasing desperation, as he pushed through thicker smoke.
POLICE DOG FOLLOWS HIS NOSE TO FIND MISSING AUTISTIC TEEN SCREAMING FOR HELP
He inched forward on his chest, feeling around through the smoke. Suddenly, he found a man lying unresponsive on a bed.
"Hey brother, come on!" he urges frantically, tugging the man’s arm.
FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT
"Come on! Come with me!"
He shouted again through the smoke to fellow officers.
"We’ve got to get him out! I have him! He’s breathing!"
Video shows him struggling to move the man.
"Hey! We need help!" an officer shouted.
Coffey pulled the limp man onto the floor. Beel crawled in to help.
Together, the four officers dragged the unconscious man into the hallway.
Then a firefighter in protective gear emerged through the smoke.
A team of firefighters carried the man out of the burning building, and extinguished the fire.
SEND US A TIP

The rescued resident was transported to a hospital, then transferred to a regional burn center. His name and the cause of the fire have not been released because those details are part of an active investigation.
GOT A TIP?
Three of the police officers also were treated at a hospital for smoke inhalation and other injuries. They were released that evening.
Officers who helped save a man from a burning house fire received valor awards from the Culpeper Police Department. (Culpeper Police Department)
All four who braved the smoke and flames were honored with valor awards on Oct. 14, Capt. Kevin Tooley of the Culpeper Police Department told Fox News Digital. He was a supervisor on the scene.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
"They went above and beyond the normal call for a police department," Tooley said of his team.

"We normally don't go into burning buildings. I mean, that's not our job. That's typically the fire department's job. But we don't know how to say no, especially when there's a life … that we know we have to save."

title: Accused teen killer's own dashcam could prove murder of two girls mowed down, lawyer says: 'Not an accident'
summary: Vincent Battiloro's own dashcam footage allegedly shows him turning to follow two New Jersey teens before the fatal e-bike crash on Burnside Avenue.
story: Fox News correspondent Eric Shawn sits down with the mother of a New Jersey teen killed in a hit-and-run on ‘America Reports.’

An accused New Jersey killer’s own dashcam could help prosecutors prove he deliberately killed two girls riding an e-bike, an attorney for one victim’s family said, after investigators say the recording shows him turning around to follow them.
On Wednesday, a Union County grand jury indicted Vincent Battiloro, 18, of Garwood, on two counts of first-degree murder in the teen girls’ deaths.

Brent Bramnick, who represents the family of victim Maria Niotis, said the dashcam recording from the 2021 Black Jeep Compass driven by Battilori could help prosecutors establish Battiloro’s intent when he allegedly struck and killed Maria, along with Isabella Salas, both 17, on Sept. 29, 2025.
Two teenagers were killed in a hit-and-run. Vince Battiloro has been indicted. (GoFundMe and FOX 5)
MAN ACCUSED OF MOWING DOWN TWO GIRLS IN ALLEGED DOUBLE MURDER EXPOSES TWISTED REASON HE KEPT STREAMING

According to court records, Battiloro had been driving up to 70 mph on a residential street in Cranford, with a speed limit of 25 mph, when he plowed into the girls on Burnside Avenue. The best friends were riding together on an electric bicycle when Battiloro allegedly struck them from behind.

Cranford police issued citations for offenses including, in part, speeding, reckless driving, improper passing and an unsafe lane change. While the citations described dangerous driving, the murder charges will require the prosecution to prove that Battiloro purposely caused the deaths, Bramnick said.
COSTCO EMPLOYEE FATALLY RAMMED CAR INTO CO-WORKER ON MOTORCYCLE AFTER SEEING HUG: DA

"So I think even more important than the allegations in the tickets, even though obviously everything’s important, is the fact that this was evidently recorded as it’s happening," Bramnick told Fox News Digital.
Vincent Battiloro, 18, was indicted in connection with the deaths of two New Jersey teenagers. (VinnieBat118/YouTube)
"And that requires a lot of work and that requires making sure you have all the evidence to show, piece by piece, what this defendant was thinking, and that it was not an accident."
MOTHER ACCUSED OF TRYING TO KILL DAUGHTERS IN FREEWAY CRASH AND KNIFE ATTACK AS SOLDIERS STEP IN
Bramnick said that he is confident, however, that the evidence will prove murder.
"We certainly believe based upon all the evidence presented so far that the intention was to commit those murders," he said.
WATCH: DRIVER SMIRKS IN MUGSHOT AFTER ALLEGEDLY HITTING GROUP OF CYCLISTS IN CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA ROAD RAGE
Niotis family lawyer Brent Bramnick speaks about seeking to move the teen suspect’s double murder case to adult court. (Fox News)

Authorities said that following the crash, Battiloro abandoned the SUV and fled the scene on foot. Police cited him for leaving the scene of an accident involving personal injury and failing to report an accident.
He’s also accused of having improper or unclear license plates, no proof of registration and insurance, and no proof of a driver’s license.
The day after the incident, Battiloro appeared in a gaming livestream on YouTube and complained that people were ridiculing him over what he called "false allegations."
Stalking and swatting accusations

Niotis' mother, Foulla Niotis, said that Battiloro, who previously attended Lincoln School in Cranford with her daughter, had stalked the girl for months before the collision, and although she had reported it to police, nothing came from it.
Foulla Niotis speaks in an exclusive interview after her daughter Maria and friend Isabella Salas were killed. (Fox News)
"Nobody said to me if there was anything I could do, restraining orders or anything against him," Niotis previously told Fox News Digital. "They just kept saying, 'Oh, he's a juvenile.' "
The defendant is also accused of swatting the Niotis residence on at least two occasions in Sept. 2025, according to Bramnick.
DRIVER ACCUSED OF KILLING 2 COLLEGE CYCLISTS IN TENNESSEE CRASH ALLEGEDLY FAILED TO BRAKE: COURT DOCS
Adult charges
Cranford police questioned Battiloro on Sept. 29, 2025, but subsequently released him to his father after Battiloro claimed someone carjacked him at knife-point.
In June, after reviewing the dashcam footage, police arrested Battiloro and charged him as an adult.
SEND US A TIP
Bramnick said Battiloro remains in custody after his defense agreed to detention without prejudice, leaving open the possibility of challenging the status later.
GOT A TIP?
Battiloro’s defense attorney, Brian Biglin, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Battiloro’s arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 27, at the Union County Courthouse in Elizabeth.

"There'll be an opportunity to have this play out, where people can see what's going on, and that is hugely important for the public," Bramnick added.
