Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson and Fox News' Courtney Walsh-Annesi contributed to this report.

title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis
summary: Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis.
story: Emmy-nominated actor Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a condition she believed she had for more than five years, leaving her “back at square one” as she continues to experience debilitating medical issues.

Applegate, who revealed the misdiagnosis on the latest episode of her podcast “MeSsy,” broke down in tears as she recalled a doctor recently telling her: “Congratulations. You don’t have MS.” She said that she was “not happy at all” about the news.

“You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I’m better,” Applegate told her podcast co-host, “The Sopranos” actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler. “I haven’t gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways.

“I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me,” said Applegate, who spent months in the hospital earlier this year and recently took a break from co-hosting “MeSsy” with Sigler, who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis roughly 25 years ago.
Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS

Applegate disclosed that she had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2021, calling her medical ordeal “a tough road.” She received a standing ovation at the 2024 Emmy Awards, appearing on stage with a cane. In an interview that year, she said she lived “kind of in hell.”

Multiple sclerosis is a progressive disease of the central nervous system that disrupts the flow of information between the brain and body. The immune system attacks the body’s nerve linings, producing unpredictable symptoms such as pain, fatigue or paralysis.
In the two-part podcast episode released Tuesday, Applegate said the lack of clarity about her medical condition was “unnerving” and “confusing.”

“It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down,” Applegate told Sigler. “It’s this weird feeling because I became this — you and I — the poster children for MS. ... I had a f---ing reason as to why my day sucked every day.”
She said her medical team will work to determine the underlying cause of her symptoms.
“Why did this happen? I had every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one,” Applegate said.

Applegate is best known for her television roles on Fox’s “Married with Children” and Netflix’s “Dead to Me.” She also appeared in both “Anchorman” movies as TV news anchor Veronica Corningstone. She has received eight Emmy nominations, winning in 2003 for her guest appearance on NBC’s “Friends.”

title: Woman accused of holding stepson captive over 20 years in abusive conditions to go to trial in February
summary: Kimberly Sullivan’s 32-year-old stepson told police last year he had spent almost his entire life being abused, starved and held in captivity, according to an affidavit.
story: The case of a Connecticut woman accused of holding her stepson captive for over two decades is expected to go to trial in February.

A judge at the Waterbury Judicial District courthouse received a series of confidential records in the case against Kimberly Sullivan  during a hearing on Tuesday. Sullivan wasn’t present at the hearing.

Over the next several weeks, the judge is expected to review the records obtained via a state subpoena from the Department of Children and Families, the Waterbury Public Schools and an undisclosed treatment facility. He will then determine which ones can be used during the trial.
Sullivan’s case drew national attention after shocking details around the allegations that her stepson had been living in captivity since he was 11 began to emerge following her arrest in March 2025.

According to an affidavit, Sullivan’s 32-year-old stepson told police that he had spent almost his entire life being abused, starved and held in captivity — prompting him to intentionally start a fire in his room in order to regain his freedom.

At the home, police found the man severely malnourished, noting he had not received medical or dental care in years and had been subjected to “prolonged abuse, starvation, severe neglect and inhumane treatment,” according to police.
At the time of Sullivan’s arrest, her 5-foot-9 stepson weighed 68 pounds.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“It was worse than the conditions of a jail cell,” Waterbury Police Chief Fernando Spagnolo told reporters last year of the man’s living situation.

In April 2025, Waterbury police released dozens of photos from inside the home through a Freedom of Information request to NBC Connecticut, showing rooms cluttered with items, walls covered in smoke and destroyed from the fire, and doors with locks on the outside.

Ioannis Kaloidis, Sullivan’s attorney, decried the release of the images at the time, telling NBC Connecticut that the move by police was “shocking, offensive and quite frankly, ethically questionable” and threatened his client’s right to “a fair trial.”
Sullivan pleaded not guilty to charges of kidnapping, assault, unlawful restraint and intentional cruelty to persons.

Sullivan also rejected two different plea deals in September: one offered by the judge, granting her a 30-year sentence to be suspended after serving 10 years, and another one from the state. The latter one included 30 years in prison, suspended after 20 years served, and five years of probation.
Kaloidis has said his client has consistently “maintained her innocence.”

During Tuesday’s hearing, Kaloidis filed a series of motions, including a request for a 12-member jury, instead of six, and another one asking state prosecutors not to refer to Sullivan’s stepson as “the victim” during the trial. The first motion will be argued in the next court hearing set for Nov. 23. The judge granted the second one on Tuesday.
Sullivan’s stepson, who is only identified in court by the alias S., is expected to testify during the trial, NBC Connecticut reported.

The judge granted a motion filed by Kaloidis on Tuesday requesting that all information that could potentially challenge or undermine the credibility of S. and his sister, who is also expected to testify, be shared during the pretrial discovery phase.
If convicted next year, Sullivan faces more than 45 years in prison.
Jury selection for February’s trial is expected to begin about a month before.

title: Kyle Kennedy, granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, dies at 42
summary: Kyle Francis Kennedy, an educator and granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, died last month after suffering a severe spinal cord injury.
story: Kyle Francis Kennedy, an educator and granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, died last month after suffering a severe spinal cord injury that resulted in long term paralysis and years of medical issues, a Massachusetts funeral home said.
She was 42.
Kennedy “passed away peacefully” on Sept. 21 “at her home in Westwood, Massachusetts,” according to an obituary by Burke Funeral Homes. Her cause of death was not announced.
She “built a career devoted to early childhood education,” the obituary said.

“Blessed with a formidable intellect, dry wit, and beauty, she will be remembered for her devotion to her children Conor, Josephine, and Declan, and her support for educational reform for disadvantaged children and for people living with disabilities.”
Kennedy grew up in Cohasset, Massachusetts, and attended the prestigious Milton Academy before matriculating to Georgetown University.

She spent a semester abroad in Florence, Italy, which “left a lasting mark” and led to her “deep love of Tuscan Renaissance art and a lifelong talent for making pasta dishes from scratch,” the obituary said.
She earned a master’s degree in early education from Pace University and another master’s in education policy from  Harvard.
Kennedy spent two years in the Teach for America program, working in New York City public school system in “an experience that launched a career in education,” according to her obituary.

“She went on to become a passionate advocate for more equitable elementary education and charter schooling, later working with technology companies focused on reforming and improving school curricula, and as a coach for educators working with young students,” the obituary said.
Kennedy was the daughter of Michael LeMoyne Kennedy, the  sixth oldest child of RFK and Ethel Kennedy.
Michael LeMoyne Kennedy was just 39 when he was fatally injured on Dec. 31, 1997, in Colorado, slamming into a tree while playing ski-football on an icy Aspen slope.
Like many in her famed family, Kennedy was fond of the outdoors and sports. She ran in the 2019 Boston Marathon, competing under her married name, Kyle Kerr.
But she spent the last several years of life unable to walk.

“In 2020, Kyle suffered a severe spinal cord injury that resulted in long term paralysis, disability, and other medical challenges,” the obituary said. “The years that followed brought struggles but Kyle fought to maintain her dry wit and determination through it all, trying to be the best possible mother to her sons and caring for her two beloved, ill-behaved Wheaten terriers.”
It was not disclosed how Kennedy suffered that traumatic 2020 injury.
“She also began to advocate for people living with disabilities, including testifying at the Massachusetts state house in a hearing on discrimination in disabled health care,” the funeral home added.
Kennedy is survived by her sons, Conor, 12, and Declan, 10, ex-husband Liam Kerr, mother Victoria Denise Gifford, brother Michael LeMoyne Kennedy Jr.  and sister Rory Gifford Kennedy.

title: Spotify says it removed 50 million ‘slop’ and spam AI tracks this year
summary: Spotify removed more than 50 million tracks created by AI so far this year, as it works to keep AI-generated music from crowding out human artists.
story: Spotify has removed more than 50 million tracks that appear to have been created by artificial intelligence from its curated music recommendations so far this year, as the streaming giant works to keep AI-generated music from crowding out human artists.
“AI-generated slop and spam don’t belong in your recommendations, and we’ve made changes to keep them out and protect the listening experience,” Spotify said in a statement Tuesday.

Last year, the company removed 75 million tracks for what it said were serious or repeated violations of its rules, which prohibit replicating an existing creator’s content or creating media artificially with technology.

The flood of AI-generated creative content online poses a major challenge to streaming services like Spotify, which need to identify and weed out instances of impersonation or deception from among tens of millions of tracks.

Here, Spotify said it turned to its listeners for help. The company analyzed patterns within songs that users frequently skipped or ignored on the platform over the past six months. These tracks consistently overlapped with the artificially generated audio sometimes referred to as “slop.”

By combining feedback from listeners with metadata and third-party AI-detection tools, Spotify was able to update its internal recommendation system to limit how often AI-generated content was surfaced.
The company acknowledged that AI-detection technology has limitations and that identifying suspicious content could become more difficult as generative AI evolves.

For Spotify, the presence of AI-generated music can also have huge implications for artists who are paid based, in part, on how often their music is played relative to the total number of streams on the platform.

“If the denominator has grown because of AI slop, the percentage that each legitimate rights holder or artist will receive is diminished,” said Morgan Hayduk, CEO of Beatdapp, which sells AI- and fraud-detection software to music labels and distributors.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
To be eligible for royalties on Spotify, an artist must reach a minimum of 1,000 streams, which is far less common for AI tracks than it is for human-made music.

But not all artists who use AI in their creative process publish what Spotify may consider “slop.” For these situations, Spotify launched an AI credits feature earlier this year that artists can use to disclose which parts of a song’s creative process involved AI.

The combined use of audience feedback, metadata and detection tools to identify AI slop is one of several features that Spotify has introduced this year to increase transparency around AI use on the platform.

It also labels the artist profiles of musicians it believes are AI-generated with an “AI Persona” badge. AI Persona artists are excluded from user recommendation streams by default. Only listeners who proactively follow a particular AI artist will see that persona recommended to them.
Spotify said these efforts have resulted in a “marked decrease” in the number of concerns from listeners about AI spam showing up in their recommendations.
“AI moves fast and bad actors adapt just as fast,” Spotify said. “But as AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more.”

title: Jane Doe says Cornell president appeared to question her allegations in letter to faculty senate
summary: Jane Doe, the woman who accused several Cornell University fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024, sent a letter to the school’s faculty senate sharing a second-hand account of President Michael Kotlikoff’s response to her allegations ahead of a potential vote of no confidence in his administration.
story: Jane Doe, the woman who accused several Cornell University fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024, sent a letter to the school’s faculty senate sharing a second-hand account of President Michael Kotlikoff’s response to her allegations ahead of a potential vote of no confidence in his administration.

In a Wednesday letter obtained by NBC News, Doe described a meeting between Kotlikoff and the then-president of her sorority, Tri Delta, months after she reported the alleged assault to the university. Doe wrote that the sorority president subsequently told her that Kotlikoff had allegedly questioned why she waited to report the incident.

“After the conversation she shared with me, with concern, that President Kotlikoff’s initial response was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’” Doe said in the letter. “She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story.”

Cornell disputed that characterization Tuesday, saying in a statement that Kotlikoff’s question during a January 2025 meeting was focused on bystanders who had not reported the allegations, rather than Doe herself.

The letter comes amid mounting scrutiny of Cornell’s handling of Doe’s allegations and growing debate among school faculty members over whether to hold a no-confidence vote in the university’s administration. Earlier this month, Cornell hired former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review, which will examine the school’s response to Doe’s allegations and broader policies governing sexual misconduct.

In a civil lawsuit filed last month, Doe accused seven members of the now-dismantled Chi Phi fraternity of plying her with drugs and sexually assaulting her at a party in October 2024 and into the early hours of the next morning.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Orazio Petito, who was named as the former president of the fraternity, was dropped from the lawsuit after his lawyer said he was “mistakenly” identified as the Chi Phi chapter president at the time of the alleged 2024 assault, according to court documents. Petito was not accused of assault in the lawsuit.
Attorneys for several of the men have denied wrongdoing or disputed her account. Doe’s lawyer did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment.

Cornell subsequently investigated the allegations through its Title IX disciplinary process, expelling two students and imposing suspensions or lesser sanctions on others. The university also launched a Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault in early 2025 and has said in a statement Tuesday that it is implementing recommendations to improve its response to sexual misconduct.

“The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account,” the statement added. “The question ‘why did it take so long for the assault to be reported’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024. He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.”

In her letter, Doe wrote that the sorority president told her that at least one other faculty member who attended the meeting “appeared distressed” after hearing Kotlikoff’s question. Doe said that the faculty member thought “the President’s response was inappropriate.”

“I felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff,” Doe wrote in the letter. “It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school.”
Doe added that she is now sharing this account because she does not know how many people know about the meeting or the president’s response.

“My intention is not to prescribe how the Senate should interpret this account, but rather to provide information that its members may wish to consider or investigate further,” she wrote. “I would not want to withhold something potentially pertinent, only for Senate members to later discover that information relevant to their deliberations had not been made available to them.”

The letter has prompted questions from at least one faculty member about how it was handled by Cornell’s dean of faculty, Chris Schaffer. A professor on the faculty senate, who requested anonymity to speak freely about the situation, told NBC News that Schaffer told members Tuesday that he had received Doe’s letter last week, the same day the senate met to discuss whether to hold a vote of no-confidence.
“If he received it on the 14th, he should have said so,” the professor said.

Cornell said Schaffer received the letter as “legal correspondence claiming to be from a law firm representing Jane Doe” and that he “subsequently turned it over to the General Counsel to verify and to share with the Independent Review.”

“Shortly before the start of the Senate meeting on October 14, I received a communication from a lawyer representing Jane Doe, which relayed a second-hand account of President Kotlikoff asking about the timing of reports about the Jane Doe assault in 2024,” he wrote. “I later received a contemporaneous account of the meeting from a university official who was present that indicated President Kotlikoff asked bystanders ‘why did it take so long for the assault to be reported’ through Cornell’s anonymous tip line, given the level of social media discussion of the events. The question was not about Jane Doe or her decision to report.”
Schaffer added that his office “does not have the investigatory capacity to properly follow up on private communications of this kind, nor is this the role of the office.”

“In the interests of transparency, I am writing now to inform the Senate that I received this communication, that I passed it on to the Office of the General Counsel, and that they have sent it to the investigatory team led by Former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates,” he added. “Any individual who has information they believe is relevant to the deliberation of the Cornell Senate may make such information public or communicate it directly.”

title: Pennsylvania warns of rise in congenital measles and infection during pregnancy
summary: The Pennsylvania Department of Health issued an alert Monday to doctors about an increase in measles infections in pregnant women, as well as a concerning rise in congenital measles — a disease that’s rarely, if ever, seen in the U.S.
story: The Pennsylvania Department of Health issued an alert Monday to doctors about an increase in measles infections in pregnant women, as well as a concerning rise in congenital measles — a disease that’s rarely, if ever, seen in the U.S.

The department said that 66 pregnant women in Pennsylvania had been diagnosed with measles since the state’s outbreak began in April. “Getting measles while pregnant increases the risk of miscarriage, early labor, and low birth weight,” a department spokesperson said in an email.

It’s unclear how many women have miscarried or delivered babies with congenital measles. The department said that state law prohibits it from releasing details of the outcomes of those pregnancies, and there is no national database that tracks cases. True numbers may also be obscured as the outbreak has largely been limited to Amish families who don’t always seek conventional medical assistance.
As of Thursday, there have been 4,410 measles cases in the U.S. this year. In Pennsylvania, there have been 1,286 cases as of Monday.

Even before widespread measles vaccination, congenital measles was rare. That’s because most women had already been infected as children. It’s only now emerging as a threat as measles outbreaks are increasing as vaccination rates fall.

Last month, the American Academy of Pediatrics added a “frequently asked questions” page about congenital measles to its website in response to ongoing and increasing measles outbreaks. According to the AAP, congenital measles occurs in newborns whose mothers have been infected during the two weeks before birth and who test positive or develop measles symptoms within 10 days of delivery.

Anecdotally, doctors have said that at least six babies were born in Pennsylvania with congenital measles. Babies can have a range of symptoms, from a rash and fever to pneumonia, neurological problems and low blood platelets. At least two developed pneumonia and were admitted to an intensive care unit, doctors said.

Congenital measles can be deadly. One father in Lancaster County previously told NBC News that his wife was sick with measles in August and went into labor a month early. Their baby died shortly after birth.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Congenital measles can also lead to severe brain and immune system issues later in life, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said. Those long-term complications can include a very rare and severe inflammatory brain condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE. It can occur seven to 10 years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. There is evidence that SSPE may occur earlier in children born with congenital measles.
There’s no specific treatment for congenital measles other than supportive care, such as fluids, hydration and supplemental oxygen.

The best way to prevent the newborn condition is for women to get vaccinated before getting pregnant, the health department said. Pregnant women who get measles are unable to get the vaccine because the shot contains a weakened but live version of the virus.

Unvaccinated pregnant women who are exposed to measles can get a dose of immunoglobulin within six days of that exposure, the health department said, to “provide protection against measles infection or reduce the risk of serious illness among susceptible people.”
The vaccine can be given to women after they deliver their babies and is safe for breastfeeding mothers, according to state health officials.

title: Democrats jump into Mississippi Senate race
summary: Senate Democrats’ top super PAC announced Tuesday it is launching a new ad campaign in the Mississippi Senate race, as Democrats seek inroads in Republican-leaning states to try to flip the Senate majority.
story: Senate Democrats’ top super PAC announced Tuesday it is launching a new ad campaign in the Mississippi Senate race, as Democrats seek inroads in Republican-leaning states to try to flip the Senate majority.

Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in the state through Election Day, beginning with a 30-second spot that boosts prosecutor Scott Colom as a Democrat who will “fight corruption in both parties” and casts GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as a “do-nothing” incumbent.

“Senate Majority PAC has been watching this race closely, and it is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” Lauren French, the super PAC’s spokesperson, said in a statement, also noting that the group will be advertising on TV and digital platforms.

Senate Majority PAC, which is aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., has been shifting its focus to deep-red states amid President Donald Trump’s sinking approval ratings. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate, which means flipping multiple states Trump won handily in 2024.
Mississippi is the reddest state the group has jumped into so far — Trump won it by 23 points two years ago. A Democrat has not won a Senate race in Mississippi since 1982.
Senate Majority PAC is also spending in Kansas, which Trump won by 16 points, and other states Trump won by double digits in 2024, including Alaska, Texas and Iowa.

Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have long touted Colom as a strong candidate. A district attorney, Colom told NBC News when he launched his campaign last year that Hyde-Smith’s vote to support Trump’s “big, beautiful” tax and spending law, which cut Medicaid funds, spurred him to run.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Colom and Hyde-Smith have history from before this year’s Senate race. Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination for a federal judgeship during the Biden administration. Colom said when he launched his campaign that he had forgiven her.
Hyde-Smith, who has Trump’s endorsement, is running for her second full term after she was appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a full term in 2020 by 10 points.

title: Top baby names heading into 2027 inspired by ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Yellowstone’ and ‘Heated Rivalry’
summary: BabyCenter released the most popular baby names of 2026 and the trends it expects to shape 2027, including “The Odyssey,” “Yellowstone” and “Heated Rivalry.”
story: Somewhere in a delivery room, a new parent is weighing a name that sounds like a Greek hero, a Montana ranch hand or a brooding hockey player from a streaming series. According to BabyCenter’s latest data, they’re far from alone.

BabyCenter, a digital parenting resource that’s been reporting on baby names and trends for more than 20 years, just released its annual lists of the most popular baby names of 2026 and the trends it expects to shape 2027. The findings, shared with NBC News, draw on more than 350,000 babies born this year to parents registered on the BabyCenter app. Because parents submit names in real time, the company can predict trends before the Social Security Administration releases its official list.
At the very top, little has changed from last year. Noah and Olivia both keep their No. 1 spots.

Just beneath them, though, one name is making a lot of noise. Eliana has shot up to No. 2 for girls, a remarkable climb from No. 14 in 2024 and No. 7 last year. BabyCenter’s baby name advisor, Steph Coffield, calls it the year’s most surprising trend and predicts that if the momentum holds, Eliana could take the top girls’ spot next year.

If there’s a theme running through this year’s data, it’s with that first letter E. E is the most popular starting initial for girls, making up 15% of the top 100 girls’ names. For boys, J leads, with 14% of the top 100.

The E-names are having a moment well beyond the top 10. Elsie rose 23 spots, Evangeline 50, Elodie 87, Elaine 143 and Esme a whopping 222. Among the boys, Josiah surged 33 spots to No. 21 and Jeremiah climbed 28 spots to reach No. 60, while Jaxon, Jaxson and Jasper all hold spots in the top 100.

Scroll further down the list and you’ll find some fresh faces. Magnolia is the only brand-new girls’ name. But on the boys’ side, Stetson, Archer and Milo all debuted, joined by Dean, which is making its first top 100 appearance this century after a heyday in the ’50s and ’60s.
Length is trending upward, too. Nearly three in 10 of the top girls’ names and 31% of the top boys’ names have seven or more letters. The longest name in the mix is Christopher, at 11.

Many of those longer, bolder picks are coming straight from the screen, and nowhere is that clearer than on the ice. In the same year ESPN logged its most-watched NHL playoff season, ice-rink TV dramas, including “Off Campus” and “Heated Rivalry,” sent names like Garrett, Allie, Beau and Jules climbing. The breakout star is Ilya, which rocketed up more than 6,000 spots to No. 2,197 for boys.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Trade the rink for the open range, and another small-screen hit is leaving its mark. The lingering pull of “Yellowstone,” with its cowboy hats, boots and line dancing, is carrying into the nursery. As mentioned earlier, Stetson rose 46 spots to No. 95, the first time it has ever cracked BabyCenter’s top 100. Walker (up 19), Callahan (up 88), Wilder (up 107) and Gunner (up 151) are riding the same wave.

But the cowboys have some competition from across the sea. Names from Greek mythology are washing ashore, boosted by the blockbuster movie “The Odyssey.” Boys’ names on the rise include Atlas (up 5), Orion and Troy (both up 9), Ares (up 32), Evander (up 128) and Perseus (up 249). For girls, Iris (up 18), Lydia (up 38) and Daphne (up 42) are climbing.
“The trends this year show parents are ready to dig into the archives with some modern appreciation for the ancient, the vintage, the classic,” Coffield said.

In some cases, that archive is a cozy Connecticut town. With a “Gilmore Girls” documentary newly announced, fall rewatches are sending Stars Hollow names soaring. Lorelai is up 12 spots and Rory up 31. Among the boys, Christopher is up 4, Luke up 7, Richard up 29 and Dean up 31, which helps explain that name’s return to the top 100.

Not every name is riding the pop culture wave, though, and one has had a rough year. Between Taylor Swift’s wedding, Taylor Farms’ lettuce recalls and a two famous Taylors welcoming a baby with Taylor as the middle name, BabyCenter says parents are over it. For girls, Taylor dropped 24 spots to No. 399. For boys, it plummeted 262 spots to No. 1,093, falling out of the top 1,000 for the first time ever.
So back to that delivery room. Whatever name new parents are landing on, whether it’s a mythic hero, a rugged cowboy or a Stars Hollow favorite, chances are it’s already climbing the charts.

title: Elderly couple pleads not guilty to murdering son-in-law, a NYT executive, at local park
summary: The couple accused of killing their son-in-law, New York Times executive Jonathan McKinsey, pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, a defense attorney said Monday.
story: The couple accused of killing their son-in-law, New York Times executive Jonathan McKinsey, pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, a defense attorney said Monday.

Defense attorney Curtis Briggs argued that his client, Shili Chen, who is married to Shouyong Zhang, did not premeditate the shooting, NBC Bay Area reported. Instead, Briggs told NBC Bay Area that the couple, both 77, acted out of concern after seeing something disturbing while their son-in-law had a supervised visit with his children.
“My client was absolutely concerned for her own life and also concerned for her grandchildren,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area. Zhang is being represented by a public defender.

Alameda County prosecutors say Chen and Zhang watched and waited in a parking lot in Dublin, California, to attack McKinsey, who was embroiled in a bitter divorce and custody battle with their daughter.

Briggs said that McKinsey, 40, had previously threatened Chen’s life three times through a hit man. The couple purchased firearms in March to defend themselves, Briggs said, and were moved to act last month in the parking lot of a popular park.
“They are not cold-blooded killers. They didn’t premeditate anything,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area.
Briggs did not elaborate on what the elderly couple witnessed that drove them to kill their son-in-law.
If convicted, they could both face life in prison without the possibility of parole.
According to local police, 911 calls started coming in around 3 p.m. on Sept. 26 from terrified witnesses, many of whom were with their young children.

Several witnesses told police they saw a black Honda speeding out of the parking lot and later identified Chen and Zhang as the shooters, police said in a statement. Officers chased down the car and arrested the couple, according to the police report.
Nearly a decade’s worth of court documents revealed a deeply troubled marriage between McKinsey and his wife, Candice Jang, who has not been charged in connection with his death.

McKinsey’s death followed years of violent struggle between Jang and McKinsey, who started dating in 2008 and were married in 2011, according to Jang’s petition for a domestic abuse restraining order. They had three children.
McKinsey had recently filed for divorce and was scheduled to appear in court the same week he died, according to court records.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In separate petitions for restraining orders, McKinsey and Jang each argued that the other was physically and mentally abusive during their marriage. McKinsey and Jang both said they wanted full custody of their children, but McKinsey had an ongoing child abuse case that granted him only supervised visits.
The children were living with Jang and her parents when McKinsey was shot.

He had been previously charged with two misdemeanors — cruelty to a child by endangering health and corporal injury to a child. McKinsey was freed on $50,000 bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program, according to court records. Had he successfully completed the program, the charges would have been dismissed.
According to police reports, Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey with his firearm during interviews with investigators. The husband and wife were each carrying weapons at the time of their arrests.
“Chen and the passenger carried out this shooting in a crowded park parking lot with blatant disregard for public safety where several children were present,” the arresting officer said.
McKinsey allegedly threatened to kill Chen at least three times, NBC Bay Area reported. A bail hearing was set for Nov. 4, followed by a pretrial hearing on Nov. 23.

title: ‘Call Her Daddy’ host Alex Cooper welcomes her first baby
summary: Alex Cooper, the host of “Call Her Daddy,” is now a mom.
story: Alex Cooper, the host of “Call Her Daddy,” is now a mom.

Cooper, 32, announced the birth of her first child, a boy, in an Instagram post Tuesday. The Unwell founder and her husband, Matt Kaplan, 42, announced in May that they were expecting. The baby’s due date was not clear.
The post featured a photo of a newborn in a fuzzy blue outfit. The caption was just a blue heart.
On Thursday, Cooper posted a slideshow of photos from her pregnancy.
“The most transformative 9 months of my life,” she wrote in the caption.

In a July post on Instagram, Cooper revealed that she was diagnosed with gestational diabetes, which she described as “when the placenta hormones cause insulin resistance — aka your pancreas cannot create enough insulin to keep your blood sugar normal.”
At first, Cooper said, she was hard on herself about the diagnosis, which she said felt “very isolating.” But ultimately, she said, she just wanted her baby to be healthy.
For Subscribers

“This diagnosis was so upsetting, I think, because during pregnancy, there’s already so much emotionally that you’re going through — I am so blessed and there’s been so many incredible parts of my pregnancy — but it’s a lot,” she said.
For Subscribers
According to the American Diabetes Association, gestational diabetes can affect up to 9% of pregnancies.
Kaplan, a Hollywood producer, married Cooper in April 2024. The couple co-founded the Unwell Network, a subsidiary of the media company Trending.
The baby’s name has not been revealed. One user joked in the comments: “call him baby.”

title: Oil prices rise, threatening to push cost of gas higher two weeks before midterms
summary: Oil prices surged in early trading Tuesday, as energy markets adjusted to a new normal in the Middle East.
story: Oil prices surged in early trading Tuesday, as energy markets adjusted to a new normal in the Middle East. The increase in crude prices threatened to drive up the cost of gas in the United States just two weeks before the midterm elections.

U.S. crude prices jumped as much as 5% to about $109 a barrel, the highest price since April, while the price of international Brent crude climbed 1.5% to more than $111, its highest price since May. Prices pulled back later in the morning, after weaker-than-expected U.S. housing starts raised the prospect of a broader slowdown and lower demand.
Prices for advanced oil contracts dated for next year also hit record highs, “implying an extended period of high oil prices deep into 2027,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Tuesday.

“The 2027 contracts are moving higher as well as the possible reality of higher for longer oil prices sink in,” Peter Boockvar, author of the Boock Report and chief investment officer of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, said in a note Tuesday.
High gas prices have become a major issue for voters in the midterms, where Republicans face dwindling odds of maintaining their control of Congress.

A recent NBC News poll found that 67% of U.S. adults believe gas prices are a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. A majority also said that current economic conditions have caused them to change their spending habits.
U.S. gasoline prices had started off the week lower. At $4.28 a gallon, the national average price of unleaded was on pace to reach its lowest level in a month.
But that trend is likely to be upended as higher crude prices filter through to the pump.
Several factors were contributing to Tuesday’s oil price hikes.
The cost of chartering a large tanker vessel to transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz has quadrupled since September, data shows.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Much of that increase is a risk premium, both for sailors and insurance. During the past two weeks, at least 18 ⁠vessels have been attacked in the strait, the ship-tracking group Kpler said in a note ⁠Monday.
The higher cost of transport has begun to offset the recent bump in supply from a growing number of ships moving through the strait.
The Iranian attacks on ships have also prompted investor speculation that the Trump administration will be more likely to escalate against Iran after the midterms, the Deutsche Bank analysts said.
Iran-aligned Houthi rebels also claimed Monday that they had hit airport, energy and military targets in Saudi Arabia, as well as a ​training camp in Yemen for that government’s security forces.
The U.K. will begin deploying fighter jets over Saudi Arabia to help protect against further Houthi attacks, the Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The entry of another country’s military into the regional hostilities was taken as a further sign of escalating tensions.

title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis
summary: Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis.
story: Emmy-nominated actor Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a condition she believed she had for more than five years, leaving her “back at square one” as she continues to experience debilitating medical issues.

Applegate, who revealed the misdiagnosis on the latest episode of her podcast “MeSsy,” broke down in tears as she recalled a doctor recently telling her: “Congratulations. You don’t have MS.” She said that she was “not happy at all” about the news.

“You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I’m better,” Applegate told her podcast co-host, “The Sopranos” actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler. “I haven’t gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways.

“I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me,” said Applegate, who spent months in the hospital earlier this year and recently took a break from co-hosting “MeSsy” with Sigler, who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis roughly 25 years ago.
Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS

Applegate disclosed that she had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2021, calling her medical ordeal “a tough road.” She received a standing ovation at the 2024 Emmy Awards, appearing on stage with a cane. In an interview that year, she said she lived “kind of in hell.”

Multiple sclerosis is a progressive disease of the central nervous system that disrupts the flow of information between the brain and body. The immune system attacks the body’s nerve linings, producing unpredictable symptoms such as pain, fatigue or paralysis.
In the two-part podcast episode released Tuesday, Applegate said the lack of clarity about her medical condition was “unnerving” and “confusing.”

“It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down,” Applegate told Sigler. “It’s this weird feeling because I became this — you and I — the poster children for MS. ... I had a f---ing reason as to why my day sucked every day.”
She said her medical team will work to determine the underlying cause of her symptoms.
“Why did this happen? I had every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one,” Applegate said.

Applegate is best known for her television roles on Fox’s “Married with Children” and Netflix’s “Dead to Me.” She also appeared in both “Anchorman” movies as TV news anchor Veronica Corningstone. She has received eight Emmy nominations, winning in 2003 for her guest appearance on NBC’s “Friends.”

title: Offshore nor’easter creating high surf and coastal flooding along the East Coast
summary: A strengthening nor’easter hundreds of miles off the Atlantic will still manage to bring several days of gusty onshore winds and coastal flooding, along with some rain that could clip Cape Cod.
story: A strengthening nor’easter hundreds of miles off the Atlantic will still manage to bring several days of gusty onshore winds and coastal flooding, along with some rain that could clip Cape Cod.

The storm is expected to stay far enough offshore that the heaviest rain will likely affect only the easternmost parts of the country. While the rain will stay mostly offshore, gusty winds and coastal flooding are still possible, especially across the Outer Banks.
Flood advisories are in place from the Jersey Shore to the Outer Banks for 1-2 feet of inundation from onshore winds.
The storm, still offshore, is intensifying. Coastline cities from New Jersey to Cape Hatteras can expect coastal flooding, beach erosion and gusty winds.
Rain and coastal flooding are expected to impact Cape Cod and Nantucket in the coming days. By Thursday, rough surf and rip currents will hit those areas.

The nor’easter could become a tropical storm but, if it does, it will only intensify as it continues east and away from the coast. It has a 40% chance of formation in two days, and 40% in seven days. If it develops, it will be named Josephine.
Winds will have the biggest impact, with 44 mph winds forecast in Nantucket. Virginia Beach could see 32 mph winds, and Cape Hatteras is expected to have 39 mph winds.
For Subscribers
Meanwhile, a storm in the Pacific Ocean is expected to bring heavy rain, flooding and mountain snow. A flash flood risk is in place from Southern California to the Rockies.
For Subscribers
A flood threat is in place for California and parts of the Southwest through Thursday, specifically in Southern California from San Luis Obispo to Santa Barbara, and across the Four Corners states.
Six million people across Arizona are also under a flood watch, including Phoenix and Flagstaff.

title: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
summary: U.S. envoys met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
story: U.S. envoys met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.

President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war. Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”

Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo, with Kushner joining remotely. Zelenskyy held talks with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb prior to meeting the U.S. delegation.

Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.

Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.

In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.

“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.

Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”

Zelenskyy said later on Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian missile attacks that he said occurred without enough notice. The change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including the phone call with Rubio earlier in the day, according to Zelenskyy.
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.

When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”

Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.

Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.

title: 1.5 million pounds of bacon and other meat were just recalled — here’s what you need to know
summary: More than 1.5 million pounds of meat was just recalled after possibly being stored unsafely — here’s what you should know if you have the affected products.
story: Don’t fire that breakfast griddle up just yet — your bacon may be at risk. On October 17, Kayem Foods Inc. issued a recall for more than 1.5 million pounds of ready-to-eat meat products that may have been stored at improper temperatures, according to an announcement from the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS). This includes bacon, deli meats, poultry and more, with an extensive list of potentially affected products that may be sitting in your fridge right now.
Keep reading to find out more about which products were affected, and what to do if you have them.
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
What is included in the Kayem Foods meat recall?

Kayem Foods, Inc. has recalled several meats because they may have experienced temperature abuse while being stored prior to delivery. The issue was found after a retail customer complained of warm product temperatures on October 1, after which an investigation was conducted.

The investigation determined that a range of ready-to-eat meat and poultry products were being stored in a warehouse cooler with inconsistencies in temperature that make them potentially unsafe to consume. Cold food should be kept at or below 40 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the FSIS — anything above that can result in spoilage and bacteria growth, potentially causing food poisoning or other illness.

Inside the USDA inspection seal, the recalled products have establishment numbers “EST. M/P 7839,” “EST. P 20935A” and “EST. M 9520”. The products were produced approximately between March 31 and Oct. 7 and shipped to retailers nationwide and in Hong Kong. The list includes hot dogs, bacon, turkey breast (deli meat), corned beef, chicken sausage and more — you can check here for a full list of recalled products and check to see if you have any (there’s also an abbreviated list with images). Consumers can also contact Kayem Foods’ customer service Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET at 800-426-6100 or email them at info@kayem.com.
What to do if you have the recalled meat?
If your meat was recalled, you should throw it out. Alternatively, the FSIS recommends returning it to your place of purchase, but above all, it stresses that consumers should not consume the meat.

Even when cooked to a proper temperature, there’s no way to guarantee the meat’s safety, and you can’t tell just by looking at it, either. “One of the most important things for consumers to understand is that you cannot reliably determine whether food is safe by looking at it, smelling it, or tasting it,” Melissa Vaccaro, senior food safety program specialist at the National Environmental Health Association, told NBC Selected in our guide to food safety during a power outage. “Food can contain disease-causing microorganisms without looking or smelling spoiled. And never taste questionable food to decide whether it is safe.”
The best products for keeping your meat safe

There are products that can help you keep your meat temperature-safe during storage and preparation. Remember that these aren’t solutions to official recall warnings, and all contaminated products should be thrown away or returned — not consumed. The products below, however, can help you store non-recalled food and ensure that your method of storing keeps it safe to eat.
Acurite Digital Wireless Fridge and Freezer Thermometer with Alarm

Digital thermometers can alert you to temperature changes in your fridge or freezer that can result in spoiled food. This thermometer includes one fridge and one freezer thermometer, each of which sends real-time readings to the LCD display, according to the brand. The LCD display has a magnetic backing for mounting to the front of a fridge, and a foldout stand for countertop placement, and includes a programmable alarm as well. This can be especially helpful to alert you of the temperature drop if the power goes out overnight, giving you the opportunity to move your food to a cooler or insulated bag.
Bodaon 2-Pack Insulated Reusable Grocery Bags

Insulated grocery bags are great for keeping your food cold or frozen on your way back from the store, and these lightweight bags can keep food cold or hot for up to an hour and a half, according to the brand. They’re also foldable, making them easy to store, and can hold up to 25 pounds of groceries in each bag.
Cooler Shock Reusable Ice Packs

You can use these ice packs to keep food and other contents cold for up to 48 hours, according to Cooler Shock. Once you add water and freeze them, the nylon exterior holds up over time, so you won’t need to restock the ice again. It’s great for coolers and totes, and comes in packs of three or five in varying sizes. These are ideal if you’re heading to the beach or pool and want to bring sandwiches, hot dogs or other food that needs to be kept at a certain temperature for safe consumption.
TempPro TempSwift Digital Thermometer

While cooking recalled meat will not make it safe to eat, a meat thermometer is handy for ensuring that non-recalled meat and poultry is cooked to a safe temperature. This one lets you read temperatures in either Fahrenheit or Celsius, and has an LCD screen with large numbers, making it easy to read, according to the brand. It also includes a storage sleeve for safekeeping, which has a protein temperature chart on the side for reference while cooking.
Why trust NBC Selected?

I am an associate SEO reporter for NBC Selected who’s been covering various topics for more than two years. I frequently report on skin care news, along with weekly reporting on sales and deals from prominent brands and retailers. For this piece, I researched the recall on Kayem Foods Inc. meat products to find out everything you need to know about its recent recall.
Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

title: Pennsylvania warns of rise in congenital measles and infection during pregnancy
summary: The Pennsylvania Department of Health issued an alert Monday to doctors about an increase in measles infections in pregnant women, as well as a concerning rise in congenital measles — a disease that’s rarely, if ever, seen in the U.S.
story: The Pennsylvania Department of Health issued an alert Monday to doctors about an increase in measles infections in pregnant women, as well as a concerning rise in congenital measles — a disease that’s rarely, if ever, seen in the U.S.

The department said that 66 pregnant women in Pennsylvania had been diagnosed with measles since the state’s outbreak began in April. “Getting measles while pregnant increases the risk of miscarriage, early labor, and low birth weight,” a department spokesperson said in an email.

It’s unclear how many women have miscarried or delivered babies with congenital measles. The department said that state law prohibits it from releasing details of the outcomes of those pregnancies, and there is no national database that tracks cases. True numbers may also be obscured as the outbreak has largely been limited to Amish families who don’t always seek conventional medical assistance.
As of Thursday, there have been 4,410 measles cases in the U.S. this year. In Pennsylvania, there have been 1,286 cases as of Monday.

Even before widespread measles vaccination, congenital measles was rare. That’s because most women had already been infected as children. It’s only now emerging as a threat as measles outbreaks are increasing as vaccination rates fall.

Last month, the American Academy of Pediatrics added a “frequently asked questions” page about congenital measles to its website in response to ongoing and increasing measles outbreaks. According to the AAP, congenital measles occurs in newborns whose mothers have been infected during the two weeks before birth and who test positive or develop measles symptoms within 10 days of delivery.

Anecdotally, doctors have said that at least six babies were born in Pennsylvania with congenital measles. Babies can have a range of symptoms, from a rash and fever to pneumonia, neurological problems and low blood platelets. At least two developed pneumonia and were admitted to an intensive care unit, doctors said.

Congenital measles can be deadly. One father in Lancaster County previously told NBC News that his wife was sick with measles in August and went into labor a month early. Their baby died shortly after birth.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Congenital measles can also lead to severe brain and immune system issues later in life, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said. Those long-term complications can include a very rare and severe inflammatory brain condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE. It can occur seven to 10 years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. There is evidence that SSPE may occur earlier in children born with congenital measles.
There’s no specific treatment for congenital measles other than supportive care, such as fluids, hydration and supplemental oxygen.

The best way to prevent the newborn condition is for women to get vaccinated before getting pregnant, the health department said. Pregnant women who get measles are unable to get the vaccine because the shot contains a weakened but live version of the virus.

Unvaccinated pregnant women who are exposed to measles can get a dose of immunoglobulin within six days of that exposure, the health department said, to “provide protection against measles infection or reduce the risk of serious illness among susceptible people.”
The vaccine can be given to women after they deliver their babies and is safe for breastfeeding mothers, according to state health officials.

title: Kyle Kennedy, granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, dies at 42
summary: Kyle Francis Kennedy, an educator and granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, died last month after suffering a severe spinal cord injury.
story: Kyle Francis Kennedy, an educator and granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, died last month after suffering a severe spinal cord injury that resulted in long term paralysis and years of medical issues, a Massachusetts funeral home said.
She was 42.
Kennedy “passed away peacefully” on Sept. 21 “at her home in Westwood, Massachusetts,” according to an obituary by Burke Funeral Homes. Her cause of death was not announced.
She “built a career devoted to early childhood education,” the obituary said.

“Blessed with a formidable intellect, dry wit, and beauty, she will be remembered for her devotion to her children Conor, Josephine, and Declan, and her support for educational reform for disadvantaged children and for people living with disabilities.”
Kennedy grew up in Cohasset, Massachusetts, and attended the prestigious Milton Academy before matriculating to Georgetown University.

She spent a semester abroad in Florence, Italy, which “left a lasting mark” and led to her “deep love of Tuscan Renaissance art and a lifelong talent for making pasta dishes from scratch,” the obituary said.
She earned a master’s degree in early education from Pace University and another master’s in education policy from  Harvard.
Kennedy spent two years in the Teach for America program, working in New York City public school system in “an experience that launched a career in education,” according to her obituary.

“She went on to become a passionate advocate for more equitable elementary education and charter schooling, later working with technology companies focused on reforming and improving school curricula, and as a coach for educators working with young students,” the obituary said.
Kennedy was the daughter of Michael LeMoyne Kennedy, the  sixth oldest child of RFK and Ethel Kennedy.
Michael LeMoyne Kennedy was just 39 when he was fatally injured on Dec. 31, 1997, in Colorado, slamming into a tree while playing ski-football on an icy Aspen slope.
Like many in her famed family, Kennedy was fond of the outdoors and sports. She ran in the 2019 Boston Marathon, competing under her married name, Kyle Kerr.
But she spent the last several years of life unable to walk.

“In 2020, Kyle suffered a severe spinal cord injury that resulted in long term paralysis, disability, and other medical challenges,” the obituary said. “The years that followed brought struggles but Kyle fought to maintain her dry wit and determination through it all, trying to be the best possible mother to her sons and caring for her two beloved, ill-behaved Wheaten terriers.”
It was not disclosed how Kennedy suffered that traumatic 2020 injury.
“She also began to advocate for people living with disabilities, including testifying at the Massachusetts state house in a hearing on discrimination in disabled health care,” the funeral home added.
Kennedy is survived by her sons, Conor, 12, and Declan, 10, ex-husband Liam Kerr, mother Victoria Denise Gifford, brother Michael LeMoyne Kennedy Jr.  and sister Rory Gifford Kennedy.
