“He sent me a picture — a still from the filming they were doing, and they’re crossing the Abbey Road crossing,” McCartney said. “The Paul character is markedly smaller!”
McCartney said he just had to pick up the phone.
“I texted him, Sam,” McCartney said during the episode, released Oct. 13. “‘Don’t do this.’”

For the biopics, McCartney is being played by Paul Mescal who, according to his IMDB page, is 5’11” — not at all a short king. Harris Dickinson, who will star as John Lennon, is just pretty darn tall. His height is listed as 6’2” on his IMDB page.
Barry Keoghan will play Ringo Starr in the films while Joseph Quinn will appear as George Harrison.
In the podcast episode, McCartney admits that he’s “got a thing” about height.

“We were all the same height and Ringo was a bit smaller,” he explains. “(Director Sam Taylor-Johnson) did a film called ‘Nowhere Boy,’ and the John character, — who she later married — he’s bigger than me in the film!”
“Nowhere Boy,” released in 2009, featured Aaron Taylor-Johnson as Lennon while Thomas Brodie-Sangster played McCartney.
McCartney, who said he is still good friends with the director, recalled that she gave him an explanation.
“She said, ‘This is a movie. It’s not a documentary,’” a disgruntled McCartney says. “I thought, ‘Well, I don’t like that explanation.’ But I couldn’t do anything because by now she’d made the film.”
He added: “There was I, little Paul. And, you know, John, the great big hero. And it’s like — no! It’s not true.”

title: Miley Cyrus Breaks Down During Tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘Me and Dolly, We Are Eternal’
summary: Miley Cyrus got emotional while honoring her beloved late “Aunt Dolly” during her comeback performance at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles.
story: Miley Cyrus got emotional while honoring her beloved late “Aunt Dolly” during her comeback performance at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles.

The singer, who made her return to the stage in her first solo show since 2022, sang a soulful rendition of Dolly Parton’s hit “Jolene.” But before Cyrus, the goddaughter of the “Queen of Country,” performed the cover, she said a few words about Parton, breaking down during the sweet tribute.
“Me and Dolly, we are eternal,” Cyrus said, speaking to the crowd as she sat at the edge of the stage. “Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart.”
Cyrus got particularly tearful when reflecting on Parton’s absence. The longtime country music icon passed away in August, following a brief battle with cancer, her estate said.
“And I’m gonna see her again,” Cyrus said. “And I can’t f------ wait. And I miss her.”

The tribute was part of Cyrus’ first performance at the iconic venue. Her second sold-out show will take place Oct. 18. The singer, who’s currently promoting her new album “Bass Persuades,” last performed a full-length concert in Mexico roughly four years ago at the Corona Capital Festival.
Her latest set of shows are particularly significant for the “Flowers” singer, who explained to the audience that she had only ever seen Parton perform live once. And it was at the Hollywood Bowl.
“Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my Aunt Dolly,” Cyrus said, introducing “Jolene.” “This is one of those songs.”

Parton, who died at age 80, was a fixture in Cyrus’ life. The Queen of Country once toured with the singer’s father, country star Billy Ray Cyrus, and was bestowed the role of godmother upon Miley Cyrus’ birth in 1992.
During an interview with Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, released Sept. 17, Miley Cyrus opened up about the meaningful relationship she shared with Parton.

“She was always right,” Cyrus said. “It’s like how your mom’s always right, and when you’re a kid, you’re like, ‘What does she know?’ And then as you get older, you’re like, ‘Everything. How? Where did this come from? You’re just a normal person. Why do you know everything?’”
Cyrus added: “Dolly was just always right about stuff.”

title: The Shocking ‘You Can See Everything’ Twist: Wait, Who Shows Up in the Elizabeth Holmes Documentary?
summary: The documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything,” takes a surprise turn that will have viewers on the edge of their seats. Here is what happens.
story: Spoilers ahead for “You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes.
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, has officially been released and people and critics have thoughts — many, many thoughts.
They also want to know what Amanda Seyfried thinks.
During the documentary’s opening weekend, the actor was asked her opinion on the film by many reporters while at the Academy Museum Gala. She remained tight-lipped, and there’s a reason for that.
Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the almost 3-hour film begins 34 days before the Theranos founder and CEO entered prison in 2023.

While Holmes invites a film crew into her home to follow her, partner William “Billy” Evans and their two children, Willian and Invicta, in her San Diego home, the second half of the film takes an unexpected and polarizing turn.
“You Can See Everything” includes an appearance from Seyfried, who portrayed the disgraced Theranos founder in the Hulu series “The Dropout.”
Holmes hoped to revolutionize blood testing. However, in 2022, after a federal investigation uncovered critical violations in a Theranos lab, she was found guilty of four counts of wire fraud.
Sentenced to 11 years in prison, “You Can See Everything” shows Holmes maintaining her innocence before surrendering to Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Texas.
To tell the rest of the story, the filmmakers ask for Seyfried’s help.
Why Is Amanda Seyfried in ‘You Can See Everything’?
Amid the questions that arise about Holmes, as well as her relationship with Evans, Fielder decides to reach out to none other than Seyfried for insight.
Seyfried portrayed Holmes in the 2022 limited series “The Dropout,” even winning an Emmy for her performance.

During his stay at their home, Fielder has Holmes and Evans watch episodes of “The Dropout.” The show ends up making Holmes uncomfortable and through tears she tells Fielder she no longer wants to watch it.
Holmes then goes to prison, but filming continues.

Holmes and Evans had been working on a new business venture, what they called Theranos 2.0. Two years after Holmes reported to prison, Evans calls the film crew and tells them he has an update on their project.
Fielder tries to get updates about Holmes, who was unreachable with cameras, but doesn’t get much. Then tensions start brewing between Evans and the film crew.

“As we are trying to finish making (the film) ... (Evans) started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him,” Fielder said at an Oct. 6 Los Angeles screening. “It was uncomfortable for us ... We sort of had to stop. Communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that state for a little bit.”
Fielder noted, at the time, that Evans had not seen the film.
How Did Amanda Seyfried Get Involved in ‘You Can See Everything’?
Fielder and Oppenheim had never met Seyfried, but was one of many people they reached out to in late 2025, according to press notes.
“A lot of people say no in this process, and a lot of people who are relevant to her story want nothing to do with her anymore,” Fielder said.
Thanks to a mutual friend, Fielder was able to connect with Seyfried, who agreed to watch their footage and talk about her experience on camera.

While preparing for her role in “The Dropout,” Seyfried never met or communicated with Holmes. However, the actor became “an invaluable key” in how the filmmakers continued their investigation and the “unprecedented” ending.
About halfway through the film, after Holmes is in prison, Seyfried and Fielder watch the footage of Holmes watching “The Dropout.”
This was the first in-person meeting between the two and it was captured “as it unfolded, unscripted and in real time.”
What came next is unorthodox, unconventional and intriguing.
Seyfried accompanies Fielder to Holmes’ San Diego home where he recounts the first time he met the biotech company founder. They then re-create that very scene.
As the documentary continues, Seyfried continues to help Fielder in his re-creations, including a meeting with the filmmakers, A24 executives and Holmes and Evans.
As Seyfried’s involvement deepens, she begins to bring her own perspective to Holmes’ life, also questioning the CEO and her partner’s intentions.

In a wild turn of events, Fielder brings Seyfried to Evans’ home, where she gets a chance to briefly speak with Holmes who calls from prison. After some shocking revelations, including Evans controlling Holmes’ social media accounts, the actor gets into a heated argument with Evans, cementing her dislike of him.
Seyfried also re-creates Fielder’s meeting with Holmes in prison, since cameras are not allowed inside.
As the documentary comes to an end, Seyfried and Fielder question if Holmes is a victim or they, too, are being deceived.

“I still am not sure to this day what I experienced,” Fielder said during the Los Angeles screening. “It’s one of the reasons I’m excited for it to come out and more people to see it because it was just a small group for so long. I actually think maybe it being out there everyone can help me understand what I went through.”
What Has Amanda Seyfried Said About ‘You Can See Everything’?
During the Oct. 17 Academy Museum Gala, Seyfried was asked how her life is right now, alluding to her unexpected cameo.
“It’s interesting, yeah, it’s interesting,” Seyfried told The Hollywood Reporter, who added that it’s difficult to do interviews at the moment.
The actor agreed, adding, “For a good reason. I don’t know, I think everything that’s happening is meant to happen ... everyone that’s in your life is meant to be in your life.”
Both did not specifically mention her role in the film, but the reporter asked if it made some of her conversations difficult.
“Only of late,” she said, before being asked what topics she could talk about.

“I like to talk about the emus. I like to talk about Halloween,” she said. “And you can engage with me if you want to talk about all things having to do with apple pie and olives and really good hard ciders.”
Additionally, in the comment section of The Hollywood Reporter’s Instagram video, Seyfried reacted to her own response.
“What AM I even saying,” she wrote.
Variety’s Marc Malkin also chatted with Seyfried at the same event.
“Don’t ask me anything,” she said, before coming up to him. “I got nothing to say.”
He then asked if she thinks there will be a second season of “The Dropout,” to which she replied, “I don’t think so. But life is long.”
She also added that she’s kept up on Holmes’ story “on and off.”

title: What the Victoria’s Secret CEO Calls the Store’s Customers, and Why
summary: Victoria’s Secret CEO Hillary Super explains why the company has a very specific way of referring to its customers.
story: Victoria’s Secret CEO Hillary Super says the company has a very specific way of referring to its customers.
“I would say, especially our younger customers want an in-store experience,” Super, who has served as Victoria’s Secret CEO since 2024, told Savannah Sellers in a story that aired Oct. 17 on TODAY.
“There is this tremendous opportunity to be a third space for her and a gathering place where she can come and shop and have fun with her friends.”
The wording caught Sellers’ ear.
“It’s interesting to me to hear you using ‘she’ and ‘her’ about your customer, like we’re talking about an individual that you know,” Sellers said.
“Yes,” replied Super.
“One of our brand values is to put her first,” Super continued. “Everything that we do, we do for her. We read all of the social comments. I read them every single night before I go to bed.”
The Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show will take place Oct. 18, live at 7:30 p.m. ET on YouTube. It’s the latest move for a company that is trying to regain trust with its customer base.

Known for making superstars out of the likes of Heidi Klum, Tyra Banks and Gisele Bündchen, Victoria’s Secret found itself making headlines when it came out that former owner Lex Wexner had close ties with Jeffrey Epstein.
Wexner resigned in 2020, while saying he didn’t do anything wrong and he wasn’t aware of Epstein’s criminal activity.

“It’s not something any of us really want to be tied to, but at the same time, it’s important to know, know that bit of history to understand how far we’ve come and how much we’ve changed,” Super told TODAY.
There have also been accusations about poor treatment of models, including harassment and assault related to the Epstein era. That environment also led to change.
“We have very strict protocols in our casting, in our fittings, in any model interaction, and it’s actually monitored by a designated individual. So we’ve come a long way in that regard,” said

There have also been changes to the way the brand recruits talent for the Victoria’s Secret and Pink brands. “We like the mix of OG angels, new talent, sports figures, influencers. It’s about the mix of the community,” Super said.
“We’re really thinking much more expansively about who an angel can be, and to me that’s about self-possession, and just personal confidence, strength, and feeling great in your own skin,” she added.

title: All About Elizabeth Holmes’ Prison Sentence: When She’s Out
summary: As the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” hits theaters, people are wondering when she will be out of prison.
story: As the buzzy new Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” hits theaters on Oct. 16, the former CEO of Theranos remains behind bars.
The film gives an unnerving and intimate look at Holmes’ life with partner Billy Evans and their two young children in the weeks leading up to the start of her federal prison sentence in May 2023.
Holmes, 42, was convicted in 2022 by a California jury of wire fraud after siphoning off hundreds of millions of dollars from several high-profile investors and misrepresenting Theranos technology.

The Silicon Valley startup had claimed that it was going to revolutionize healthcare with a machine that could conduct hundreds of medical tests on a single drop of blood. Prosecutors said that Holmes knew the technology was faulty and still solicited investors and business partners like Walgreens — something she denied during the trial.
In “You Can See Everything,” comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim spend extensive time with Holmes and her family.
A trailer released in September shows that Fielder moved into her house during the filming.
“I think this is the moment in time to capture this story before I’m gone,” she seemingly tells the comedian at one point.
Given Holmes’ backstory, Fielder asks her why she should be believed.
“That’s because I don’t have anything to hide,” she tells him.

News of “You Can See Everything” went viral after it was screened at the Telluride Film Festival in September, with attendees having strong reactions. Rebecca Keegan of NBC News Digital was among those in the crowd.
“There were audible gasps and ‘no ways’ consistently throughout this almost three-hour film,” she told NBC News correspondent Erin McLaughlin on TODAY Sept. 8.
The buzzy film also hits theaters three weeks after news broke that Holmes is expected to be moved from prison to a halfway house next year.
How Long Is Elizabeth Holmes’ Prison Sentence?
Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison in November 2022, but it has since been reduced.
In May 2023, U.S. District Judge Edward Davila ordered her to pay $452 million in restitution to the victims of her crimes.
Also, former Theranos president Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani was sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison and three years of probation after being convicted of 12 counts of fraud.
Holmes has been serving her sentence at a minimum-security prison in Bryan, Texas.
When Will Elizabeth Holmes Be Released from Prison?

Her original prison sentence was reduced from 135 months to 123 months in March 2026 when a judge agreed she did not cause “substantial financial hardship” to her victims, according to a court document.
Her scheduled release date is now Feb. 22, 2030.
Holmes is also scheduled to be transferred from the minimum-security prison in Bryan to a halfway house in 2027, according to one of her victims. There has been no change in her release date.

Alan Eisenman, who invested about $1.2 million in Theranos, told NBC News on Sept. 24 that he was alerted by the Justice Department’s victim notification system that Holmes is to be transferred to the Austin Transitional Center. The halfway house is in an unincorporated community that borders Austin, Texas.

He said he has not received any money in restitution from Holmes that was part of the court ruling in 2023. Holmes’ attorney from her trial did not respond to a phone message from NBC News requesting comment.
Eisenman told NBC News he plans to watch “You Can See Everything.”
“She’s obviously manipulative,” Eisenman said. “If people don’t see that, then they’re blind. She’s the most conniving person I’ve ever met.”

title: Did the ‘Cheers’ Cast Drink Real Beer on the Show? George Wendt Revealed the Answer on TODAY in 1988
summary: “Cheers” star George Wendt spoke with TODAY in 1988 about whether he drinks beer on the show and what he hoped to do after the series ends.
story: Welcome to the “TODAY Archives,” where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment features “Cheers” star George Wendt on TODAY on Dec. 8, 1988, talking about the success of the show in the middle of its lengthy run.

“Cheers” remains one of the most beloved and critically acclaimed sitcoms in history, thanks in large part to a stellar cast that included George Wendt. The late actor played barfly Norm, the unmotivated accountant whose love of beer and the bar trumped everything else in his life.

Wendt, who died in 2025, would have turned 78 on Oct. 17. He earned six Emmy Award nominations for his portrayal of Norm, coming in six consecutive years from 1984 through 1989, the heart of the show’s 11-season run, from 1982 until 1993.
“Cheers” was a massive hit, so did Wendt feel any pressure to perform for a live audience?
“You get to like pressure after a while. If you don’t, you’re really in the wrong business because there’s so much of it,” he told Gene Shalit on TODAY on Dec. 8, 1988.
Did They Drink Beer on ‘Cheers’?
Norm’s greatest love was beer, so did Wendt actually drink real beer while shooting his scenes?
“It’s not beer. It’s ‘near beer,’ which I guess it’s not available in draft or in kegs, so they pour cans of ‘near beer’ into Coca-Cola dispensers and out it comes,” Wendt said.

“They do that before the audience gets in and it’s flat and warm and just horrible by the time we have to drink it,” he continued. “In the first couple of seasons, I used to just be swilling it, be a real actor, sort of behaving as a bar patron onstage. Now, I have a feel for where the cameras are, and I only drink it when I’m on camera.”
Would There Be a Letdown After He Finished ‘Cheers’?

“Cheers” rolled with the punches with cast turnover, including the death of Nicholas Colasanto, who played Coach, and Shelley Long’s decision to leave after the fifth season. Wendt said there would be a “huge letdown” when the show wrapped up, but he missed the mark in saying that the end of the comedy was on the horizon.

“I can get sentimental right away,” he said. “I mean, we had so many reasons to be sentimental, anyway. When Nick Colasanto died, when Shelley left, and now, you know, the imminent end of the show — not all that imminent — but the end is certainly closer than the beginning.”
“Cheers” would remain a ratings juggernaut until its series finale aired in May 1993.
“It’s kind of a sobering thought that Norm might be the best role I’ve ever had,” he said. “I mean, it’s definitely the best role I’ve ever had. Might be the best role I’ll ever have.”
When Was the Last Time George Wendt Had to Pay for a Beer?
Wendt may not have had real beer on the set, but he certainly was taken care of whenever he was out.
“I know, it’s one of the great perks of employment history. I get free beer wherever I go,” he said.
“Too bad you’re not in the series where you’re a Cadillac salesman,” Shalit said.

While the role of Norm afforded Wendt fame — and free beer — he also wanted to keep acting in any form once his time on the show ended, whether it was TV or film, something he would do for the duration of his career.

“We just want to do good work, if possible, and the medium isn’t really important. Let’s say stage, feature films and television. The more you can spread it around, it really stays interesting for you,” he said.

title: Who Is Billy Evans? Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Seen in ‘You Can See Everything’ Documentary
summary: Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall as the disgraced founder of Theranos is the subject of the new A24 documentary “You Can See Everything,” which premieres in limited theaters on Oct. 16.
story: Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall as the disgraced founder of Theranos is the subject of the new A24 documentary “You Can See Everything,” which premieres in limited theaters on Oct. 16.
The documentary, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, goes behind the scenes to tell the story of how Holmes, 42, vowed to revolutionize blood testing only to end up a convicted felon.

After a 2022 federal investigation of Theranos labs uncovered critical violations, Holmes, who was just 19 when she founded the biotech company, was found guilty of four counts of wire fraud and sentenced to 11 years in prison.

“You Can See Everything” also delves into Holmes’ private life. The movie includes footage of Holmes with fiancé William “Billy” Evans and their two children that was shot in 2023 during her final days of freedom before she reported to a Texas federal prison.

According to the filmmakers, they revealed at a Los Angeles screening of the doc, Evans has yet to see the documentary. Fielder noted that after Holmes went to prison, Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process” that made it difficult to continue filming and “communication broke down.”

In February 2025, Holmes broke her silence to give her first prison interview to People. She described life behind bars, which includes two visits a week from Evans and their kids, as “hell and torture.”
“The people I love the most have to walk away as I stand here, a prisoner, and my reality sinks in,” Holmes said.
Read on to learn more about Holmes’ fiancé Evans.
Evans’ Grandparents Founded Several Luxury Hotels
In 1953, Evans’ grandparents, William and Anne Evans, founded Evans Hotels, a hospitality group consisting of several luxury hotels in San Diego, according to NPR.
Holmes and Evans Got Engaged in 2018, a Year After Meeting
Holmes met Evans at a charity event in Oct. 2017, she told People in her 2025 prison interview.
A year after meeting, Evans popped the question by presenting Holmes with a silver snake ring he bought at a Taylor Swift “Reputation” tour concert.
“I asked him 20 times if he wanted to spend his life with me,” Holmes said. “There were a million reasons why not.”
Evans Spoke of His Love for Holmes in a Pre-Trial Letter
Evans poured his heart out about Holmes in an emotional pre-trial letter to the judge in her case, reported The Independent.
In his 12-page letter, which also included photos of the couple, Evans wrote that he fell instantly in love with Holmes, whom he called “Liz.”
“I was captivated by her childish wonder and authenticity,” he wrote, adding “She listened more intently than anyone I had ever met.”
Evans praised Holmes’ vision, writing, “Her capacity to change the world is limitless.”
He also included the story of how Holmes competed in a Golden Gate Bridge ocean swim event in 2021 while pregnant with William.
“There were fifty reasons I thought it was a bad idea, the sharks, the tides, her complete inexperience swimming post age 14,” Evans wrote.
“You would think by now I would learn to not discount her perseverance,” he wrote.
Holmes and Evans Share 2 Kids
Holmes gave birth to the couple’s first child, son William, shortly before her fraud trial began.
She and Evans welcomed their second child, daughter Invicta, in 2023.
According to People, Holmes sat in the back seat of a Ford Expedition pumping breast milk for three-month-old Invicta as she approached the prison gates to begin her term.
Holmes ‘Always Wanted to Be a Mother’
While speaking to People, Holmes addressed speculation that she and Evans schemed to start a family to depict Holmes as more sympathetic so she might avoid time in prison.

“I know how the optics look, but I always wanted to be a mother,” Holmes said. “I truly did not think I would ever be convicted or found guilty. I kept talking to my lawyers and they also assured me we would never get this far.”
“It wasn’t planned and I can’t worry about what others think. It’s just when the timing happened,” Holmes added.

title: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
summary: U.S. envoys met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
story: U.S. envoys met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.

President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war. Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”

Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo, with Kushner joining remotely. Zelenskyy held talks with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb prior to meeting the U.S. delegation.

Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.

Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.

In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.

“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.

Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”

Zelenskyy said later on Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian missile attacks that he said occurred without enough notice. The change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including the phone call with Rubio earlier in the day, according to Zelenskyy.
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.

When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”

Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.

Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.

title: Oil prices rise, threatening to push cost of gas higher two weeks before midterms
summary: Oil prices surged in early trading Tuesday, as energy markets adjusted to a new normal in the Middle East.
story: Oil prices surged in early trading Tuesday, as energy markets adjusted to a new normal in the Middle East. The increase in crude prices threatened to drive up the cost of gas in the United States just two weeks before the midterm elections.

U.S. crude prices jumped as much as 5% to about $109 a barrel, the highest price since April, while the price of international Brent crude climbed 1.5% to more than $111, its highest price since May. Prices pulled back later in the morning, after weaker-than-expected U.S. housing starts raised the prospect of a broader slowdown and lower demand.
Prices for advanced oil contracts dated for next year also hit record highs, “implying an extended period of high oil prices deep into 2027,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Tuesday.

“The 2027 contracts are moving higher as well as the possible reality of higher for longer oil prices sink in,” Peter Boockvar, author of the Boock Report and chief investment officer of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, said in a note Tuesday.
High gas prices have become a major issue for voters in the midterms, where Republicans face dwindling odds of maintaining their control of Congress.

A recent NBC News poll found that 67% of U.S. adults believe gas prices are a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. A majority also said that current economic conditions have caused them to change their spending habits.
U.S. gasoline prices had started off the week lower. At $4.28 a gallon, the national average price of unleaded was on pace to reach its lowest level in a month.
But that trend is likely to be upended as higher crude prices filter through to the pump.
Several factors were contributing to Tuesday’s oil price hikes.
The cost of chartering a large tanker vessel to transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz has quadrupled since September, data shows.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Much of that increase is a risk premium, both for sailors and insurance. During the past two weeks, at least 18 ⁠vessels have been attacked in the strait, the ship-tracking group Kpler said in a note ⁠Monday.
The higher cost of transport has begun to offset the recent bump in supply from a growing number of ships moving through the strait.
The Iranian attacks on ships have also prompted investor speculation that the Trump administration will be more likely to escalate against Iran after the midterms, the Deutsche Bank analysts said.
Iran-aligned Houthi rebels also claimed Monday that they had hit airport, energy and military targets in Saudi Arabia, as well as a ​training camp in Yemen for that government’s security forces.
The U.K. will begin deploying fighter jets over Saudi Arabia to help protect against further Houthi attacks, the Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The entry of another country’s military into the regional hostilities was taken as a further sign of escalating tensions.

title: Tech stocks erase $1 trillion of wealth as oil surges to $110 for the first time since May
summary: Tech stocks shed more than $1 trillion in value Friday, as the price of oil soared to its highest levels in five months.
story: Tech stocks shed more than $1 trillion in value Friday, as the price of oil soared to its highest levels in five months.

The Nasdaq 100 index, which tracks most of the country’s largest tech and AI-linked companies, sold off by 2.5% and now sits about 7% below its most recent all-time high — a record it had only notched last week.
The S&P 500 dropped 1% and the Russell 2000 index fell 1.6%. The Philadelphia semiconductor index dropped 3.8% for its eight straight day of losses, the longest such streak since 2008.
The sharp drop in tech shares came as worries about ballooning debt, high interest rates and rising oil prices all resurfaced.

Brent crude oil, widely considered to be among the most important prices in global energy, surpassed $110 per barrel shortly after 2:30 p.m. ET, its highest level since May. It ended the week at $109.86 per barrel, still its highest closing level since May 19.

U.S. crude oil, which also steers gas prices, jumped 3.5% Friday to close at $101.41 per barrel. It was the first time West Texas Intermediate crude had crossed the $100 threshold, closely watched by both traders and the public, since September.

The continued upward trend in energy prices increases the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again this year. The Fed already boosted rates by 0.25% in September to tame inflation that had risen as a result of higher oil and gas prices.
Diesel futures also jumped Friday by more than 1%. The cost of this commercial fuel critical for farming and other industrial sectors has risen even faster than regular gasoline in recent months.
The steady rise in the price of fuel around the world began this spring, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February and triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
But an escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months has caused an even more dramatic price spike for diesel.
Russia has traditionally been one of the world’s largest diesel exporters. But attacks by Ukrainian forces on its energy infrastructure has taken much of its refining capacity offline.
On Friday, another Russian refiner suspended some crude oil operations. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”
Energy assets in Ukraine have also been targeted by Russian strikes.

As the world seeks alternative sources for diesel, there are few clear opportunities to expand diesel production. Refineries in the U.S. and Europe are already running at nearly maximum capacity to churn out as much diesel fuel as possible.
President Donald Trump is intensely focused on the high cost of diesel fuel because of its key role in driving up inflation — a top issue for American voters in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Trump has tried multiple actions to lower prices, but those have not resulted in a significant step-down for diesel prices.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The president has also touted a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin as a way to lower prices, but as of Friday, no actual Russian diesel had been identified as having reached the global market.
Additionally, a group of American lawmakers introduced a bill that would block Trump’s Russian diesel deal. It has little chance of passing the Republican-controlled House.

But polling indicates that Republicans are unlikely to maintain a majority in the House after November’s elections. The Russian diesel-blocking bill offers a preview of the kind of legislation that could advance under Democratic control.
Yet even now, the legislation adds to “growing doubts that a U.S.-Russia diesel deal will come to fruition,” said Mason Mendez, global real assets analyst at Wells Fargo.
“Investors also remain concerned about further military escalation in the Middle East, as attacks on commercial shipping and regional infrastructure have increased in recent weeks,” he said.
“Looking into 2027, the need to rebuild depleted global inventories could create an additional source of demand and keep energy prices elevated for longer.”

At the same time that inflation pushes interest rates higher around the world, trillion-dollar tech companies are borrowing and spending hundreds of billions of dollars to develop AI and build their vast data centers.
This week, fresh cracks began to show in the AI business model, as investors raised questions about when their massive injections of cash into AI companies would pay off.
The two worst performing stocks in the Nasdaq 100 on Friday were both data center companies: Nebuius and CoreWeave.
The value of CoreWeave’s shares has plunged more than 25% over the past month.
But these companies are just two of the dozens that have borrowed billions of dollars at high interest rates to expand at a breakneck pace.

Just a day before Friday’s sell-off, Ed Yardeni, a highly regarded market analyst, cut his year-end S&P 500 target to 7,900, down from 8,400, over what he said was rising investor caution about the artificial intelligence trade and lingering doubts about inflation and higher interest rates.

title: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
summary: An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.
story: An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.

Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away.

Local media reported that one of Haines’ legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports.
Australian lawmaker in critical condition after car ramming

Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then did a  U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car.

“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the network that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time.
The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well.
She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and his partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement Tuesday.
“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added.

title: Dramatic images show violent unrest sweeping across France
summary: France unrest protest photos over the weekend Macron election buildup
story: Widespread violence erupted across France over the weekend, as rioters and looters ransacked storefronts, clashed with police and set fire to municipal buildings.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured, the French Interior Ministry said, after some of the worst unrest the country has seen in years.

title: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
summary: The “historic” mission comes as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia.
story: Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the front lines by drone.
The “historic” mission comes just as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia.

Shared by the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade on Monday, the video shows the soldier strapping himself into a large drone and being flown at what appears to be relatively low altitude over blurred-out territory. The drone carefully lowers him, and the drone operator greets him with “Welcome back to the ground!” The video also shows blurred faces of drone operators who carried out the mission.

The post said the unidentified infantryman was wounded at his position. “Due to intense enemy drone activity and the presence of landmines, evacuation using conventional unmanned ground vehicles was impossible,” the brigade said.
Injured Ukrainian soldier rescued with a drone
“At that point, the specialists in our unit took it upon themselves to attempt something that had never been done before: evacuating a serviceman using an aerial drone,” it added.
The craft was a heavy-lift hexacopter, it said, originally designed as a bomber by a Ukrainian manufacturer. It looks about twice the size of the soldier in the video.
The specialists working on the mission had to ensure the drone could carry a human being without flipping over or swaying excessively, according to the unit.

The rescued soldier is undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, the brigade added. The squad leader and programmer with the brigade, identified only by his call sign, Napalm, called the soldier a “hero” for agreeing to the mission, “having seen and heard the kind of machine that had arrived to get him.”
In a separate statement, Ukraine’s Ground Forces said its drone units are already conducting operations “that were recently considered science fiction.”
The war has increasingly become a technological arms race, with both Ukraine and Russia relying on drones to reduce human casualties.

The conflict has taken a severe toll on both armies, although neither side reports up-to-date numbers of those killed, injured or missing. Ukraine in particular has faced a severe shortage of manpower as it has tried to ramp up recruitment.

Ukraine took a major leap in drone technology this year, allowing it to limit Russian logistics in occupied territories, as well as strike deeper inside Russia to target Russian oil refineries, commercial warehouses and data centers.
“This mission proves once again that Ukrainian service members, working in tandem with Ukrainian manufacturers, are setting global trends in the conduct of warfare,” the brigade’s statement added.

Despite hoping its drone innovation would give it the upper hand at the negotiating table, Kyiv has faced pressure from the U.S. to halt its strikes on Russian oil sites after President Donald Trump signed a diesel deal with the Kremlin this month.
Kyiv has since also reported gaps in intelligence sharing and restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink service, which is crucial for its drone missions, battlefield communications and air defense.

The drone evacuation comes just days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the Ukrainian government had approved an “experimental project” to use drones for medical logistics. Koretskyi said that flights would require coordination with the military and that drones would be given a special status and be identifiable in the air.

“During the war, moving medical cargo by road can cost critical time, especially for transplants,” he said. “Drones will be able to carry medicines, medical products, blood samples and donor organs between hospitals, including from remote areas.”

title: France moves to impose curfews as it reels from worst violence in years
summary: Rioting and looting erupted across the country over the weekend, with authorities conceding they had “lost control” in major cities.
story: Only shattered glass and the skeletal frame of the Haussmannian roof remain of Limoges’ 19th century town hall.
The town was among the places hit hardest by the rioting and looting that erupted across France over the weekend, leaving the country reeling from its worst violence in years.

The towering spire at the heart of Limoges ultimately collapsed in flames, drawing cheers from the crowd below that were captured on video. In Paris, the Louvre Museum said it was closed after protesters announced their blockade of the iconic tourist site.
Authorities conceded they had “lost control” in major cities, and said Monday they had asked some cities to impose a partial curfew in a bid to restore order.

“Despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed and that is a miracle,” Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said after an emergency meeting with top officials. About 3,000 businesses had been looted or vandalized, he added.

The unrest came on the heels of an anti-government movement that had seen days of largely peaceful protests over rising living costs and poor school conditions. On the weekend, this unrest descended into violence on the streets of cities across France: Rioters, often hooded and masked, looted stores and torched cars and government buildings as they faced off with the police.

title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
summary: The strikes that took place over several days earlier this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers.
story: From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout, millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life.

“I ended up in a situation where I had absolutely no money. Well, I had the money, but it was inaccessible,” said Irina, a blogger from St. Petersburg, who had not been able to access her money for four days when she spoke with NBC News last week.

Irina, who like several other people did not want her last name shared while she was speaking with a foreign news organization about a sensitive matter, said her rent was due the day the first outages happened, when she hoped “that it would be fixed in a few hours.” Days later, she still had no access to money to pay for utilities or even food for her small child.
The strikes that took place over several days this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers as Ukraine seeks to bring the war home for Russians.

The disruption hit myriad services provided by Yandex, a tech giant akin to Google whose services are deeply integrated into daily life in Russia and whose digital infrastructure other third-party platforms rely on.

Many people took to social media to complain about not being able to order taxis or food delivery. Others reported not being able to access their files on the company’s storage service, while some even struggled to get into their homes after their digital keys went offline.

title: Priest in Ecuador dies after crucifix falls on him during livestreamed Mass
summary: The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari was the parish priest at the Church of Perpetual Relief in Guayaquil.
story: A priest in Ecuador died Saturday after a crucifix fell on him during a livestreamed Mass, according to church officials and video of the incident.
The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died Saturday, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil announced.
He was the parish priest at the Church of Perpetual Relief of the Central Vicariate, the archdiocese said.
Molinari “has left to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory,” it said in a news release.
The Mass was livestreamed, but the video was taken down. The video, reviewed by NBC News, showed a large crucifix hanging on a wall behind Molinari suddenly falling forward onto the back of his head.
For Subscribers
Molinari was behind the altar, facing the congregation, and did not see the crucifix falling behind him.
For Subscribers
Molinari did not stand back up, and parishioners are heard on the video shrieking and crying. Some rush to tend to him.
A Eucharist in his memory is scheduled for Sunday evening.

title: U.S. taking Putin’s side would be a ‘historic mistake,’ Zelenskyy says
summary: The Ukrainian leader told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Ukrainian officials believe the decision to limit Starlink, imposed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, came from the U.S. government.
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S.’ formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake” but said he still sees President Donald Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill.

“We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday, referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.”

Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, saying in an executive order that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.” Passed with bipartisan support and signed by Trump last month, the sanctions were intended to target Russia’s revenue streams by punishing global buyers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump defended his decision Sunday, writing on Truth Social that he did not want to “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” Trump added that Zelenskyy was targeting diesel refineries in Russia, which he claimed was “seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.”

Trump added that “Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way,” a claim that comes the same day the Russian Foreign Affairs Ministry announced that Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov would travel to Tehran this week.
The waiver came days after a deal with Putin to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar was announced.

At the same time, Zelenskyy said, U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” blinding Ukraine to incoming ballistic missiles, while limits have been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercept jet-powered drones.
Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe the decision to limit Starlink, imposed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, came in response to a “message from American government.”

The U.S. has been Ukraine’s most significant backer across 4½ years of war, but personal relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have appeared severely strained in recent weeks, with each publicly criticizing the other.
Asked about Trump’s remark last week that he was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelenskyy said he was “very honest” with Trump.
“Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.”
Zelenskyy, who accused the U.S. of betraying Kyiv last week, said his feelings have not changed. He warned that Trump’s diesel deal with Russia “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.”
Announcing the deal last week, Trump expressed hopes that it would go some way to address soaring fuel costs.
But Zelenskyy said the deal wouldn’t have “a real influence” on the price of oil in the U.S. because the rising prices were due to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine.
“I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said.
Of the prospect of the U.S.’ more formally siding with Russia, he said: “If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Zelenskyy said it was a “pity” Trump had waived the sanctions in a bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who he said was “a great supporter of peace and of Ukraine.”
“He invested his life and time because he really believed in Ukraine,” he said.
In a separate interview on “Meet the Press,” Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., defended Trump’s decision to lift the Russia sanctions.

“He’s trying to walk this fine balance between trying to be able to put pressure on Russia, but also to be able to help the American people, so he is choosing the American people first is what he’s doing,” Lankford said, pointing to high gas prices.

Asked whether Trump’s moves indicate the president is siding with Putin, Lankford, a member of the Intelligence Committee, said Trump was “siding with the free people of Ukraine,” adding later that Trump was working to get the two countries “to the table to be able to negotiate.”

The war has seen little recent movement on the front line, with Russia continuing to occupy around a fifth of Ukraine. Trump had vowed to end the conflict within days of the start of his second term, but peace talks have effectively stalled, with Ukraine saying that Russia has rejected a short-term ceasefire and that Putin’s terms for peace are tantamount to a full surrender.
Meanwhile, another difficult winter looms for Ukrainian civilians, with a critical munitions shortage limiting Zelenskyy’s ability to defend infrastructure against Russian strikes.

Zelenskyy said he was due to speak to U.S. negotiators by phone later Sunday and was still hopeful of a meeting in the days ahead. “I’m very open for this, even with all the difficult circumstances,” he said.
He cited some progress after a multiday interruption in U.S. intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which he said has now been “deblocked.”
“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”

European and Ukrainian officials previously told NBC News they believed that a move to limit sharing intelligence, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia, was most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv to make concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

While Zelenskyy indicated that the intelligence problem has been resolved, he said Ukraine was still facing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service.

Asked whether he thought Trump or Musk had directly made the decision to limit Starlink, Zelenskyy said he did not know but thought “both” were involved. He said that if Trump decided tomorrow to lift the restriction, “it will immediately work as it was before.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with his surgeon saying he could be fully recovered in about 10 days.
story: Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with his surgeon saying he could be fully recovered in about 10 days.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News there were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pontiff from making his planned trip to Latin America next month.

The pontiff, who had been recovering at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday, walked out unaided before spending a couple of minutes speaking with well-wishers. He appeared to accept a gift of a homemade smiling Pope figure before getting in a car and being driven back to the Vatican.

“Following the conclusions reached by the medical team this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital, where he was admitted for surgery on his right lung,” the Holy See Press said Saturday in a statement, before the Leo left the building mid-afternoon.
He is expected to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica on Sunday, according to the statement.

The pontiff’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and Margaritora, said that in light of blood tests and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, and after an assessment of his clinical condition, “the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge from the hospital.”
So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.
Leo, who is a Chicago native, resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported.

The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass inside the hospital, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.

The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.
His discharge from the hospital comes less than a month before Leo is scheduled to jet off for a two-week trip to South America, which is set to start Nov. 11.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru.
“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said Wednesday.
Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.
Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer last week.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.
As Margaritora led the procedure, Gemelli’s medical staff recited the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel.

title: Trump says Ukraine resuming strikes on Russian oil sites is a ‘disgrace’
summary: President Donald Trump has labeled Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace,” the latest salvo in his campaign to pressure the U.S. ally over rising gas prices that could cost Republicans in next month’s midterm elections.
story: President Donald Trump has labeled Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace,” the latest salvo in his campaign to pressure the U.S. ally over rising gas prices that could cost Republicans in next month’s midterm elections.

Kyiv said Thursday that it would no longer abide by Trump’s “energy ceasefire,” citing Russia’s refusal to halt its own attacks on Ukraine’s power grid. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the U.S. of costing civilian lives by striking deals with Moscow and withdrawing support that is crucial to Kyiv’s defense against the invasion launched by President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian officials had raised alarm after gaps in intelligence sharing left Kyiv vulnerable to Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink satellite service disrupted military operations.  Zelenskyy said Friday that the technology was still not fully restored.
With Ukraine defying his demands to halt strikes, Trump responded late Thursday.

“If you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty. “I think that’s a disgrace. There’s plenty of other targets; they don’t have to hit,” Trump said.

“Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with” on the war, he said, adding that “I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
As his clash escalated with Trump, Zelenskyy was in Brussels on Friday to shore up support from European allies, whom he called “real leaders” as they gathered for a crucial summit.

Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery Thursday after Zelenskyy said he was “done” with the truce, which Trump had announced to the apparent surprise of both sides in the war. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv reported any new strikes on Russian refineries Friday.
Trump has sought to blame Ukraine’s strikes for destabilizing the price of diesel globally, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.
But this campaign of attacks deep inside enemy territory has given Ukraine crucial leverage, sparking a major fuel crisis inside Russia.

Kyiv hoped this would give it a stronger hand at the negotiating table, but as Washington pushes for an end to the conflict it has taken a series of steps that have caused surprise and alarm among Ukraine and its backers in Europe.

Last week, Trump announced a deal to buy diesel from Russia, an apparent attempt to relieve pressure at the pump for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections but which reversed years of U.S. policy. Trump then called for Kyiv to stop all strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and said Zelenskyy had to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader.

It comes amid mounting questions about whether the U.S. is still sharing critical military intelligence with Ukraine after a pair of major strikes earlier this week that Kyiv said came without a usual advance warning from its partners.
Ukraine also reported a slowing down of the Starlink satellite terminals, which are critical for its army’s communications, drone missions and aerial defenses.
Kyiv said that Starshield, the military version of the technology that is used by Ukraine’s troops, had been limited without any warning.
SpaceX chief Elon Musk, the billionaire Trump ally, said that such decisions were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.

After repeated requests for comment about Musk’s statement, a senior U.S. official told NBC News that “no such request was ever made by the president.” Trump has also denied restricting military intelligence for Ukraine.

Kyiv said Thursday the Starshield service was being restored, but the episode only added to the mounting suspicion in Ukraine that the U.S. was willing to cut it off from battlefield support in order to exert pressure for a peace deal. Asked about the service on Friday, Zelenskyy said that issues were ongoing. “Has the speed been fully restored to what it was? No. Is the speed returning? Yes,” he told reporters in Brussels.

European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid the stalemate in peace talks.
The Kremlin agreed with Trump on Friday, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was clear that “Zelenskyy doesn’t want to take responsibility and move toward a peaceful resolution.”
Russia has always stated it’s open to a peace settlement but only on its own hard-line terms, which would see Ukraine ceding significant territory.

title: ‘We’re done’: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries as anger at Trump mounts
summary: Satellite internet functionality via Starshield — the military version of the SpaceX service in Ukraine — has resumed at previous speeds for the moment, according to Ukraine.
story: Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the United States of betraying Kyiv with a “dangerous” withdrawal of support critical to its defense against Russia.

Ukraine held off on attacks for three days after President Donald Trump’s unilateral “energy ceasefire” announcement, but it accused Russia of repeatedly attacking its power grid. Zelenskyy voiced mounting frustration over the Kremlin’s failure to abide by the truce and what he sees as U.S. attempts to pressure Kyiv following gaps in intelligence-sharing about Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink internet service.

Satellite internet functionality via Starshield — the military version of the SpaceX service in Ukraine — has resumed at previous speeds for the moment, Ukrainian Chargé d’Affaires Denys Sienik told NBC News on Thursday.
“We hope it will remain unchanged,” Sienik said. “Speed is critical for logistics and for intercepting the jet-powered Shahed drones.”
The Ukrainian government still has received no response from SpaceX or the U.S. Defense Department about the reason for the recent limitations, a Ukrainian official said.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday, Zelenskyy indicated his patience had already been exhausted.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying.

Hours later, a fire was reported at an oil refinery in the western Ryazan region, Gov. Pavel Malkov said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”

Ukraine has been reeling from a sudden shift from Trump, who struck a diesel deal with Russia in an apparent bid to relieve pressure at the pump ahead of the midterm elections. He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil facilities and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader.
Trump’s “energy ceasefire” appeared to take both warring sides by surprise. He has blamed the Ukrainian campaign for fueling a rise in energy prices, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.
The moves caused frustration and confusion in Ukraine and Europe, intensifying concerns over how much of an ally the U.S. remained in the fight against Russia.
That worry was aggravated Wednesday when Kyiv said it was facing a slowdown of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite terminals, disrupting battlefield missions and its ability to intercept Russian drones.

Russian drones swarmed Ukraine on Wednesday, and more than 850 had filled the skies over Ukraine since early Thursday, Zelenskyy said. “And this comes precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted,” he said, referring to the Starlink slowdown.
Musk, a staunch ally of Trump, wrote on social media that decisions about restricting the use of Starshield were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.
Overnight, Musk said it was “time for Zelenskyy to go.”

The Defense Ministry source said Kyiv was still seeking clarification of the reasons for Wednesday’s throttling of the technology, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communication, drone operations and air defense.

Questions are mounting about whether the U.S. has stopped or limited the sharing of critical military intelligence with Ukraine after Zelenskyy said several ballistic strikes on Kyiv did not come with the usual warning from its partners.

European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

Ukraine was concerned that the chain of events amounted to an effort to pile pressure on Kyiv and backtrack on years of U.S. promises to help fend off the Russian invasion, one of the Ukrainian officials said.

Ukraine relies heavily on U.S. intelligence and the Starshield satellite network to defend itself against Russian drone and missile attacks, as well as to target Russian forces with its own drones. A reduction in intelligence assistance or satellite access could seriously undermine Ukraine’s battlefield prospects just as winter sets in, according to military experts.

Ukrainian military officials were told by their U.S. counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence,” Zelenskyy said, according to the Financial Times, although the incident was subsequently presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch.

The withdrawal of the intelligence and the simultaneous weakening of Starlink satellite internet were “dangerous” for Ukraine, he told the newspaper, adding that fighting without the U.S. would be “very difficult.”
In a separate interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy acknowledged that he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s actions.

title: Kevin Warsh says Fed is focused on taming rising prices, but gives no hint about next rate hike
summary: Two inflation reports this week set the stage for a rate hike potentially sooner than previously expected.
story: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Friday said that the U.S. economy has “broadly” moved in the direction that the central bank expected during its last meeting in September, when it raised rates for the first time since 2023.

In the weeks since, inflation as measured by the consumer price index jumped to 3.7%. For businesses, inflation has hit even harder. That turned investors focus to Warsh’s appearance at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank for a signal about whether the Fed would hike rates in October or December.

“We made very clear we’d deliver price stability,” Warsh said Friday morning in Bangkok (Thursday night ET), a signal of his focus on inflation and that another interest rate hike is likely on the horizon.
But Warsh stuck to a familiar tone and refused to give any clear hint about how soon that might come. “We’re not in that business anymore,” he said.
However, Warsh, the head of the world’s most important central bank, spoke at length about one major economic force that is causing prices to rise across the economy.
“In the United States, we’re having a massive investment surge,” he said, referencing the seemingly ever-expanding AI boom.
“It’s probably the most important thing that’s happening in the global economy on the upside,” Warsh said. “I think it’s going to fundamentally change the conduct of monetary policy.”
Warsh declines to give hint about Fed's next rate hike
A central feature of the AI boom is an expansive buildout of data centers around the country.

To fund all that building, trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components. Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices for consumers as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June.

Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds.
Warsh said AI could also “change the real economy,” though he  acknowledged not knowing how deeply it would impact employment.

But he projected optimism about the technology’s prospects, predicting that “it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive.” He said it should also generate “more wealth.”
“But the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one,” he warned.
Warsh said a Fed task force of outside experts studying the impact of AI on the labor market would hold a public hearing on the topic in November.

“So I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose to the day jobs that you and I have,” Warsh remarked. “I think it’s an exciting development and it’s an innovation that I think a decade from now they’ll look back on and they’ll say this was hugely consequential.”

His comments will be closely scrutinized because they are the last from any Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28.
The price of politics
Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month.

Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms.

In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully.

“Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term.
But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story.

By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again.

Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them.
Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.”

“I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.”
“They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump.
Diesel and the damage done

Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for.
“Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America.

The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods.

“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview.  “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.”
Despite the challenges facing the U.S. economy, Warsh concluded on an optimistic note, saying that those should strengthen it in the long run.

“What is striking to me are two things: almost everywhere in the global economy showing resilience that I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago, given what’s happening in geopolitics and hot spots around the world.”

Warsh added, “I believe, optimistically, you might think naively, at least in the U.S. we’re going to come out of this stronger, with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.”

title: Harry and Meghan cheered in first joint appearance since returning to U.K.
summary: The couple are visiting three charities in Nottingham as they remain locked in a public row with Buckingham Palace about their status and security in Britain.
story: LONDON — Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, were making their first royal-style public appearance together Thursday since they returned to the United Kingdom with their two children.
Harry, 42, and Meghan, 45, were visiting three charities in Nottingham, as they look to rebuild their image in Britain six years after walking away from royal life.

Nottingham, a city in central England known as the setting for the famous “Robin Hood” legend, holds a special place in the couple’s history as the place where they made their first joint public appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.
“It’s almost a full-circle moment because it looks very much like a royal engagement,” NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash said.

title: Pope Leo slept well after cancer surgery, but recovery could take ‘longer than expected’
summary: Peru’s president said the 71-year-old American pontiff’s planned visit might be in jeopardy as he recovers from surgery to remove part of his right lung.
story: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV’s recovery from lung surgery could take “longer than expected,” the president of Peru warned Wednesday, as the leader of the Roman Catholic Church continued to mend at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital.
Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru, which was set to start Nov. 11.

“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said. “We will also be watching for any announcements from the Vatican, because we understand that his recovery will take several weeks longer than expected and, therefore, we also understand that there could be some changes to the schedule of his visit.”
Leo, who is a Chicago native, spent more than two decades working in Peru and maintains close ties with that South American country.

Fujimori’s announcement was somewhat at odds with the Vatican’s assertion on Wednesday that the pope was recovering as expected after an operation to remove part of his right lung, which confirmed a cancer diagnosis.
